I'd never even heard of Mary Osborne until Guitar Player magazine gave her a page and recommendation for this album. I looked it up and saw so many positive reviews I (as a fellow guitarist) would be nuts not to give it a try.

I was greatly surprised. Not only in her outstanding playing, and her tasty band, but the recording as well. It's crisp, clean and you can hear all the instruments well. It says in the notes she was taken aback by how good Charlie Christian's playing was, and how it put the bee in her bonnet about taking up the guitar. You do hear some of that influence in her playing, but there's much more to her than that. As jazz oriented as it might be, some pieces are solidly rooted in Blues and some cuts border on Rock-a-Billy.

There are a few songs (such as How High the Moon) I was familiar with, but most of the cuts were new to me. She is an ace player. If you are a guitar aficionado, you'll love this CD. And even if not, it is more than listenable.

I became aware of Damon Fowler and his lap steel guitar work in the band Southern Hospitality that also includes JP Soars on guitar and victor Wainwright on keyboards.

Damon sings lead on this his seventh solo effort after previously performing with ex Allman Brother Butch Trucks’ band. When Damon’s mentor passed he then played with the Dickey Betts Band.
Also of note is a connection to Rick Derringer (Edgar Winter band) who produced Fowler; and this album the Whiskey Bayou Session which has reintroduced me to the album’s producer, Tab Benoit! Benoit performs acoustic guitar on 3 songs, too.

The Whiskey Bayou Sessions (2018) is a pretty steady diet of rocknroll tunes that I like better than Warren Haynes and Gov’t Mule. Fowler is a soulful singer and I had a difficult time trying to find a comparison—which is a good thing. I did finally think of Jeff Healy during the song Holiday.
The album is not as down home Louisiana gritty as I thought it might be but, again, this is good modern rocknroll as the rhythm section of Todd Edmunds and Justin Headley keep the songs centered as Damon does his thing whether singing or playing a solid guitar solo.
The Whiskey Bayou Sessions is a fine and nuanced rocknroll album. Nothing fantastically rocking but easy to hear subtle musicianship changes upon a better second listen.
4.4 stars

I particularly like Johnny Mandel and Dave Frishberg's "You Are There" -- both are among the finest composers/lyricists of their generation.

Right off, this set of songs doesn't sound anything like what most people would expect to hear on a Beach Boys album. There is not even a hint of the beach, surfing, fast cars, or summer fun. By the time this album was released in 1967, all of those subjects were in the Beach Boys' rear view mirror...at least for another 7 years. There have been numerous books, movies, documentaries, etc, detailing the history of what the group was trying to navigate through in an attempt to keep their music relevant to the times. One very risky offering was Wild Honey, an album of 11 R&B flavored tunes with some soulful and sometimes dark subject matter. Brother Carl Wilson belted out many of the lead vocals with some gritty and powerful singing.

Another factor setting this album apart from earlier releases is the sound itself. Starting with the previous album, much of the recording was done in leader Brian Wilson's home studio, with simpler arrangements and fewer instruments. Gone were the spacious reverb-drenched orchestrations by the famous Wrecking Crew with the Phil Spector-ish wall of sound, backing up the Beach Boys' layer upon layer upon layer of vocal harmonies. Wild Honey is all about straight ahead R&B flavored rock. And it all works well with the more intimate close-mic'ed sounds.

The downside, though is that the album was only originally released in mono and fake stereo. To me, this is the one thing that made this music sound dated. For so many years I wished for a true stereo remix, which I always felt would compliment this somewhat modern sounding music from a group that rose to fame at the tail end of the doowop era. Four years ago I got my wish with the release of a double cd called Sunshine Tomorrow. This set featured, among a wealth of other related Beach Boys material from 1967, the complete Wild Honey album remixed in true stereo. I was not disappointed!

I am a rather casual vinyl collector. I listen to music mainly on cd, but occasionally I like to spin some vinyl, mostly for nostalgia's sake. I don't get into debates on which sounds better. Some things sound better on vinyl and many of my cds sound superior. I think it's mostly a matter of taste....and your audio set up.

So, do I think this Lp sounds better than the Sunshine Tomorrow cd? I wouldn't say one sounds better than the other, but I would say slightly different. There is a little bit more warmth in the bottom end on the Lp, but that could be my stereo, too. All I have to say is that it sounds amazing, and the true stereo mix opens up the sound of these vintage tracks. And this is a great Lp for someone who is strictly a collector because you'll never walk into a used cd shop, thrift shop, or garage sale and find a vintage true stereo album of Wild Honey (beware: the original 1967 release is labeled STEREO, but it's not!)

text.301:
West African griot artists, particularly those who have come to the attention of world music fans, for all the baggage of such terminology, can come to sound somewhat rangebound. There are differences, of course, but to the ear raised on rock, or any other style from elsewhere, parsing the differences requires education, as is always the case. Part of this, undoubtedly, is that Western audiences mostly hear Malian, Nigerian and a few other countries’ traditions, but there really are differences, just as Mississippi blues can be distinguished from Piedmont, even though one raised on Indian classical music or Tuvan throat singing may hear the similarities more than the differences. So here we have Mamar Kassey, not a person, but a band. Curious persons can trace the origin of the name, but what is more important here is the music, which is outstanding, and quite different from Ali Farka Toure, King Sunny Ade, Fela Kuti, Baaba Maal, or any of the artists to break on through to the other side of the Atlantic and achieve a level of fame among the world music-conscious.

What makes Denke-Denke, and more generally, the sound of this band special? Certain rhythms, instruments and tones will sound familiar to fans of artists from Mali, desert blues, and related styles, but what is immediately distinctive about Denke-Denke is the contrast the band builds between traditional instruments and modern. Electric guitars and bass, played against African flutes and other West African instruments. This is not precisely new. Listen to Ali Farka Toure, and you will often hear his electric guitar played against not only African percussion, but African bowed instruments and other contrasts, and that is merely one highly prominent example. Yet in many of these cases, the band construction has the feel of a group picking up the instruments available and playing. The guitar because the guitar. That’s enough. Then, add what is there. Mamar Kassey builds the music by thinking through the tones of each instrument, and placing them thoughtfully in context rather than just jamming. There is nothing wrong with jamming. Great music results that way. Yet the intentionality of Denke-Denke and the manner in which the distinct tones work together lend the music something altogether unique, even aside from the distinct rhythms and melodies of Niger, which can be separated from Mali, Guinea, or whatever tradition with which a listener may be more familiar.

And they are all just a well oiled operation. This band works. It isn’t a backup band for a star guitarist, as thrilling as that can be. It is a composed group. Good stuff here.

I live on the coast of Florida, own a BMW convertible Z4, and have found the ideal driving music, in Govi! I have been spending the last few days collecting as much of the CD collection as is available. I can't believe I am just finding Govi.

Growing up, one of my closest family friends left at the end of high school to study with Andre Segovia, in Spain. As I climbed the educational heights at Columbia University and Princeton, his mother dropped in to leave me a copy of his music he wrote for the new Paris ,Cirque du Soleil. He was not only a great writer, 12 string Flamingo guitarest, and leading figure in the German, Berlin Symphony orchestra. So, the next time your parents try to dissuade you from a career in music, and you believe in your talent, why deny your happiness. The beauty I listen to in the music of Govi , sounds like the beauty I search the heaven's for as an Astrophysicist. I will be carrying a CD of Govi's, around the world, to all the great observatories. Until I leave on my next voyage, I will be driving along the sea shore of Florida , with 14 speakers surrounding my 2 seater. The beautiful sounds remind me of driving across the evening bridges of Miami, in the 80's, to the sound of Gato Barbieri.

I am so pleased to be the last person to discover Govi. At least for this month! 5 🌟s

In The Good, the Bad and the Ugly Blondie (Clint Eastwood), Angel Eyes (Lee Van Cleef) and Tuco (Eli Wallach) are Good, Bad and Ugly, respectively. The film begins with Blondie and Tuco as a team of con men in Texas during the last days of the Civil War.. Blondie captures Tuco, who has a bounty on his head, and claims the reward then frees him as he is about to be hanged. But Blondie tires of the arrangement and leaves Tuco in the desert to die. Of course he survives and now wants revenge. The plot takes a twist when Tuco and Blondie find a dying rebel soldier who tells them about a huge sum of gold that he has buried. Each of them know part of the location so that they have to work together. Angel Eyes is a corrupt Union soldier who also wants the gold. The rest of the film centers on the efforts of the three to find it. The film includes a dramatic battle scene that is reminiscent of a Dino de Laurentiis spectacular. The film ends with the three facing off in a triangular shoot out.

This film is well worth watching and far from the poorly made “Spaghetti Westerns’ that are modeled on it. It is really a morality tale about the harm that greed can cause. I think Wallach steals the film as a comical, not to be trusted, bad guy.

text.513:
I've always found my Music On Vinyl reissue of AIC's Dirt to be underwhelming. The pressing quality of my copy is fine. It just doesn't sound particularly good to me ... not enough detail or bottom end focus compared to the CD for my liking. Expecting a similar experience from MOV's JOF/Sap reissue, I put off purchasing it. I recently pre-ordered the forthcoming Facelift reissue from Sony Legacy and, impulsively, added this title to the order. I'm very glad I did. It just arrived and I'm happy to report that my copy is excellent.

There was some very minor out of the sleeve debris that was completely removed by a vacuum cleaning. A thorough brushing would've accomplished the same. There are a couple of isolated scuffs on my copy that, at first, concerned me. However, I noticed almost no surface noise on playback ... on par with the audiophile label pressings I have. Nutshell plays through on my copy without a locked groove as mentioned in other reviews.

And, finally, the mastering sounds fantastic to my ears ... clear and detailed without being too bright, and a nicely focused bottom end. Based on my experience, I highly recommend this pressing ... a great listening experience. Oh, and the music is pretty special too ... but you already knew that.

text.573:
Classic Ulrich from over 20 years ago still has a universal appeal. You enter this album expectant and it takes you on a carefree journey of relaxation and mental release. This was one of the first electronica albums I ever heard and it is not as layered as "Goodbye" or later albums. It has a purity of sound that is unique to Ulrich's earlier albums. There are however more rhythmic elements on this album that make you feel like you are on a train riding into the future to some new adventure.

What captivates me about this music is its solitary beauty and the beginnings of the metamorphosis that has led to Ulrich's brilliant later albums. But I think Ulrich was always on the cutting edge even at the beginning because there is a sparkle to his music that has kept me a fan all these years. It is rare for me to want to collect all of an artist's albums as I am doing lately!

The tracks on this album are also long enough that you can saturate in the sounds for an immersive experience. So if you want to go back in time and are intrigued with electronica's evolution you will find this still has a lot of warmth and memories but the synthesizer sounds and persistent drum beats do date this album a bit here and there.

"Nobody's Home" on this album seems like a breakthrough into more like what Ulrich was really capable of and what his music was becoming.

The bonus disc has music that also emphasizes the heavier drum beats. "Sunday evening in your street" has an experimental feel. "Crazy for You" is worth hearing and has a soothing repetitive nature and is almost hypnotic. "Wherever you are" has echoes of future albums that branch off into musical ecstasy like Goodbye.

To be honest, this was my introduction to Ulrich's music and I'm glad I got to hear it again. It shows me what electronica used to sound like and how far things have progressed.

~The Rebecca Review, a fan

text.593:
Ok, let’s get something out of the way immediately: I’ve always had some sort of a love affair for Flotsam and Jetsam. In my personal opinion they have always deserved way more attention and recognition than they had, they are a top-notch band destined to forever play second fiddle to the media behemoths, like Metallica, Slayer and Megadeth. Flotsam and Jetsam will forever be known as the band that Jason Newsted played in before joining Metallica after the death of the previous bassist Cliff Burton, however people tend to forget the tiny fact that back in the ages when the thrash movement was a very well established one, with acts like Metallica, Dark Angel and Slayer belting out more than two albums out there; they stepped into the scene with their first effort “Doomsday for the Deceiver” album that nowadays have garnered the status or a genre’s classic, a monumental speed-thrash statement capable of producing multiple auditory orgasm, and likely Jason Newsted’s highest career moment ever. Truth is there was a period in their musical career when releases like “Unnatural Selection” and “My God” were uneven and pale in comparison with previous efforts, with frequent line-up changes and even periods of dormancy, but wait a minute… can you name a single band on Earth which hasn’t had a slip? I’m sure you can’t, even the mighty four have had their shadowed moments (Yes “St. Anger” and “Risk” I am looking at you).

Anyways, historical rant and Flotsam and Jetsam‘s Earth shattering debut aside, they have managed to stay in the game for at least three decades, and next May 20 they will be treating the fans with a new musical journey, a eponymous album for which the diehard Arizona veterans come back sporting a revamped line-up. The current incarnation of Flotsam and Jetsam comprises Eric ‘AK’ Knutson, Mike Gilbert, Michael Spencer, Steve Conley and Jason Bittner (Shadows Fall’s drummer). They got together in January 2015 to start rehearsing for their 2015 European tour dates and to commence writing for the band’s 13th record. After a 5 month initial writing process, the band completed 18 rough ideas to start having Bittner track drums to. At first the band thought about a double release, but realized it would be better to concentrate on an album’s worth of killer material by what essentially is a new band with a 30-year history.

So what is the new album like? It is like taking a ride in the heavy metal machine and setting the destination for the late 80s, a simpler time where hair was big, the pants were spandex, and Metallica was still playing metal. The band has returned to what they do best: pure in-your-face metal. All their thrash metal roots are here, all the ingredients they became well-known for are in place; this time driven by an increased vigor and a brash, aggressive sound. However the album sound isn’t stilted and locked in the 80′s; on the contrary the band sounds more current staying true to their roots than they ever did chasing a trend: this record is a robust and lethal mixture of heavy highly-melodic and intricate thrash metal; frantic and forged by pure fire, strength and experience. If I ever found myself thinking “this riff might get stale if it is repeated one more time”, it changes before I can finish my thought. The album never gets boring, it just rips face from start to finish, then afterwards pisses on your corpse.

The guitar’s riffing is unstoppable and intense, although they have always been a guitar-driven band, this time the twin guitars of Mike Gilbert and Steve Conley serrate, thrash and churn over the venomous vocals of Eric ‘AK’ Knutson, who sings his lungs out spitting pure angry along the verses, proving a seemingly ageless vocal performance (I’ve always been a fan of his delivery and willingness to stretch beyond the standard thrash snarl) Jason Bittner’s drumming injects a new life to the band’s overall sound: astounding and precise drumbeats, mixing complex patterns in the speedy parts and dropping some nasty double bass drumming here and there. He’s a drumming school on his own, and his tight playing paired with Michael Spencer’s infectious and killer bass lines (he goes tornado most of the times and you can feel it!) weave the perfect backbone for the two guitars to outstretch themselves. Fans can judge by themselves by listening to the dynamic bass intro of “L.O.T.D” or his effortless impersonation of Steve Harris’ playing style in the album’s first single “Iron Maiden”: a fine homage to the UK’s finest heavy metal band in which the band employs the classic Iron Maiden gallop, twin-guitar attack and certainly a bit of a nod to the Maiden’s classic tune “The Trooper” on the verse; while Eric’s vocal channel Bruce Dickinson admirably.

The temptation to parallel “Flotsam and Jetsam” to “No Place with Disgrace” is irresistible, particularly when you consider the band recently re-recorded the latter album in order to be able to offer their fans with a remixed version due to the difficulties in obtaining the original master tapes. With far more finesse but no less speed, this new effort rolls with a vengeance; it’s vicious from the get-go and doesn’t die until it’s over: it simply epitomizes what a thrash album should be. Many older bands in recent times have failed to successfully reinvent themselves, become irrelevant to their original fan base or never been able to top their first few releases. That a band can come out some 30 years later, after suffering all the setbacks, and deliver an album this good and fresh is inspirational and utterly admirable, to say the least. To put it in a few words: this is the sound of a band downright rejuvenated and ready to remind the world that they were once contenders for metal’s hallowed throne for a darn fine reason. They are back with a vengeance and are giving the vast majority a run for their money. For me the strongest contestant for the thrash metal album of the year.

I guess record execs are all the same regardless of race, color, or creed.
It has everything: Theme, instrumentation, lyrics and remains relevant even OUT of its historical context. For me, it is reminiscent of my high school years in an inner-city high school and remained with me throughout the 70s. I always associated it with rolling on the Cross Bronx Xpwy with my brother behind the wheel of my dad's 71 Riviera.
I wish someone would do this work justice with a proper remaster by someone who knows what they're doing!!!!
There's a DEEP Christian message there too, and I know you can guess why the album was "33" minutes long ( Coltrane's "A Love Supreme" ran the same 33 ).

In my teens and twenties, though I was only a passive listener of Sonic Youth, I tended to prefer Thurston Moore as a singer and mostly disliked Kims vocals. This wasn't a male over female sexist view, as I enjoyed many female artists, singers, musicians, front-women for their art and vocals. There was just something that annoyed me to the point where I didn't want to hear another vocalist other than Thurston on a Sonic Youth record. Fast Forward to 2019. Where Kim became my favorite member, and this record did it. Her sass, her clear and stinging vocals made me truly listen for the first time. I went from a passive listener to an active fan. My year end Spotify review listed Sonic Youth as my top band though I listened to over 3k different artists. All thanks to Washing Machine.

Then came "The Promise," a wonderful return to the R&B mainstream via Jimmy Jam & Terry Lewis (and a host of others), which seemed to be a bigger and better step in the right direction.  NOW, she presents with a Whitney Houston tribute that should have, as with "Destination Moon," found certain tracks scattered across albums that (might have) followed rather than one whole set of Houston covers, which, for ME, comes off as more of a karaoke album that it does anything else.  Granted, she has the lungs to DO IT, but, Whitney alREADY did it, so what's the point?  Had she stayed with her own ORIGINAL songs, I think she would have succeeded more.  Even with the Dance hits she had along the way, they were too noisy and didn't sit (again for ME) comfortably enough alongside what else was being presented.  Don't get me wrong.  Deborah Cox's voice is a force to be reckoned with, howEVER, "Deborah needs to do DEBORAH" (as one reviewer points out) and leave the covers for American Idol auditions.  She's SO MUCH MORE TALENTED than that.  With that powerful vocal instrument of hers, there's no reason why she can't have another go around with Flyte Tyme Productions giving her what she does BEST:  soulful up and midtempos and beautiful ballads that she wrings every ounce of emotion out of. text.829:
If you listen to samples of this recording on one of many internet sites available you might hear what I hear- Pollini displaying his trademark tradeoff of command and coldness. I have many recordings of the WTC, and many recordings by Pollini, but for years I have avoided this recording because I was turned off by what sounded like a dull straight reading as compared to that of so many others. Since then I have come to appreciate Pollini's musical persona, and this reading now strikes me as unique in that is delivers the feeling of absolute control without eccentricity. Pollini's Bach is a constant and consistent stream flowing as if from a spigot through a big modern piano. Once in a while I like to hear Bach keyboard music played this way. The next best alternative in the same vein is Jeno Jando, who plays (as another reviewer here put it) the way your piano teacher wanted you to play. Jando is Pollini without the mighty commanding hand sensation, and that can be too dull for me even when I'm in the mood for this sort of thing.

That said, you might have a totally different impression. I post this here for those who are just curious about other's take on this recording. If you want to know which WTC to buy, then quit reading these reviews and go sample a bunch of different recordings on the internet. Nobody needs a music critic to make purchasing decisions anymore.

With that said, and I realize this opinion puts me in the minority, Karajan/BPO's best rendition of the 9 is their late 1970's effort recorded in the Berlin Philharmonie. Compared to this release, it has no audible tape hiss, the tempii are brisker and more exciting, and the adagio passages are lusher and more beautiful. And, it's available on Blu-Ray audio as well, in a lovely 24b/192khz transfer! (ASIN: B07H62PFS4)

It's my two cents, of course. But I wager that most people on a blind listen would agree with my take. I came to both recordings with no preconceptions (I only recently took a deep dive into classical) and 1977 was the clear winner over 1963.

Please note: Jarrett recorded this work on both harpsichord and piano. This is the piano version.
I unwittingly bought the piano version of Book I and the Harpsichord version of Book II. But this provided a nice chance to compare, if not the same pieces on two instruments, at least a sense of his playing on both.
While I find both outstanding, I was surprised to find the harpsichord the more natural and rhythmically fluid. Now I think I need both versions of each!
While I have been listening to Bach's keyboard works for years, I always resisted the WTC mainly because it seemed more like practice or technical demonstration than music that could just be enjoyed on its own terms. But I recently got into trying to find a really listenable, enjoyable version of this music. My sense is that this is one of the very best (this or the harpsichord version by same). I have also enjoyed Richter, who takes a more dramatic approach. What I find so good about Jarrett's approach is that he instinctively finds the right tempo for each piece, which really lets the music develop and shine. Rather than just rushing through, he allows you to hear the melody and rhythm of each piece. The music breaths. It is kind of unfair that Jarrett has been both the greatest jazz pianist of his era, and also outdone some very fine musicians who devoted their whole careers to Bach.

The album is 56 minutes and the sound quality is OK. I can't tell if this is a studio or live recording. I think it is mostly studio. Maybe it has one live track or audience applause was edited on to a studio track (they wouldn't be the first one to do this).

This is more of a producer's band and album than a group effort. The liner notes, describing who the band members are definitely come from the producer. Someone who had an idea to pull together some jazz musicians and play some Dead. And some great musicians were chosen. Billy Cobham may be the best jazz drummer of all time.

Sometimes, the band sounds like the Dixie Dregs (J Lavitz's band). The Dregs did do some interesting work but I found much of their music to be tedious. I remember being bored at times during a Dregs concert on their first tour.

The guitarwork on this album is surprisingly subdued and not very exciting. This is surprising because Jimmy Herring has done some interesting work with Widespread Panic (after their guitarist died) and Phil Lesh.

It probably deserves 3 stars as it gets better near the end. I just don't seem to enjoy the opening tracks.

text.1003:
Having stumbled upon this album, I am pleased to report to anyone interested that it is undoubtedly the finest musical purchase I expect to make this year. Here's why:

1. Sheer value for money: At this writing this two-CD set is priced at $7.65. There are 50 tracks altogether. Do the math. That's fifteen cents per track. Nowadays fifteen cents won't buy you fifteen cents.

2. Limited availability: Right now this set is unavailable on iTunes. Even if it were, you would pay a lot more than 15¢ per song. I almost feel guilty about this. Shouldn't the artists or their heirs be receiving proper royalties for all this?

3. Historical value: Here we have a compilation of five of Dame Julie's first seven albums (the earliest being the original cast recordings of "My Fair Lady" [1956] and "Cinderella" [1957]). The tracks preserved are from the lady's earliest solo ventures: "The Lass with the Delicate Air" (1958), "Julie Andrews Sings" (1958), "Broadway's Fair Julie" (1961), "Don't Go in the Lion's Cage Tonight" (a.k.a. "Heartrending Ballads and Raucous Ditties," 1962), and "Julie and Carol at Carnegie Hall" (1962). How many of these are available as free-standing CDs I've no idea. Few, I suspect; at this price (see #2, above), none whatsoever. In any event, with CD manufacturers tottering before the onslaught of streamed music, one dare not assume that these discs will forever remain in press.

4. Variety: The selections range from music hall and vaudeville numbers from the performer's youth (some, before she had been born), Tin Pan Alley classics, wonderful numbers from the 1940s songbook, comedic novelties done with tongue convincingly in cheek, and many of the artist's most beloved Broadway songs by 1962, from "My Fair Lady" and Camelot," which, of course, she introduced in the mid-1950s.

5. Arrangements and orchestrations: Absolutely superb support from musicians under the supervision of Irwin Kostal (who arranged the songs for "Mary Poppins"), Henri René, and Robert Mersey. The arrangements support the singer and the song, never overwhelming either.

6. Last and foremost: Julie Andrews to the nth degree. One is tempted to say that here she is at the peak of powers, but, good Lord, "The Lass with the Delicate Air" was recorded when she was twenty-two. By then she had sung onstage for ten years and, in 1946, had rendered a command performance before Princess Elizabeth (who, now Queen, is also still with us). Miss Andrews's popularity may have peaked in the 1960s, but, years earlier, her voice was already flawless: pitch, diction, breath control. Her talent was so great that it was impossible for her to sing poorly. Yes, the precision of her singing may suggest to some an English primness, but that was her style—which she could bend to inhabit the song's character. There's simply no point in comparing her with, say, Ella Fitzgerald or Rosemary Clooney (whom I also adore). Julie was and is Julie. That's that. And that is sublime.

Have I mentioned that the two discs comprise fifty songs, twenty-five per disc, with no sacrifice of audio quality? Altogether this amounts to seven minutes shy of two hours and thirty minutes of Julie Andrews in concert.

If your taste cannot accommodate Julie Andrews, then you have my sympathy. If it can and does, if ever there were a must-buy, this is most assuredly is it.

text.1025:
Thirty-seven years ago in a musty record store in Hollywood, an aged clerk saw me rummaging through the classical music bins, and came to ask if he could help me, and that simple act had a profound effect on my inner life. He was strangely animated, like he had a secret he was dying to share, even if it was with this gangly kid in a faded Clash t-shirt. "You like classical music?" I nodded. He said "Then you've got to hear this new recording that just came in. It's extraordinary!" He put it on the store turntable, dropped the needle on the first track, and turned up the volume. It filled the air.

I don't need to remember how listening to this magnificent piece of music for the first time made me feel, because I have owned one after another copy of this recording for every one of the 37 years since, and I still feel the same goosebumps and shivers I did in that long ago, long gone store, listening to this work of unutterable beauty. Pachalbel's "Canon and Gigue in D Major" is perhaps the most routinely, universally butchered entry in the Western Canon, yet this recording of Musica Antiqua Koln performing absolutely flawlessly on antique instruments in the original tempo is a revelation. Every time I listen to this it fills me with absolute awe that a mere human being could compose something so intricate and beautiful, and even more so that other mere humans could finally, finally do it justice. To me, this amazing recording is celestial mechanics in music form. It is so unlikely that something as sublimely breathtaking as this even exists, yet thankfully it does. Please, listen to this piece and be reminded that, unlikely as it seems, there can still be things unsullied and pure in this vulgar world.

text.1061: I am very pleased at the price point at which I purchased this.  At $14 this is one of the finest 180g reissues that I own.  This is the first of the VH vinyl reissues that I decided to try and am greatly amazed at the attention detail put into this project.  First, the cover sleeve is made with high quality card stock. Next, there is an audiophile vinyl lined white paper sleeve over the record itself, and yet included inside is the extra original inner sleeve as well with all of the liner notes.  The vinyl itself is well pressed, high quality and dead quiet.  The first 4 Van Halen projects were just fantastic recordings in the first place so the remaster just kicked the clarity up a notch.  The drum mix on Alex alone is just incredible and Michael Anthony has never been clearer.  As far as Dave, not much changes here, he’s straight down the middle as he should be.  But Eddie...we get to hear some actual power amp hum and hiss.  Truth is, these recordings were made for analog moments like this.  Fair Warning has always been my favorite of all of the VH projects.  It’s a little more dark and colorful with no covers.  Mean Street is unmatched, Unchained, well it’s Unchained and the songs that follow on both sides are loaded with creativity.  It’s classic Van Halen laid down at a time when Rock innovation and creativity were on the rise.  A solid piece of music history at a great price...

text.1161:
Until last night I couldn't remember the last time listening to a record made me laugh out loud. (I couldn't remember the last time anything made me laugh out loud, but I digress.) In 1961 twenty-seven years separated Bobby Darin, an up-and-coming singer, and Johnny Mercer, lyricist extraordinaire for three decades ("Moon River," "Blues In the Night," "One For My Baby (And One More For The Road)," "Skylark," "Ac-Cent-tchu-ate The Positive," and too many more to name). Somebody had the smart idea to put them in the same studio to record duets. Not just any songs, mind you, but some items that no one had heard since the days of vaudeville ("Paddlin' Madelin' Home," "I Ain't Gonna Give Nobody None Of My Jellyroll," "My Cutey's Due at Two-to-Two Today"), sparkled with some of Mr. Mercer's older numbers ("Bob White," "If I Had My Druthers"). Until hearing this album you've no idea how much fun you'd have listening to pop antiquities vocalized by two pros having the time of their lives: harmonizing, scatting, impersonating other singers, ribbing, ad-libbing. (One take is labeled #17, probably because they couldn't stop laughing while the tape was rolling.) But that's only two-thirds of the magic. The touch of genius was to hire Billy May to arrange these songs for the best LA session artists from the Big Band era. Talk about swinging! This is May's patented "Be-Bop-BAM-She-WHOP-Bum-BUM-Bee-Bum-Bop-WHAAAAM' swing, done with unbelievable musical precision that fills the bars between those tongue-twisting lyrics. And talk about musical invention: who but Billy May would have turned "Lonesome Polecat" into a cha-cha? You like your chestnuts roasting on an open fire? This is it. This album is really Three of a Kind: Darin, Mercer, and May.

This disc remasters the thirteen songs on the original LP, plus seven bonus tracks, four of which are alternative takes of the first thirteen. Call 'em encores, so good that the producers tore their hair over which take was better. Now you have more than one: almost an hour of freewheeling joy that never sacrifices impeccable musicianship.

I played this album straight through twice because I couldn't believe how much I enjoyed it the first time. It's lightning caught in a bottle. If you are determined to be depressed, look the other way. If you're ready for a heart-lift, buy this gem right now.

Personally, this was a great rockin CD. It was heavy but also melodic and harmonious; I just loved it!!!. I liked every song on the disc; to me there was no filler. Lizzy still sounds great vocal wise and is really an underrated vocalist, one of my top 10 of all time.

Some ppl did not like this disc too much because it probably was not dark enough for them. That's alright because he did plenty of dark stuff in the past but this output holds alot of merit by itself because it was the Harges brothers and a keyboardist doing the entire album. I like the keyboards throughout the album but it was not very dominant and overburdening, just a nice touch for some flavor.

I actually feel bad for these guys and for some other METAL bands from the 80's that are still alive today just trying to stay alive and relevant in a bleak and dim world musically polluted by fake and pretentious garbage that will never matter or never stand the test of time. The Harges bros will be lucky if they can attract a crowd of 500 at a NYC club like the Gramercy Theatre or be invited to play at a weekend fest like the Maryland Deathfest in May. I wish them the very best and hope to see them live again someday. Long Live Lizzy Borden and Give 'Em' the Axe!!!

text.1505:
I was intrigued by this recording the first time I heard it. Hearing timeless music, given a modern facelift, just seemed to work. Bach's music was perfect for this project, and a mammoth project it was. The Moog (rhymes with "rogue") was able to produce only one sound at a time, and the process of cutting, splicing, and making it all work seemed gargantuan. But Wendy did it! The rest is musical history.

First released on Columbia Masterworks, S-OB became, perhaps, the best selling classical album of all time. It was one that I used to show off my modest, but nice, stereo system, and the response was often something religious, starting with "holy". Add your own second word; you would probably be right, since there were many.

A few years later, I had upgraded to a quadraphonic system. Music took on a new life, and S-OB was no exception. The processing in the receiver could make stereo records come to life in a whole new way. So when Columbia decided to release an SQ quadraphonic version of the album, I jumped on it...but something was wrong. Some of the sounds I clearly heard when playing the stereo LP were missing when I played the quad disc. It didn't sound like the same album. Turns out Wendy wasn't happy,, either. She let Columbia have it with both barrels, and convinced them to pull the album. The SQ matrix created all kinds of problems that destroyed the sound of the record. The Q8 tape, which was pure discrete, didn't have the problem.

This edition of S-OB is pure stereo, as it was intended to be, with all the dynamics the LP couldn't quite achieve. If you're a fan, you gotta get it. If you're not a fan, you will be after you hear it. I'm hoping that, someday, Wendy will authorize a full 4.0 discrete release on hybrid SACD. That would truly be the ultimate.

text.1556:
Monaural recordings, like dinosaurs, came close to extinction by the mid '70s. For some reason "audiophiles" have taken it upon themselves to reissue mono recordings of albums from the1960s and 1970s, when record buyers had the option of choosing either monaural or stereo. In my opinion, stereo records always sounded much better than mono, but monaural recordings were cheaper to purchase. Since most record buyers were teens, and few had the money to buy sophisticated stereo systems, mono records were just fine.

I actually have several mono lps that I purchased during the mid to late 1960s, but that doesn't mean I'm anxious to add to my collection. This album is disappointing not because it is monaural, but because the Amazon listing Did Not So Indicate.

text.1722: I remember as a teen circa Y2K having a vague notion of "'80s" sound.  I knew it was synthy and modern, but other than that, the early 2000s were a time with significantly less internet power and the '80s was actively being ushered out to make way for Pink, Avril Lavigne, Destiny's Child and Usher.  I later found out the sound I was hunting for had been known as "New Wave" and in this, the 'Like...' CD set excels.  Lots of one hit wonders and just about every MTV staple.  However, the more obvious hits are indeed missing.  This is probably due to licensing.  Still, it gives a very extensive and accurate window into the past and will hopefully provide for you some good leads on deeper (or far more shallow) dives.  All recordings are high quality with no evidence to my ears of tape hiss or blips.  This is exactly what these songs sounded like on '80s hits radio stations of the '90s and 2000s.  Of course we are talking about an era prior to iTunes and all the more recent remastering projects.  The versions here may be a touch soft compared to the very latest remasters.  Then again, I typically prefer the old flat transfers over remasters for authenticity.

Released the same year as his debut album Got to Be There, this Michael Jackson second solo foray is another beautiful listen for fans of the Future King of Pop. Especially since in his first track, he performs the Main Theme for Ben, a Horror film very popular in 1972 whose main theme song got major nominations at many movie awards such as the Golden Globes and the Oscars. Ironically, that same song sort of foreshadows Michael’s future dive into horror cinema which he would accomplish in his masterpiece album Thriller with Vincent Price.

As always, Michael sings a great range of Soul/R&B songs. Songs about love for someone he longs for, but also some related to world issues. Like People Make the World Go ‘Round; not an original composition from Michael since it was written by Thom Bell and Linda Creed. Still, it foreshadows future Michael compositions like Healing The World and its humanist concept; but also the singer’s lifelong interests over helping others in need. As such, the album Ben is a forewarner of the main important thematics in Michael Jackson’s personal compositions.

As for his new versions of classics such as My Girl (by Smokey Robinson and Ronald White) and People Make the World Go ‘Round, I love Michael’s new take on them; to his own style and emotional range; making them as moving as the original releases done by groups such as The Temptations. In sum, through each of his songs, his voice performances for them are stunning and the emotional range of his melodies are as memorable as ever. A shame the album isn’t as available for purchase in stores such as Amazon like other Jackson tracks. Though it is fortunate that Amazon.co.uk offers the cd in special printings through their Autorip program which offers together MP3 versions of the songs as well. Still, it would be nice to see that album in more massive demands as big as his Thriller, Off the Wall, and Bad releases for Michael is an amazing artist worth discovering right from his early debut as his prodigal talents shine right on the vinyl/cd/mp3 listening.

In sum, I strongly encourage everyone to discover this Michael Jackson release. Another jewel in the musicography of the King of Pop.

text.1941:
At some point in most peoples' lives, they have been told to sit down and listen to the canon. The canon being defined as a set of symphonies, operas and chamber music pieces that western culture has collectively elevated for a variety of reasons. Many of these pieces of music truly do deserve to be studied, at least in a scholarly way. Many have a kind of emotional resonance that can be uncovered by those with a proper education in the language of the relevant musical traditions.

But few are truly fun.

This is fun. It is an education in musical history for those uninitiated, a vital resource for those who are, and fun for all.

Louis Armstrong. For good or for ill, he is a musical icon, but largely for a vocal rendition of What A Wonderful World. The man was so much more than that. Moreover, for those who would think of New Orleans jazz as parade music, an education is necessary. A fun one. Louis Armstrong is, to a significant degree, the root of jazz. Arguing about who started jazz is pointless, and Armstrong himself had a mentor in King Oliver, and all that, yes, but Armstrong was, in many ways, the source, and New Orleans was the source. So here is the source of jazz. Everything to come is here. Everything to come in New Orleans is here. Everything to come in swing, bebop, and modern jazz, that's here too. You can trace it to Louis. You can trace it to his rhythm, his timing, his virtuosity...

and his fun. Jazz can easily lose that sense of fun. And there can come a point at which century-old music can sound quaint or silly, until you step back. Think of it as educational. Step back from preconceptions, and simply step into the moment, and nobody could swing like Armstrong. Learn, if you are uninitiated, and enjoy if you are.

The collection itself? Here is your basic rule. When in doubt, get the JSP boxed set. This applies to all the old stuff. Jazz, blues, country, whatever. When in doubt, JSP. Here's the thing. They do the best job possible with remastering, keeping in mind that getting rid of all the noise means losing substance, and they keep the cost down. At this point, if you really want extensive liner notes, you can find all information in other documentation anyway. They give you the basics, and then if you want to collect books, do so. This is simply the most efficient and effective way to collect the classics. JSP. Just stop looking, because every time you go with another company, you will be disappointed. I have been.

The JSP 4 disc set is classic Armstrong, remastered well, minimal repetition, giving you the fun history. A true understanding of the roots of jazz. What more do you need?

text.2197: The early Van Halen remasters so far have been great and this is no exception to the rule.  Re-Released on 180g vinyl by Warner Brothers this heavy vinyl is ultra quiet.  The cover is made from heavy card stock and the original inner sleeve with artwork is included.  Also as an extra bonus the record itself is in an audiophile quality while paper sleeve that is plastic lined. Every care and careful detail has been  put into these vinyl re-release projects for Van Halen and they really are amazing.  Having Ted Templeman as a producer from 78-84 was a plus for the original audio capture for instruments and voices so the original material was laid down well.  With the exception of Pretty Woman.  I’m not sure what happened here but I’ve heard this on everything from vinyl, CD, to cassette, to 45 and now the Remastered version and they all sound similar.  Maybe they were trying for an AM type retro sound.  Don’t get me wrong, this is still the best that that Pretty Woman has ever sounded, it just wasn’t captured well from the start.  Everything else is great.  Most people prefer the Dave albums that got the most airplay and are the most recognizable like Van Halen 1 and 1984.  But the albums from Van Halen 2 to Diver Down all have a similar format and order and are loaded with creativity.  This may be the most diverse collection of tunes for this band.  It’s certainly entertaining to listen to.  The cover tunes are fun and pretty good.  Cathedral is an innovative instrumental.  Secrets is a wonderful song showing the band’s ability to scale it back a bit.  Intruder is the intro to Pretty Woman and it is captured well with a phenomenal sound.  Each song just shows off that Van Halen with Dave was capable of so much.  If you’re considering it, it’s worth it!  A truly wonderful vinyl experience...

text.2210:
When I bought this recording, I already knew some of the performers did not evoke the plight of the French poor as well as did the original London cast: Jauvert (whose character, like that of Valjean comes from extreme poverty) is less sinister and menacing in this production; and some of the "comic relief" characters do not manage sarcasm as well. Nor, frankly, do they tap-into their "entertaining hostility and nihilism" as well as the London cast.

But so many little pieces are missing from the London cast recording that it is much easier to follow the story in this two-CD set -- and to understand the developing characters. On the whole, this is rounded-out better and (as mentioned above) easier to follow.

I wish there were a London-cast recording more "fleshed-out" with characters and their interaction -- that, combined with the subtle lyrics and nuanced delivery, would be worth whatever it cost to acquire it!

The headline above is the title to the English liner notes in the disk. More like in their dust. I am not a musicologist, but if you are writing symphonies in the 19th Century, if you don't come up with hummable melodies that stick to the inside of a listener's head, you have -- nothing.

I heard the last movement of Symphony #1 played by a different orchestra in Sirius/XM, and it sounded interesting enough to buy. I found this set by Leipzig/Masur for a very good price, and said to my self what better combination to play such music firmly in the tradition of the greats? The question is, as the composer of the Scottish Fantasy, G Minor Violin Concerto and Kol Nidrei, how did things go so awry?

As it turns out, Symphony #1 is ok to listen to, some interesting themes. Parts are straight out of the Felix playbook, such as the scherzo which sounds like drafts of Midsummer's Night dream that hit the cutting room floor. Others are Schumann on a bad day -- but fairly nice nonetheless.

Symphony #2 - what fat, turgid lump of coal, a mass of sound like Wagner without his charm! I had to pull my index finger away from the stop button more than once.

Symphony #3 is far better than #2. Much more interesting, give it a listen.

Crimes of the Mind is a real gem. It has songs of sillyness, such as "Self", which is an egotistical satire, and "Bitchin' again", which is the only track with a female vocalist and she complains about how her partner never gets anything done. The album also contrasts this with more serious and dark songs like "Lucy in the Subway", which is a great interpretation of the aftermath of The Beatles' "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds", and "King of Nothing", reminiscing on dreams of that the speaker had as a child and where he is now, holding his nihilistic world view.

The drums, guitars, keyboard and vocals are great and the artists play very comfortably with each other. The bass can be a tad wacky sometimes but I think it adds to the comedic effect.

It is a great collection of creativity and is definitely worth a listen

The best thing about this compilation is that all songs are in STEREO !! I bought this cd mainly for the song "SLEIGH RIDE " and much to my surprise found it in STEREO !! These songs were recorded in the '50s , '60's, and later and appear to be the original recordings ! I liked most all of the songs that I used to hear as a kid growing up.
The skip / repeat from 1:38 to 1:47 on "CLASSICAL JUKEBOX" ( track 10 ) is not an error but a clever way of revealing jukeboxes that would skip / repeat until jarred , shaken , or beaten . This is NOT A MISTAKE !! I reccommend this cd to anyone who wants to listen to great instrumental music of the '50's and '60's.

I bought this as a gift for my vinyl loving friend, thinking that if you're going to collect vinyl, Kind of Blue is an essential album to own. He reports that it is a good quality 180 gram pressing. The blue disk looks really cool, and he says the audio quality is great. So it would seem to be a win.

However, through some interesting social media cross traffic, a representative of the Miles Davis estate saw it on Instagram, and commented that it appeared to be a "weird bootleg." So I started doing some digging. It definitely appears that this is an unauthorized release, by London-based Not Now Music, under EU public domain law. It is not licensed by Columbia Records or the Miles Davis estate. It is not technically illegal, but it is definitely shady, especially being sold in the United States. That is the reason for the different cover art. It is also impossible to know what the audio source is, but it seems entirely likely it was mastered from a good quality CD.

So I guess whether you want to buy this will depend on whether you care about artists and their estates. I would not buy it again, knowing what I know now. In fact, I plan on buying another officially released copy. Let your own conscience be your guide.

This album is cut incredibly well and frankly the sound quality for a single-disc 33 1/3 RPM album is phenomenal. Almost like hearing the album again for the first time. Nearly silent in terms of surface noise. Huge bass extension. Ultra wide soundstage and stereo image. Crisp yet incredibly smooth and detailed highs. Outstanding. I've encountered *no* IGD whatsoever in the latter portion of either side that another reviewer mentioned. This is the copy that I will stick with for all time. It is nearly perfect.

I am however deducting 1-star for the handling of the Hi-Res download for the digital files that should be included. Upon visiting the noted link on the card for redemption one is greeted by a paragraph of text explaining that something has changed in the hosting of these files and the code on the included card needs to be replaced. To do so you must send a photograph of the card itself AND the album to a support email address. They noted it will take up to a week to receive a response. Frankly, this if this is the best system anyone could come up with for problems on the back-end it looks embarrassingly amateurs and unprofessional. I'm waiting for my response.

Another complaint is Amazon.com's utterly atrocious packing/shipping of the album but I will not count that against the review here of the actual product (thought the shipping would receive 1-star at best). It was "in stock" yet delayed for well over TWO WEEKS, and when it did finally ship Amazon simply tossed it in an oversized sized box with next to no packing material so the record just bounced around inside during shipping. As a result it arrived with one corner of the jacket *severely* dented and bent. I'd have returned it if there were more in stock but as the LP itself is not damaged I chose to just hold onto it. Amazingly poor shipping practice for most any item, but particularly so for a vinyl record.

Both of those headaches aside, it really comes down to the record itself, and again it is nothing short of phenomenal. Find this one.

Update: Real World got in touch with me within four days for the digital download code/link, which wasn't too bad. Even that replacement code was a bit kludgy (could not be copy/pasted and *had* to manually keyed in for it work on the Bandcamp site) but the nice thing is that Bandcamp supplies pretty much any digital format you may want and it stores the purchase/download noted in your account (if you have one there, and you should) so you can go back to it again at a later date. I give a half-star back.

By listening to this album and seeing the videos that accompanied the album's hit singles, it was easy to tell that MCA Records wanted Jody Watley's debut solo album to be a big hit. And I bet Watley wanted it that way too, so she could show America that she could make a hit record on her own without her former group Shalamar's help.

Well, less than 10 months after its release Watley's debut album went Platinum which certified her as a bankable solo artist.

Me personally, I was too young to understand this album in its prime in the 1987-1988 buying season as I wasn't even in preschool yet. But as an adult I've been able to appreciate the album more.

This album was a dance pop effort bar none. There was only one ballad on the album (track 8, Most of All) and even that song had some dance pop elements to it.

Watley was this album's main attraction but don't forget the likes of Andre Cymone, Bernard Edwards (from Chic fame), Jeff Bova, Tony Thompson, and others who shaped and curated the beats on this album, which were also a major part of this album's success in 1987.

One more thing, adding the super hot at the time George Michael to track 9 (Learn To Say No) was a very good touch by MCA Records. The duet he did with Watley was underrated in 1987 and it still is today.

In conclusion, the abundance of dance pop songs and adding George Michael to the mix were MCA's attempts to make this album a commercial hit. And that formula worked.

Just to temper this. I am a John Carpenter fanatic. I own most of his soundtracks. I think no one compares to him. I think everything that made him so effective and brilliant vanishes the more advanced his equipment gets, and the more time he spends on things. He is notorious for in his early years spending a very limited amount of time on his soundtracks, which is the key ingredient to making them brilliant. The second most important ingredient to making his soundtracks great is the primitive limited synths he used. That limitation of sound imparted a great purity and simplicity to his compositions.

Here, he has time, budget and his son to help him and it all goes completely against everything that makes Carpenter's music work. It's tired, rote, lazy, stock, and something I will never listen to again, not even to revisit because of doubts caused by shock and disbelief in how bad it is.

The only good thing I can say about this soundtrack is, it matches how bad the actual movie is.

Worse than the Zombie remakes, worse than any of the later sequels.

This is the Last Jedi of Halloween movies.

This is, for me, the most pleasing recording of Beethoven's perfect 9th Symphony, though perhaps only because it was the recording I grew up listening to. I was born in 1989 and this particular re-release of George Szell conducting the Cleveland Orchestra through this piece came out in 1991. Through twenty years, this Sony Essential Classics release heightened my ecstasies and eased my defeats. Then, around 2012, I had to change cars, meaning I no longer had access to a cassette tape player. So, I could no longer listen to my favorite 9th ever. For the intervening 8 years, I was content with "other" versions of the 9th that I could find for free on the internet, but it was tough to find "the one," particularly because I didn't remember the conductor or the orchestra or anything. Anyway, COVID-19 happened and I suddenly had time to do some research! I found it! The shipping was fast and all that. The product was delivered in excellent condition. And the people on here complaining about the audio quality of this disc must be some seriously tough customers, because I was blown away by the clarity of the piece, especially compared to that old cassette I used to listen to in the car. Listening to this recording through quality headphones or on a nice stereo system may cause you to weep uncontrollably or experience unusually potent philosophical thoughts.

As a closing remark, I just want to say what a cruel and criminal act it is to place the Fidelio Overture after the 9th Symphony chronologically on the album, which in 30 years is really my only complaint about the whole thing. Fidelio is a great piece itself, but it can't possibly hope to directly follow the 9th Symphony, nor could really any other piece of music, but that's just me. They should have put it at the beginning, if it was necessary to package them on the same disc. Who am I anyway? It's beautiful, get it. Get it NOW!

John Rutter has made quite a living for himself writing easy-on-the-ears choral music, many of them mid-tempo ballads and sacred anthems, and so it is here on John Rutter’s Christmas Album. I am largely familiar with Rutter’s arrangements of carols and original sacred Christmas music from Sir David Willcocks’ multiple volumes of Oxford's Carols for Choirs, and they introduced me to Rutter’s gentle, lightly challenging style of choral writing, that is at once gently simplistic, but with stabs of colourful progressions, soft jazz harmonies, and often perky accompaniment. Much of the 78-minutes of music on this album are original works by Rutter, most if not all are sacred, with around 8 of the 23 offerings based on traditional carols and arranged by Rutter, so unless you are familiar with Rutter’s music, many of the tunes will be unfamiliar. In addition, John Rutter’s The Cambridge Singers Christmas [[ASIN:B0000DJEOL on Collegium Records]] has more familiar Christmas carols alongside classical offerings which makes a nice companion to this collection.

John Rutter definitely has a blueprint for his 4-6 verse carols settings: Full choir and orchestra on the first verse, with alternating women’s voices and men’s voices taking the lead on the ensuing verses, a gentle a cappella verse, and tutti chorus on the final runaround. But Rutter mixes things up with more complex choral writing as each song progresses, often with close-knit jazzy harmonies that keeps the music from just repeating. Since much of the music is 3-4 minute mid-tempo ballads or lyrical settings, this can get a bit tiring in one sitting, but Rutter has some gems that immediately rise to the top. The opening Wexford Carol has some nice modal chord progressions that are immediately haunting and attractive, the more jovial Jesus Child and Donkey Carol along with his famous Shepherd’s Pipe Carol are a lot of fun and provide more rhythmic interest, and the classic Angel's Carol, Candlelight Carol, Very Best Time of Year, and What Sweeter Music bring quite a bit to the table musically and spiritually. Most appreciated are Rutter’s familiar carol arrangements, which show his ability to take a carol and really make it his own, such as the Baroque-tinged Joy to the World, the humorous We Wish You a Merry Christmas, the sprightly I Saw Three Ships and Deck the Hall, a haunting I Wonder As I Wander, and a decent Silent Night arrangement.

Most of the works on the disc are orchestrated and the City of London Sinfonia adds so much more colour than piano or organ accompaniment, Rutter enjoying adding the occasional wind solo, and the orchestral sound here is plenty full, but rarely brazen. The Cambridge Singers are captured here between 1985 and 2002 and there is a slight evolution of sound, with the sopranos adding the lightest bit of vibrato to their tone for a pleasantly healthy sound to the straight-toned English chamber choirs that influences their earliest offerings. And of course, John Rutter is leading all of these performances for an authoritative programme of his own music, and these are in much better sound than his original performances [[ASIN:B00461VXTG on EMI]] with Clare College from yesteryear.

The John Rutter Christmas Album is easy to recommend to any John Rutter lover, choral music appreciator, and for something different during the Yuletide season. [[ASIN:B0000DJEOL The Cambridge Singers Christmas]] is an excellent companion to these performances, and of course you can tread back to those early Clare College performances [[ASIN:B00461VXTG on EMI]]. Highly Recommended!
text.2874: Nowhere on the planet does the blues tradition thrive so robustly as a living, breathing force than in the work of Eric Bibb.  Firmly grounded in its roots, the durable and prolific singer/guitarist’s originals and adaptations- and his performances of same- make an inarguable case for the blues as powerful contemporary expression acutely conscious of its past. Mr. Bibb’s current offering is primarily a trio affair, ably assisted by guitarist Michael Jerome Browne and harmonica player JJ Milteau.  The threesome’s chemistry generates a constant incandescence, adding just the proper amount of heat underneath Bibb’s tales of folks on the move, most often not by choice.  Originals “Delta Getaway”, “Prayin’ For Shore” and the title track stand out, as does a haunting take on Dylan’s “Masters Of War”. (Duane Verh, Roots Music Report)

Dr. West (skit): The perfect way to start the album. Bring back Slim Shady, boom, let's go. (10/10)

3 A.M: Eminem perceives himself as a serial killer, and has one of the best flows of the album. (10/10)

My Mom: Although Eminem doesn't give a f***, this track is a little long, and of course, "We get it, you hate your mom." I have to go with a 6. (6/10)

Insane: If you could kill the skeletons in my closet... This song is one of the best, but if you can't get past Relapse's horrorcore theme, this ain't it. (9/10)

Bagpipes from Bagdadh: He has better flows, not the greatest, but still fine! (7/10)

Hello: This is one of the best, of not only the album, but his carrer! (10/10)

Tonya (Skit): What a way to bring Hello, one of the best, into another highlight! (9/10)

Same Song & Dance: Same situation as Hello, but this one's even better! (10/10)

We Made You: Classic Slim Shady, insulting celebrities! (9/10)

Medicine Ball: I think this is another My Mom/Bagpipes-type song. (6/10)

Paul (Skit): Paul's pissed at Eminem for not giving a f***! (8/10)

Stay Wide Awake: Wow! It's another hidden gem! (10/10)

Old Times Sake (ft. Dr. Dre): Classic Slim Shady, and Dre! (9/10)

Must Be The Ganja: While not one of the better of the album, it's passable. (7/10)

Mr. Mathers (Skit): Transforming a song about him thinking recording is a drug, to a song about his 2007 overdose! (8/10)

Deja Vu: Oh my god! This song is the best of the album, period. (11/10.)

Beautiful: Not too much Slim Shady here, but it's still great! (10/10)

Crack a Bottle (ft. Dr. Dre & 50 Cent): Pretty catchy, and has good flows! (9/10)

Steve Berman (Skit): Part 3. Mentions Eminem's hiatus! (8/10)

Underground: Woah. (10/10)

Relapse: Refill:

Forever: While it's a good song, Em blows every other rapper out of the park! (9/10)

Hell breaks Loose (ft. Dr. Dre): So good! (9/10)

Buffalo Bill: I'm not the biggest fan, but it's still good! (8/10)

Elevator: There once was a saying that I used to say! So good, and what a flow! (9/10)

Taking My Ball: Well, it's good! It's kinda weird, but it's still good! (8/10)

Music Box: Wow. (10/10)

Drop The Bomb On 'Em: Yeah, boy! (9/10)

Overall: 9.5/10.

Jeez... for $24, I expected it to come on colored vinyl or something. But nope, regular ol' black wax, albeit 180g like most modern pressings. Comes in a seemingly unnecessary and somewhat poorly-constructed dual-pocketed gatefold which constantly tries to bow open. Album sleeve contains lyrics on one side and a nice photo on the other. The other pocket contains a haphazardly-folded mini-poster that contains production credits, which could've been printed on the inside of the gatefold or on the other side of the sleeve (instead of the photo.) Whoever managed this project is fired, especially the print producer.

That being said, this is a *really* solid album, and I'm not even a hardcore Robyn fan. Compared to the bombast of 'Body Talk' and 'Robyn,' 'Honey' is a relatively laid back and intimate album that's perfect for vinyl. Moments of greatness include the stellar one-two punch of "Baby Forgive Me" and "Send to Robyn Immediately" as well as "Between the Lines" and "Because it's in the Music." It's a respectable feat to put out a 9-track album that can be listened to all the way through without even an itch to skip a song. Looking forward to seeing her in concert in July.

An excellent album highly recommend! This is one of a hand full of LPs/CDs that all tracks are great. Released in September 1980, I was fortunate to get an original vinyl LP back in early 1981 at a JPN record shop in Los Angles. This LP "opened my eyes" into the wonderworld of J-City Pop. Before then, I would only find traditional Japanese Enka, and a few 60's, 70's pop music that to me, sounded like a copy of American pop music of the time. When I first listened to this album I was captivated by the up to date (1980's) rhythm and catchy melodies. My favorite tracks are いつか(someday) and 夏への扉(The Door into Summer). What's best about most JPN LPs, C/Ds, and cassettes is they come with lyrics so (if motivated), can find out what each song is about.

For those that follow Japanese music Enka was and Stil popular toady. I believe the genre is called Sohi Enka (壮士演歌). I still enjoy new and old Enka music but love City Pop most.

A classic album ruined by engineers who clearly don't understand remastering beyond making things louder. Further proof that in music's digital age the term "remastered" doesn't always equate to "improved".

Clearly mastered for playback on mobile devices, this mix is boomy, peaky, lacks most low-end, mid-range guitar action is muffled, and highs are thin and tinny. In fact, many of the mixing flaws from the original LP master are actually EXACERBATED here rather than repaired.

As with too many digital "remasterings" of analog material, it's clearly been remixed solely for improved playback on inferior devices, rather than superior playback on audiophile Hi-Fi systems or even studio headphones.

If you care at all about quality, skip this release.

text.3250:
Two reference points are immediately obvious when considering Sonny Sharrock’s relatively anomalous 1986 album, Guitar. First, his duet album with Nicky Skopelitis, Faith Moves, and second, Joe Diorio’s Solo Guitar.

Sonny Sharrock recorded Guitar in an unusual way. He recorded it by himself, playing multiple guitar parts. It is not a jazz album per se, but Sharrock was always an instrumentalist of many influences, incorporating styles from post-bop to fusion to free jazz to crunching noise. On Guitar, Sharrock ranges from jazzy passages to bits of rock, and even some classical, all with his characteristic crunch. The pieces have the exploratory feel of jazz, even though the recording techniques required forethought. Very interesting, yet very different from those two reference points even if they come to mind. When Sharrock recorded Faith Moves with Nicky Skopelitis, the basic sounds and concepts came to fruition with the kind of spontaneity that one would have expected because Sharrock and Skopelitis could react to each other in real time, of course. That album has the feel of a sequel, and a realization of Guitar, even if it also has the feel of a throw-everything-at-the-wall experiment in and of itself. That makes the pair of albums interesting to consider in light of each other. Guitar stands alone as a way to understand how Sharrock thought, and how he tried to compose. The guitar parts, by necessity, could not respond to each other, yet he had to do them in sequence, thinking first about what he would play second, constrained then by the initial recording.

This brings us to Joe Diorio, and that classic recording that wasn’t really the first experiment in “looping,” which is now common for solo performers on the stage, but one should still go back and study Joe Diorio’s Solo Guitar. Diorio was remarkably skilled, and could do it all, yet on Solo Guitar, he chose to lay down multiple tracks on guitar, improvising on top. That album is, at least technically and conceptually, closer to what Sharrock did here, but Diorio stuck closer to jazz, without dipping into crunchy, noisy oddity the way Sharrock was wont to do. That doesn’t necessarily make Diorio’s album better or worse, just different. Sharrock wasn’t laying down a track with the intent of laying down some bebop improv on top of it. That’s a different process. He was more interested in layering sounds.

That, perhaps, is why listening to Guitar in context of Faith Moves can leave a listener feeling like this album is a bit of a rough draft. That’s not quite true. They are conceptually different. Nicky and Sonny interacting and improvising with each other? That’s just a different thing altogether. This is more like Tibbetts putting down layers of sound. One could hear this as an almost New York version of ECM.

It is, then, a strange album. Strange within the history of jazz, and even within Sharrock’s discography. It requires a different mindset to appreciate, but of course, Sharrock’s fans will generally appreciate something different, so this is well worth tracking down. It may be harder to find than his collaboration with Skopelitis, but it is worth it.

Bavouzet... what to say? -Is Bavouzet a Gulda reencarnation? Why do I hear things of the great Gulda technique when I hear Jean Effram? Jokes aside, there is something of the Gulda genius in Bavouzet's playing. Am sure am going to find that, in a broader sense, in his Beethoven Piano Sonatas. For heard some in YouTube and there it is. He never was a Gulda pupil, but that brilliant (wherever there was one!) piano, can also be heard here. That joy of being doing Art and playing at once, that powerful and alive touch and sound...May I say that if you haven't heard Gulda you haven't heard Mozart, for instance ? Well, this Debussy is so good, as I expected from the winner of the Beethoven International Piano Competition Bavouzet is. And not because Von Beet had to see much with the Debussy innovative harmonies. Although Beethoven explored atonality in his last period, the timber harmonies of Debussy, his well tone pitch architecture is another thing. You can see how he manages the timber harmonies in the Isle Joyeuse, for instance. Find JEB has a strong, resounding piano sound, convenient so, to play Beethoven, no doubt. But he's equally owner of a delicate touch and a wonderful technique and sense of rhythm. What makes his interpretation the appropriate receipt for a good Debussy. His Jardins sous la Pluie and Pour le Piano or L'Isle Joyeuse are just great. And prefer his Preludes to the Benedetti more distant ones. Also, compared to the Paul Jacobs ones, find they are as good as them. Although the Jacobs ones still are a bit rarer for me, surely because am not familiar with them, yet. In the case of Bavouzet, as in the Jacobs ones, we are face to pianists who are fond of Jazz.. So they may incorporate somethings from there, besides an alert sense of rhythm. In this sense it has been compared JEB Beethoven Sonatas surveys with those of Gulda. Is this so, a mix of a jazzy approach with an Impressionistic one? Wouldn't go so far. But still find the alert and rhythmic touch of Gulda also here. And Gulda was another Jazz lover... - though comparing the Bavouzet Preludes with the Pommier ones... still liking the last ones more. For me, Pommier is better for instance, in the Jardins Sous la Pluie, my prefered Debussy work. But this happens also with the Preludes. I prefer Pommier to any other. Maybe because bought first the Pommier album. JEB is a different, distinctive multi awards winning Debussy set, and will have to keep hearing it. Have to follow the mainstream, in this sense. Before arriving to a definitive conclusion. Obviously Bavouzet is a gifted pianist, and will have to buy his Beethoven Sonatas account, for one can easily understand why he is the adequate pianist for such a composer. And because I love Bavouzet's playing, as love the Gulda one. Don't understand instead the complaints about the sound recording quality, for frankly, it is excellent in all the cds. As a whole this seems if not the better, a very good Debussy survey. Can't tell about the Tirimo one for choosed this one instead. The Tirimo one may be a more romantic approach, considering his Schubert and his other recordings trend. But the Bavouzet Debussy does not lack sensitivity and so he meets the inner poetry of this music. Therefore, as many others say, this is an excellent nowadays Debussy. Of another brilliant pianist of the French
cool pianists of our century: as Le Sage, Tharaud, Amoyel, Angelich, Couteau or Aimard. We are very lucky to have such a group of awesome artists at work presently. In the Bavouzet case, have heard his Ravel is also one of the best we have. Wouldn't be astonished. This is a pianist to follow and to recommend. Don't miss him. Excuses if I made a bit of a mess...!!

The fact that the otherwise excellent Rhino label would package this collection of terrible recordings in a nice book-style box I find to be quite desceptive. Such nice presentations of music collections are - in my experience, anyway - reserved for special content. This is so far from special content - in terms of sound quality - that it makes for a major disappointment. The first three disks consist of muffled soundboard recordings with very little high frequencies. As such, the drums are barely audible. The 4th disk has markedly improved sound quality BUT the song selection is awful - especially for boomers like me who favor the early stuff. The DVD of the Rockpalast performance keeps me from giving this collection a 1-star rating. It is, as others have noted, an excellent performance. It's a bit dark and high in red hues but still clear enough to see the band in excellent form. Terry is overweight and not appearing to be at the prime of health but plays his guitar like nobody's business.

Regarding the Isle of Wight set - I was scratching my head at how dull the sound quality was throught both disks. I didn't recall the Jimi Hendrix recordings from the same festival sounding so muffled - they've been a favorite of mine. On a revisit to the Hendrix recordings, they are significantly better than the Chicago recording but some of that has to do with the fact that, with Jimi, there were only three instruments to be represented in the mix - Chicago had 8 or 9. However, the relistening of the Hendrix set reveals that it also has some limitations in high frequencies but I'm inclined to believe the Hendrix tapes are of a better generation. I would be very surprised if the Chicago Isle of Wight recordings used in this collection are 1st or even 2nd generation tapes. They sound to be 5th gen with the hiss removed.

Maybe even my fave on the album. There are some mighty long empty gaps at the end, not sure what that is about, but all in all, the boys did a wonderful job of putting this together.  I wish, the tribute song  to Freddie was on it, but other than that, it is perfect. Haunting…sometimes, amazing…always. It is now my most listened to Queen album. It’s beautiful. Not as rock and roll as typical Queen. A much different feel to it.  But it seems, and this is what I really like, as if it is Freddie saying goodbye, in his own way, on his own terms, just like he always did everything. 'Exile' may be the band's last great album. I could say it's their best but I probably prefer BEGGARS BANQUET. The rock critic Robert Christgau wrote a book ranking the 100 greatest LPs. I remember the top 3, and Exile was #2. Number one was Rod Stewart's "Every Picture Tells a Story'; third was 'Astral Weeks' by Van Morrison. I love those two and would rank them among my top favorites. 'Exile' would rank below them, as it would with Morrison's MOONDANCE and others in different genres like John Coltrane's "Giant Steps". (excluding live albums, which deserve their own category). I don't really have any aesthetic criteria or empirical system of judging. Anyway, albums may be overrated but making lists of the greatest definitely is, though it's fun;i it's also hard, which is part of the fun.
'Exile' is a seventies albums that doesn't sound like one. Rock was fragmenting into divisions, including progressive, metal, punk, and glam. The Stones remind fans where the music came from. These songs could have been from the forties or fifties. That makes the album timeless; it's not tied to an era, It is for that reason that, best of all, there's no tired nostalgia about it, unlike the lame eighties musical Rock of Ages.
