text.3412: Juan Diego Florez, a star belcanto tenor, adds another distinction to his illustrious career with this album dedicated to tenor arias by Wolfang Amadeus Mozart. Florez is equally adept in brilliant virtouso selections from Mozart's early operas as well as in tender and reflective moments from masterpieces like Don Giovanni and Cosi fan tutte. The album starts in solid mode with the florid "Fuor del mar" from Idomeneo, Re di Creta, where the tenor adds some fascinating ornamentation and a final cadenza up to high D. This mastery of ornamentation extends to the whole album, where mordents, grace notes and other ornaments are introduced on the repeated sections of arias, all done with respect to the music and technical mastery, as natural as speech. Florez is also involved and expressive, conveying the feelings of the characters. It is truly delighful to hear his rendition of Il mio tesoro incanto (a number that have taxed so many tenors) done with such panache and legato. All this demonstrates the beauty and power of the belcanto tradition, and its prevalence during the eighteenth century, way before Rossini, Bellini, and Donizetti. It will be great if this great tenore di grazia continues exploring earlier composers, like Handel, Bach, and Haydn, and their relation with the tenor voice. Highly recommended!

text.3431: Had the LP years ago and picked up a Japanese CD import about 10 years or so ago.  One of Felix's best and most successful solo projects.  The lovely Only a Lonely Heart Sees was a Top 40 hit for him, and it went all the way to number two in Billboard's Adult Contemporary chart.  Sizable hit, yes?  Then there was a change at the top of Columbia / Epic, and the new regime didn't consider Felix much of a priority.  The follow-up single, the very catchy Good to Have Love Back, barely charted due to lack of promotion, and the album sank without notice.  In my world, however, the second single would've been the Cavaliere / Eddie Brigati songwriting reunion Love Is the First Day of Spring, as Rascal-y a bit of pure pop nirvana as you could hope for.  Heck, it even features Eddie on beautiful backing vocals.  Shoulda, coulda, woulda been a smash!  Another standout track is a rockin' rearranged version of the Rascals' biggest hit single, the powerfully moving People Got to Be Free.  The lilting title track (Castles in the Air) is another beauty.  All in all, if the fates had been kinder and the stars aligned, this would've been a very big album back in the day (1980-81).  Four stars and highly recommended to fans of Felix, the Rascals, and classic sixties-inspired pop.

I am really baffled that this score is getting so many fours and fives out of five. Stand this score up against the classic original trilogy music - and even some of the stronger tracks from the prequels - and it's clear that this is serviceable, but definitely not William's best. Die-hard fans are quick to resort to talk of 'Williams is taking cues from the film itself and the score is subverting expectations etc', but that's just 'meta' type nonsense. This score is just not as dynamic or memorable as the others he has done. It feels like a muted greatest hits tapestry - fusing previous more memorable tunes from the past, with more muted murky new stuff. To the die-hard fans who are bizarrely rating this highly I say: 'search your feelings, you know it to be true!'

It speaks volumes that the strongest sparks of brilliance in this soundtrack are the re-use of the classic themes from the original trilogy - albeit greatly recycled and rejigged. Kylo and Ren's themes (the best 'new' signature themes from Force Awakens) are also interwoven well. This 'lack of pop' from new themes was also a problem with the Force Awakens, but that score at least had the benefit of new themes for Rey and Kylo, which hold up well vs original signature themes. I'm a huge Williams fan, and on his best day, he's the cleverest composer in the biz. However, this soundtrack is a pale ghost of his previous work in terms of impact. Despite listening to this album multiple times I can barely remember any of the new music afterwards - although I agree that the music certainly works well enough during the movie scenes themselves (as atmospheric backdrop). That's the key issue here, it sounds like background backdrop music - the music just doesn't feel as immediate to me as it does in the older films. The stand out tracks for this score are:

Main title and Escape - has some good zip to it.
Ach-To Island - mysterious sounding.
Revisiting Snoke - mostly muted, but some nice use of Kylo's theme to ramp tension.
The Battle of Crait - complex and interweaves a variety of themes, although (again) the interjection of classic themes (Tie Fighter attack from New Hope) substantially enlivens it.

For me, Revenge of the Sith is the last truly great Star Wars soundtrack by Williams - both for textual variety/complexity, inventiveness and overall memorability. In that score, Williams did a great job of juxtaposing the catchier signature set piece tunes - Battle of the Heroes/ General Grevious - with the more muted and subtle emotional scenes e.g. Palatine's Teachings and Padme's ruminations. That approach worked brilliantly, and is a reminder of just how sublime William's top work is. Here's hoping the next Star Wars film score fares better. Beaming positive thoughts William's way in the meantime.

text.3568:
Huntley Dent, Fanfare magazine

Some great recordings—and I’d call this a magnificently great one—return to mind in the mood of lest we forget. Although Karajan’s early-digital Alpine Symphony has received its share of accolades, it received knocks as well, with the blame not entirely his. At the time Strauss’s score was still routinely ridiculed, and Fanfare’s Roger Dettmer wasn’t alone in his disparagement: “If Eine Alpensinfonie warned of serious erosion in Strauss’ creative chemistry—the frequency and bulk of self-quotation from Zarathustra and Don Quixote through Salome and Rosenkavalier is only one symptom of starved soil—Strauss had preserved a formidable craft on which he could fall back, without serious bodily injury.” (Fanfare 5:6)
I’d like to be shown the bulky self-quotations being disparaged, but Eine Alpensinfonie clearly suffered from its overweening size, often viewed like a brontosaurus with a correspondingly tiny brain. Strauss was as reverent before Nature as Beethoven, but his worship was considered showy, shallow, and vulgar compared with the “Pastoral” Symphony. In the midst of wholesale dismissal by many critics, the beauty of the music was overlooked. Now the score is an audience favorite, and its discography is full to bursting. As orchestral virtuosity continues to rise and sonic improvements advance, one would expect pride of place to go to the newer recordings by great orchestras.
Yet in my experience nothing touches Karajan’s reading despite its one objective flaw, the recorded sound. The defects of early digital in the glassy highs, hardness in loud dynamics, and a sense of artificiality compared with an orchestra’s natural sound were serious drawbacks from the start, and a later remastering for DG’s Karajan Gold series offers only a fair improvement. In some ways bad digital sound is harder to adjust to than historical monaural sound, but once forewarned, listening to Karajan’s Alpine Symphony is far more than bearable (it helps to have a pair of forgiving loudspeakers with the fullest possible dynamic range—this stupendous orchestral showpiece isn’t for headphones).
In one way this CD could stand as the greatest Strauss recording by one of the century’s premier Strauss conductors. Karajan’s Berlin Philharmonic comes across as a force of nature equal to the natural forces Strauss apotheosizes. There is heart-stopping playing at every turn, even keeping in mind modern recordings by the Berlin Philharmonic under Zubin Mehta and by the Vienna Philharmonic under André Previn and Christian Thielemann. As purely sonic experiences they are thrilling, but Karajan, if I dare to say it, grasped the spiritual underpinning of Strauss’s intentions. If Furtwängler had recorded the score, even he would have been hard pressed to extract the moments of epiphany that Karajan achieves.
I think of Furtwängler’s Symphonia domestica, which resurrected and redeemed another ridiculed Strauss score in one stroke. There as here, your expectations are shattered. True, Karajan’s recording was preceded by two very fine ones under Rudolf Kempe, which still hold up musically. However, there was nothing on the scene to rival Karajan and his Berliners, a fact many have resented but none can honestly dispute. The revelations of “On the Summit,” “Sunset,” and “Quiet Settles,” all of which come in the less virtuosic parts of the score, are uniquely moving to me when I listen to Karajan.
In general I am reminded how pitifully inadequate to an artist’s gifts are the public image and media blurbs that surround him. Karajan’s public image while he was alive was imperial and imperious, but his posthumous image has been besmirched by issues of politics, morality, and character under Nazism. In An Alpine Symphony the pitfalls of vainglory set a snare for both conductor and composer. I might not be able to forgive their biography, but I am willing to set it aside while listening to their art.

I attended a performance by the National Philharmonic at Strathmore Hall outside Washington, D.C. It was my first orchestral concert since the beginning of the pandemic. The program included Henryk Gorecki's Symphony No. 3, "Symphony of Sorrowful Songs" conducted by the Philharmonic's long time conductor, Piotr Gajewski, who offered a perceptive introduction to the work, together with the beautiful Metropolitan Orchestra soprano, Aleksandra Kurzak performing the sorrowful songs. It was a beautiful, appropriate way to return to live orchestral music.

Together with the live performance, I listened again to this 1994 Naxos CD of the Gorecki Third Symphony with Antoni Wit conducting the Polish National Radio Symphony Orchestra with soprano Zofia Kilaowicz. It was an outstanding way to hear the symphony and to enhance my appreciation of the live performance. Several excellent recordings of this music are available for those wanting to hear the piece, and this recording is among them.

The Symphony of Sorrowful Songs is one of the rare works of contemporary classical music that has achieved widespread, almost notorious, popularity. Composed in 1976, it came into popular consciousness more than a decade later. Much of Gorecki's earlier writing had been in a difficult serialist style. This symphony abandoned serialist music for an atavistic, primitive simplicity. It features basic, repeated and simple notes, harmonies, and figurations which gain in intensity with repetition and variety among the instruments of the orchestra. The symphony is in three slow movements, each marked "Lento" but with variations in mood and pulse throughout.

The tone of the symphony is sorrowful indeed but it lacks a specific programme or reference to a particular event. The three sorrowful songs include a 15th Century lament from the Virgin to her Son, a prayer of a young woman imprisoned by the Gestapo, and a folk song from a mother whose son had been killed in war. The vocal line for the songs are full of lament and sadness with a ray of hope. The songs are surrounded by the simple, dense orchestral score.

This Symphony is heavily religious in tone with its throwbacks to an earlier musical idiom. Its simplicity and its anguish speak to contemporary listeners particularly in these difficult days of pandemic, dissension and war. Keith Anderson's 1994 liner notes to the CD references the symphony's "peculiar relevance to the mood of today, its anxieties, sorrows, and hopes." I was moved to hear the symphony live for the first time in the performance by the National Philharmonic. I was also moved to hear the symphony again on this CD which has long been part of my collection. I was glad to hear the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs live and on recording and to share my thoughts briefly in this review.

Robin Friedman

My parents had this album around the house when I was young (not sure why - they weren't into it) and I confiscated it. :-) I fell in love with folk music because of it, which became one of my favorite genres of music. I slowly started getting CDs to replace some of my vinyl, and this one was a must-have. I can now listen to it at my computer, and obviously it sounds a lot better than that old record.

Over time, and with the advent of Youtube where I can listen to a huge variety of stuff, I discovered that Peter Paul & Mary are one of the best mixed vocals and arrangements. They take things and make them uniquely their own, and it's a sound I love. I'd be remiss if I didn't also mention the great guitar work of Peter & Paul, really shown off in A Soulin'. I know all (most) of Mary's parts on this and I tend to sing those. My voice fits folk really well. At first that was a disappointment since I wanted to do musicals, but after a while I accepted it and found I really enjoyed the folk music.

This includes some popular things like Puff, The Magic Dragon and This Land is Your Land (that I learned in elementary school). But my favorites are probably Flora and Man Come Into Egypt, and also I quite like Tiny Sparrow, Morning Train and Gone the Rainbow.

I was also lucky enough to see PP&M live, for less than 25% of the seat price, about 10 rows back on an aisle. (Before Mary passed obviously.) It was a wonderful night. They're also pretty amusing, so pure live entertainment.

I'm old enough to have bought the first US pressing of this record when it came out in 1973, and have come to appreciate it as Lou's finest creation on record. I also remember how awful RCA pressings could be back in those days (anyone remember Dynaflex?) yet the production of this album always shines through. I've owned it on vinyl, cassette, 25th anniversary CD edition, and high res download. At last I can hear it in its perfection on the original medium it was intended for.

This is a clean, quiet pressing from a very balanced remaster that is a wonder to listen to. Those quiet moments where Lou's naked voice sings out with a lone piano or guitar, and the cadences in the title track, are not spoiled by pops and clicks, and every nuance of this voice and its intimacy, cruel and tender in the same breath, and the reverb that surrounds it, are clear as a bell. The sharp attack of the piano keys from Rick Wakeman, the magnificent drum fills of Aynsley Dunbar and Jack Bruce's inventive bass lines, it's all here. It's an extravagant production, to be sure, and nothing is wasted or superfluous.

I've only recently got back into buying and listening to vinyl again, and this pressing is one of the finest I've come across of any rock recording, along with the 50th anniversary edition of Love's Forever Changes and a couple others. Don't hesitate to buy this LP reissue.

text.3816:
When one of the greatest pianists of all time (Martha Argerich) is fond of your playing, this will certainly help your career. No one has benefitted from this more perhaps than when Argerich took a liking to Ivo Pogorelic in 1980 during the Chopin competition. In 1999, Evgheny Brakhman would gain recognition from Argerich, this time at first Dino Ciani competition where he would take first prize. This led to this CD debut of his where he plays the works of Mozart, Liszt and Beethoven.. The works include:

Mozart : Piano Sonata No. 10 C Major, K. 330
Beethoven : Piano Sonata No. 17 in D Minor, Op. 31, No. 2 'Tempest'
Liszt : Piano Sonata in B Minor, S. 178

All three of these are wonderful works and represent some of the best piano sonatas in the literature to date. His Mozart is certainly enjoyable and has an understated sense of charm to it with going too far. The Beethoven Sonata is adequately played as well. Finally with the Liszt Sonata Brakhman adds some interesting components to the work that make it unique which is tough to do in such a crowded list of performances that have played this epic piece. He starts the movement with a very low sound level and right from the start you can tell it is not simply his goal to play this work as fast as he can. In the slow sections of the sonata, he really highlights some of Liszt's most angelic melodies that juxtapose the demonic elements in the faster sections. These tempo selections bring the work to a slower overall time of over 33 minutes in playing time. In some aspects this causes the work to lose some of its overall cohesive with the other two movements, but I still admire his approach and originality.

Brakhman continues to concertize and perform and has subsequently recorded/performed at the Lugano festival with Argerich in 2002. This recording was the Mozart Piano Quartet on a day where Argerich played Beethoven's Piano Trio. Unfortunately there are no other recordings of his to date that I am aware of, but this CD is still well worth acquiring for those interested in listening to any of the works performed.

Darin returned to folk rock in the later 60's as did Dion; think Abraham, Martin and John. I feel sorry for the fans who bought this upon release, being inspired by his cover of Ruby Baby. That's the only song that rocks on this disc.
If lounge style music is your thing you'll be happy with this disc. If you revere the rocking side of Dion, you'll listen to this once. That's it's fate with me. For me it's back to the likes of Bronx in Blue, Yo Frankie, The Son of Skip James, Tank Full of Blues and many more.
If you want Dion of the early sixties on a disc that includes Ruby Baby, I recommend Bronx Blues: the Columbia Years. Of course there are the Laurie years.

This is the second 2-disc collector's set I've bought by The Who where I thought that the one-disc version (released in 1995) was the better version. Whereas the 1995 disc is arranged to sound like a seamless double-album, with B-sides and unreleased tracks that were often as good as much of the material on the original album, this one includes alternate, mostly inferior versions of album tracks and a live CD that is about half awesome and half extremely rough, unfinished sounding versions of songs. Although this material is VERY interesting, as it lets you into a bit of the song-writing process, it doesn't make for a bunch of repeat listens. The live show is often somewhat sloppy (at least by The Who's standards) if you don't know that the show was meant to be part of the song-writing process - gauging audience reaction and fine-tuning the songs afterwards. For most of the tracks, this isn't the fine-tuned band you hear on Live at Leeds or Live at Hull, which is a bit of a disappointment to me. The live versions of Pure and Easy, Getting in Tune, and Naked Eye are pretty incredible, though.
The original album itself sounds SLIGHTLY crisper to me in this version than the 1995 edition (particularly the drums), but not enough that I feel it warrants double-dipping.
NOTE: THERE WILL BE A NEW EDITION RELEASED IN 2022. I'd save my money if I was you.

text.3898:
The Aristocrats are about as talented an instrumental trio as one can find, yet if we are fully honest, their studio albums are not always as satisfying as the live albums. This is understandable, all things considered. For the guitar fans, anything Guthrie Govan does will be of interest, which is to take nothing away from Minnemann or Beller, and really, this is an outstanding trio. Yet, We’ll Do It Live, for example, stands just above their studio work. This is true for many such combos, so that’s par for the course, if such a statement can be made for a group on this level, but it just is. Yet Culture Clash manages to rise above the challenge of studio work. At their best, The Aristocrats manage to capture some of the magic of 70s era Jeff Beck. Govan, of course, is a guitarist in that tradition, blending hard rock and jazz with peerless virtuosity, yet Jeff Beck’s 70s classics, like Wired and Blow By Blow were group efforts, with Beck surrounded by similarly talented virtuosos capable of working with the funked-out fusion ideas he had at the time. Even though they were studio albums, Beck and company managed to capture the vitality of what they could really do. Those albums are rarely matched, and rarely even attempted, for whatever reason. That particular blend is just a hard thing to do. Yet, The Aristocrats are similarly capable and similarly minded, even though they bring with them everything that came to pass in the decades since. This is no mere follow-up to Wired, but Culture Clash is an album in the spirit of Wired, drawing on jazz, funk and hard rock with a similar ethos. With that in mind, rather than merely a group of virtuosos trying to show off chops in the studio, something different can be the result.

Perhaps this is why many such albums fail. Get some supergroup together, throw them into a studio, and they’ll try to one-up each other, yet without a live audience providing the critical component in real time, and the vitality in real time, it can fall flat. So many supergroups have failed, and so much of the time, it’s in the studio. Beck got the star players together in the studio with a coherent vision, and Culture Clash has the feel of carrying forward that vision, with the full range of what has come in the wake of Beck’s influence.

Done with the skill of Govan, Minnemann and Beller, that’s how to recapture the Wired/Blow By Blow magic, even without the live audience.

Realistically, this group’s live albums are better, but they can do great work in the studio as well, as long as they are composing it thoughtfully and willfully. Beck did it. There is no reason these cats can’t too.

I got this set sometime ago in 2016 when Real Gone was having a sale...the two discs individually were out of print, but this two-fer box was available, so thank goodness I snatched it up...now I just read that Dionne's whole Warner period is being anthologized in February, 2023 on Soulmusic/Cherry Red UK as a 6CD clamshell box called "Sure Thing: The Warner Bros Recordings 1972-1977", which explains why this set is out of print...Real Gone's license ran out, and all these 40 tracks are going to be included, appended to their proper albums, at least half of them as bonus tracks...

Until that exciting box comes out, this sumptuous set will whet your appetite...I have a friend who loves Dionne Warwick but had no idea about this middle 70s period between her rich, hits-laden, golden Scepter years in the 60s & the 80s comeback years on Arista, and he had bought this 4CD Cherry Red box called "Gotta Get A Good Thing Goin': The Music of Black Britain In The Sixties" and was highly disappointed in it because 1 of the discs was mostly, if not all, reggae, and he doesn't like most reggae like Bob Marley, just soul reggae like Jimmy Cliff, so he wants to sell it to me so as not to take a loss...I want that set but had expenses to take care of first...so the ideal solution is to trade this DW set for his box & neither of us takes a loss...only thing is the price...he paid $70 but it's now used...this DW set, I just saw one here for like $40 & was going to trade it but give him $30 to cover the difference, but it sold, it's now here & most places for basically $100, one place for like $75...I think it should be an even trade cuz the value is now going up, yet my copy is used but in good shape & his 4CD "Gotta Get" set is used...

Anyway, the music, how is it?? Stylistically, how does it fit in relation to her Scepter period & her Arista period?? Well, the music is superb, utterly sublime vocals & harmonies, musically rich, soulful & complex, kind of a hybrid of her Bacharach/David sophisto-pop & the Philly soul style of Thom Bell & MFSB, plus the songs feel closer to the Scepter years but with richer production than Scepter, while not as commercial as her Arista years...I wish her Arista years were as good as this (maybe just "Deja Vu" is) because the music here is of a much higher level, maybe TOO high for radio, which is why these records didn't get much airplay, which led to minimal sales...it's too bad that these cuts were basically buried, which led to people like my friend not knowing about her Warner years at all...hearing this stuff now, both the singles & unreleased tracks, it's SUCH a revelation, it sounds amazing, the songs fresh & not dated in the least...Corinne & Andy from Swing Out Sister, Lisa Stansfield & Rumer would eat these tracks up instantly, if they don't know em already, and likely they do...Rumer covered "Hasbrook Heights", which is from DW's first Warner album from 1972, which will be on the upcoming box...in the meantime, this little taster is amazing listening, and the booklets on both discs have well-written essays with excellent background information & photos from the period...

Amazing, just amazing stuff...

text.3963: I've read a lot of reviews from people talking about not knowing many of the songs and saying it's not the best compilation available. I won't disagree totally, however, it's not often that an artists # 1 hits collection is the best compilation. Hag' had many songs that just missed the number one spot and were far more popular. These include "Swinging Doors", "The Bottle Let me Down",  "I Take a lot of pride in what i am", "Ramblin' Fever", "If we're not back in love by monday", "I'm always on a mountain when i fall", "It's been a great afternoon", The way i am", "Misery and Gin", "Are the good times really over", "What am i gonna do (with the rest of my life"; not to mention some that were not even A-side singles like "Today I started loving you again", "Silver Wings", "The Farmer's Daughter", "Holding Things Together" to name a few. This Collection is unique because it contains a rare number one single "Bar Room Buddies", a duet with Clint Eastwood that was a 'tongue-in'cheek' buddy song recorded for the Bronco Billy Movie that somehow hit number one due to the popularity of both entertainers and a big movie. It was lost for many years, but it's nice to hear it now and finally have it on a CD format (albeit it's a rough record copy). Haggard had 38 Billboard number one's good enough for 3rd best all time behind George Strait and Conway Twitty. This CD is a one-of-a-kind and very solid. Yes, some songs are dated, some are even forgotten, but they are gems regardless.

text.3998: Great album and given the timeframe, bereft of digital samples.  All sounds are created using analog synths and percussion, bass guitar. Japan was as much Mick Karn as David Sylvian but you'd never know it given the overwhelming shadow cast by Sylvian - the consummate perfectionist and i might add, control freak. It is in fact Karn's creative bass lines, played purely on instinct, having VERY LITTLE MUSIC THEORY that make these songs work so well. Karn just had a hell of a good ear and a home grown technique that allowed him to craft clever and interesting bass lines (and I haven't even mentioned his exceptional woodwind work). Mick added his parts AFTER the synth, drums and vocals were laid down. Having no training on bass, and being raised in Cyprus and being exposed to middle eastern music, he was free to get (very) far away from traditional pop/rock root note bass work - and thank god for that. The songs are alive because of Karn, not the mournful, Ferry style vocals of Sylvan. Sylvan wrote 99% of the bands songs, but not a single note of Bass - that was all Mick.  This album showcases Mick's natural untrained talent and is well worth having in your collection.

Loved this album when it first came out and still do. I was buying CD's at the time when this came out. But I decided to get back into vinyls and this was one of my favorite bands from the 90's/00's, that I had to get it on Vinyl. It was a big album for No doubt and has some of their biggest hits on it such as "Just a Girl" (their first break out hit), "Spiderwebs", "Don't Speak", "Sunday Morning and few others. This is definitely the definitive No Doubt album to own. It's definitely a 10 star album. Unfortunately, the vinyl pressing is not! I was disappointed by the sound quality on this. I had to turn my speakers up all the way, and it was still too low. I suspect it's this 2017 pressing. And looking back at some of the reviews, I see a similar complaint is made for this pressing. Hopefully earlier pressings and/or future pressings will be better. I'm hardly an audiophile. Though, all my other Vinyls I've recently purchase doesn't require me to turn up my speakers all the way up to hear it. It definitely sounds very compressed and muffled at times. Specifically the first song on the album, it's almost hard to hear Gwen's vocals. The B-side sound a little better than A-side, but maybe I just got used to it sounding so low, that I imagined it got better.

All in all, Tragic Kingdom is definitely their best album to date. Though, they had some pretty incredible follow ups. Unfortunately, the Vinyl, at least this 2017 release is quite horrible sounding. I'd be interested if earlier pressings sounded better and if future pressings do as well.

Released in Michael Jackson’s teens, this Soul/R&B release of songs follows similar themes present in his precedent albums, though they are still as pleasant to listen to. Indeed, songs about Love or about childhood; topics precious to the singer, and many of them composed by legendary figures. Stevie Wonder, Oscar Hammerstein II, Michel Legrand, Stephen Schwartz, Sylvia Dee, Billy Page, and many others composers. Especially for the song Happy, which was used in the movie Lady Sings the Blues, and whose soundtrack was a Michel Legrand piece.

As always, hearing Michael singing is a very spectacular experience. For right at his young age, his singing skills were exceptional, capturing the precise tonality of the music notes in those ballads, but also the emotions those songs ask. Making everyone who listen to this album realize that Michael Jackson was a prodigal music performer; which everyone could observe in his concert presentations.

And with all these music streaming services like Spotify and Amazon Music services available, it is quite refreshing to see them broadcasting Michael Jackson’s earlier releases. Albums that I wish could have had the same success as Thriller, Off the Wall, Bad, and Invincible. Especially when the sound transfer on Streaming or MP3 is as excellent as its original vinyl release.

To conclude, I encourage all fans to discover this great piece of musicography from Michael Jackson. The one who would become the Immortal King of Pop.

text.4151: One of the first CDs I purchased when I began switching from vinyl was the Rock of Ages 2001 deluxe edition. Rock of Ages had been my introduction to the group when I bought it in 1978 and was one of my favorites. So, when I heard of the 2013 re-titled,re-sequenced, and remastered Live at the Academy of Music 1971, I was hesitant. Could the new sound and sequencing be enough to warrant purchasing it? Finally, when the new two CD set seemed to be falling out of print, I decided to take the plunge. After one listen, I can make the following statements. (1) Although I haven't made a comparison to the original Rock of Ages, I think the mixing changes have improved the listening experience on my inexpensive sound system. (2) The horns are pushed into the background so The Band is more audible. (3) Integrating the bonus tracks into the concert probably gives a better feel for what the audience heard in December1971. (4) No amount of tinkering will improve Bob Dylan's dismal encore performance. (5) I plan to hold on to my Rock of Ages CD because its first disc reproduces the original double LP I trasured for almost 25 years. (6) Since Robbie Robertson and Capitol are producing a series of 50th Anniversary Band sets, you may want to think twice about tracking this set down. I would not be at all surprised to see them put out all four nights of the  Rock of Ages concerts. Even with that caveat, I give this set about four and a half stars, down from five mostly because of Dylan's disappointing showing.

text.4185: I’ve listened to this disc more than a dozen times in the past few days, and it’s just not for me. Although I’ve loved Lugansky for nearly two decades, I just keep finding his discs duller and duller to me; having seen him live quite a few times over the years, his recital of Schubert was lifeless and listless. So I took a break from him for awhile, before buying the Schubert disc. Then when I finally got it, my opinion hadn’t changed. Basically since his Chopin/Grieg/Prokofiev concerti, he’s tried to be more like Koroliov or Volodos, and it just doesn’t work for me. Some of his discs I will hold in the highest regard forever, but for me he is currently in a lull. He’s growing away from who he was and has not yet fully become who he is or will be — something like that... This preludes disc is big heavy thick buttery gravy Rachmaninoff, but it never causes me to dream, and it never drives me wild, and I don’t really find any of them particularly exemplary or extraordinary. For these pieces, for now, I will continue to return to my beloved Weissenberg & Richter.

Just a beautiful swinging record with 3 great cuts in the -- surprisingly -- stride piano style: "Ain't Misbehavin'", "Honeysuckle Rose", "You Took Advantage of Me". text.4290: Cinderella The Mercury Years is quite an impressive package. In a 5 disc set you have all 4 studio albums beautifully remastered along with a bonus disc of live tracks and b-sides previously only available outside the US. The quality of the remastering of the individual albums was astounding. Too often, record labels will use the "digitally remastered" banner to describe a hastily packaged reissue that relies on volume enhancement in lieu of painstaking attention to detail. This was Not the case with Mercury Years. To begin with Night Songs, the first of the four albums has never sounded so crisp and clear. All 10 tracks are presented in a manner which surpasses the original 1986 release, with the guitars sounding richer and fuller, the bass more prominently featured in the mix and Tom Keifer's vocals sounding more sublime than ever before. Each subsequent album in the set is presented in a similar manner, playing to the strengths of the original LPs as opposed to simply turning up the volume across the board. This is particularly noteworthy on Heartbreak Station, where metallic riffs and thunderous percussion give way to steel guitars and arrangements found more often in bluegrass than hair metal. Along with extensive liner notes presented in a glossy booklet, these factors and more create a superlative experience for all Cinderella aficionados, both new and experienced.

text.4303:
Bombino has a sound. He has a sound, and he is sticking to it.

Desert blues is having a kind of musical moment, and that's a good thing, as far as I'm concerned. While Tinariwen get plenty of accolades, I have generally found myself more interested in slightly more southern sounds from Mali's Ali Farka Toure, who has heavily influenced most desert blues practioners, even if that isn't how he is generally classified himself. And here, it becomes important to tell the famous story about Ali Farka Toure. Toure's sound, which is more of a Malian griot sound translated onto guitar than what people today think of as desert blues, is closely related to desert blues, but distinct from it. Upon hearing him for the first time, a westerner once remarked that he sounded just like John Lee Hooker. His response: "who?"

Ali Farka Toure's music developed with minimal direct influence from western blues. West African music is just foundational to western blues, given how the blues developed. So, Ali Farka Toure and John Lee Hooker were kind of like the musical version of convergent evolution.

Then came Ali's son, Vieux, who is a musical genius in his own right. That next generation winds up sounding more western, simply because he takes in more global influences. So, you get a live album with guest spots from musicians like Derek Trucks, and my favorite, Jeff Lang. Vieux took in the influences from around the world, and created something different, but still rooted in Mali's sound, and still rooted in the influences that formed desert blues, like Bombino, Tinariwen, Group Inerane, Aziza Brahim, Songhoy Blues, and so on. But Vieux did it consciously, knowingly, purposely.

Desert blues, of course, is an evolving sound. If you listen to early Tinariwen, it sounds different from Bombino. You can hear them combining sounds the way one would expect from travels, not all of which were voluntary (euphemisms). And in that, you can hear the influence of the Malian griots, which is a better classification for Ali Farka Toure. His guitar style is now a big influence on the desert blues scene. As we get to the current generation, with Bombino, there is more cross-fertilization. As with Ali's son, Vieux, Bombino is taking in more influences. He is not quite as brash and bold with his recombinations as Songhoy Blues, but his guitar chops show an ear for alternative picking styles.

And with a sound built around that, he has established himself. There is now a Bombino sound. It's a good one. He'll branch out a bit, and by the time you get to Takamba on Deran, does anyone notice that this thing is built around a Sly Stone vamp? Go listen to Stand! Track 7 from Stand!

This is what Bombino is now doing.

When that guy asked Ali Farka Toure about John Lee Hooker, Ali really didn't have a clue. Bombino and Sly Stone? Bombino knows Sly Stone at this point. He's making the rounds at music festivals. I guarantee you he's heard that track. This is what's happening these days. It's pretty cool. Bombino's sound is a weird, westernization of desert blues.

There is horrible distortion on the first track starting at 1:35. At first I though something was wrong with my expensive audio system but then I checked the CD on a different system (and with headphones) and the distortion is actually part of the recording. I even ordered a second CD hoping, PRAYING that somehow it was the CD. NOPE, the second CD has exactly the same distortion. This tells me that the master recording used to create the CD's actually has this recording error "baked in". Right when Hannah's voice is reaching a wonderful, expressive high...."CRACKLE"!

It is incredibly distracting and horribly frustrating.

In technical, studio terms the vocal track was overloaded during the peaks. Somewhere in the audio chain either the mic., the mic. preamp or the mixing board channel was overloaded. This is when distortion is created. The goal of recording is to keep your signal from "going into the red" and being distorted during recording.
Somehow this basic skill was totally missed here and the distortion got recorded AND THEN MASTERED onto the final recording.

How this idiotic error got past numerous quality control steps ie: the audio engineer, the producer, the mastering engineer and finally the band themselves is completely beyond me. This was not a recording made in someones garage, with cheap equipment, on a laptop.
This is the ONLY CD I own of hundreds which actually has a recording error like this.

I have read other reviews which mention a similar problem on the vinyl version although no one has mentioned the exact timing point so I can only speak about the two CD's I paid for.

There is also a theory floating around that this distortion is somehow intentional. What?!
If that is the case, someone in the production chain (including possibly the band) has rocks in their head.

"Lets write and perform some beautiful music, but record it badly because that will somehow make it sound better..." What?!

Whomever is responsible for letting this otherwise fantastic music be trampled on by either careless OR intentional poor recording should be fired and never allowed to come near London Grammar's material again.
text.4308: Out of the many Nutracker recordings I have heard, this one is the LEAST rooted in Romantic traditions and stylings. Michael Tilson Thomas seems to have had little idea how to make this music "dance" - if I were to make an analogy - this recording is the awkward teenager at the prom, all elbows and knobby knees, waiting on the sidelines for an invitation to the floor, but then flailing about rather than gracefully gliding. Tempos and moments seem to lurch about suddenly, rushing at times, halting at others, but rarely feeling at ease with itself, and unsure how to relax into the lush orchestrations which Tchaikovsky excelled at. It's a nervous performance, which is odd, since Tilson Thomas was 41 years old when he made it - surely mature enough to understand the nuances of the grand Romantic tradition, but it never settles down - and it's not a good kind of nervous energy which can crackle and spark - this one stumbles when it should float. There's no feeling of mystery or longing in the performance, just uncertainty and an odd sense of disquietude.

text.4429: This eclectic selection of songs shows off everything Gary Allan does well. His raspy voice is one of the strongest in country music; he sings with a no nonsense conviction that is impossible to resist. Everyone who follows him knows about the tragedies in his life, and the album deals with the recovery from them. This is a concept album in that an arc runs through the songs he chose to record, some of which he co-wrote. But there's another arc running through the album: his singing career and how his personal life affected it. Gary has no problem getting the people he doesn't like told. And he's pretty hard on himself, never resorting to pity or false hope. That is why the tunnel out of which he emerges in the final song, Good as New, brought me to tears. Several songs did.

My only complaint would be the lack of credits on the artwork in the book. They do have a list of contributors on the back page but it doesn’t specify who took what photos. Hey, I’m a curious girl! I’m so glad I waited for the price (originally about $60) to come down. At $30 it’s a steal.

I love this opera. I love the music, the scenes, the characters. The structure of the music moving from tense bullying to a pretty chorus from distant festival goers and then moving into a sad, heartfelt prayer. It continues to strike all the right emotions and pacing throughout (this is without the dialog, which is often redundant or overwrought. You can read the play in the included booklet.)

The voice of the lead, Laine, is beautiful and clear. She acts with dramatic truth without losing any musicality. The Devil and Jacqueline are equally enjoyable, and their Act 2 duet where the devil forces his pawn to dance to exhaustion is one of the highlights of the score. Saida's large scenas and arias are so aching and beautiful. The orchestra plays expertly, bringing both lovely and funny moments to life. I particularly enjoy the long beauty contest, and sometimes skip straight to it. It runs through all the emotions from seduction, to innocence to vanity and then into witch burning. It is just really good music.

I would highly recommend this recording to anyone who was interested in obscure opera, fantasy opera or the works of Sir Arthur Sullivan. My only complaint is not about the recording, but about the plot, where the innocent maiden ends up with the awful prince and we are supposed to be happy about it. Very odd decision, and may have been part of why the original audience didn't quite go wild for it.

text.4521: I was pleasantly surprised when I listened to these recordings.  I was afraid that the sound might be too bright.  Not at all!  The piano Ashkenazy chose has a full, rich sound.  It is perfectly miked and the sound of the hall is just right.  Those who prefer more "historical" performances, though, might be a bit disappointed.  I am not one of them.  I think that whole concept is merely an intellectual exercise.  I mean, seriously, would they prefer to watch "I Love Lucy" on a fuzzy television from the 1950's because the picture would be more authentic?  I feel certain that Mozart would have wanted us to hear his music sound as beautiful as possible, and that is what we have in these recordings.  There is an anecdote about Beethoven where a violinist complained to him that his music was too awkward and difficult to play.  His response?  "Do you think I am thinking about your puny violin when I am listening to the music of the spheres?"  I already owned a copy of the Concerto No. 21 in C played by the great French pianist Robert Casadesus.  I studied that concerto in college and especially loved playing the cadenza that Casadesus wrote himself.  Nevertheless, even though Ashkenazy does not play that particular cadenza (he plays a cadenza that he wrote himself), his playing is equally expressive and his overall technique is more virtuosic than that of Casadesus.  Another reviewer made the complaint that there has to be a disc change in the middle of one of the concerti.  Yes, this is unfortunate, but it was a necessary evil in order to fit six piano concerti onto only two discs.  The break comes after the end of the first movement of the Concerto No. 25 in C.  For one thing, this is not one of the most famous concerti.  Secondly, the break comes at a good point.  After all, if the first movement of a piano concerto is well played, and the audience is not sophisticated, applause often occurs at this point.  This little break is no more distracting than that.  I thoroughly recommend these recordings to anyone who wants to hear these Mozart concerti recorded under the best possible conditions of performance and sound.

text.4613: These are very good solo piano works of Eschenbach, winner of the Clara Haskill Competition and considered one of the best pianists of the XXth. Century. Is good to have him represented in any Classical Music collection and because of that and because I like what he recorded, I got him. Have his excellent Mozart Piano Concerts (don't miss them!!) and his Beethoven ones, and with this set, think is good enough. We can hear him playing the Mendelssohn Songs Without Words, and think he does wonders with. Like specially the slow pieces. This is worthy to have, for these works rank among the best of this underrated composer. His Schubert is also a nice one. Like specially his sensitive Impromptus. His Schumann is also good. The Waldszenen, though not complete here, are among my favourite Schumann with the Carnaval, the Kreisleriana and the Chants de L'aube, to mention only some of my prefered ones. It's also always good to have the complete Schubert Impromptus too, for once again, find are perfectly performed in this Eschenbach recordings. It is a sober but colorful, sophisticated and still yes, quite objective pianism. Though would say the approach keeps a romantic line be it only because everything here are great pages of the Romantic catalogue. So,  this is not in the trend of a Radu Lupu, mean to just play the music as it is. Here you find a clear, delicate romantic touch. The cleaness and dexterity of Eschenbach show us quickly that we deal with a pianist in command of a great technique. You won't be disappointed if you buy this charming set.

text.4853:
Johann Heinrich Schmelzer (c. 1623-1680), violinist and composer to the Habsburg Imperial Court under Leopold I in Vienna, is one of my great personal favourites among baroque composers. His instrumental music, in the then-new 'stylus phantasticus' manner, is soulful, imaginative, graceful and full of emotion; and his violin writing, in the right hands, is irresistible.

For this recording, violinist David Irving and his Australian-based ensemble bring us the six violin sonatas of the 'Sonatae unarum fidium' collection of 1664. The players use period instruments and, in addition to Irving's beautiful-toned copy after Jacob Stainer, the basso continuo varies between combinations of theorbo, harp, organ, harpsichord and bass viola da gamba. This is the first time I had come across Irving, and I think he is a fabulous violinist who plays Schmelzer's beautiful works with virtuosity, panache, delicacy, feeling and impeccable baroque style. The other four players offer first-class support in these deeply-considered performances.

Typically each work consists of a multi-section, seemingly fluid but spiritually unified structure, whereas a couple of the works comprise theme and variations in a chaconne-style pattern. I especially love Sonatas II, IV and VI (tracks 2, 7 and 5 respectively) for their engaging melodies, compelling flow and subtle textures. We also get a solo organ Passacaglia by Schmelzer's contemporary Johann Caspar Kerll (track 4), which provides a change of texture to the programme but which I don't find quite as engaging as the Schmelzer works.

The recorded sound is outstanding, while David Irving's own booklet notes are interesting and extremely detailed on the composer, his music, the instruments used and performance considerations. There are a handful of excellent recordings of Schmelzer's music, including at least a couple of others of these same sonatas; but this one from Irving and his team is probably the finest rendition of Schmelzer's music I've heard, and that's saying a lot.

P.S. Please ignore the very detrimental review from a customer who appears regularly to write spoiler reviews for reasons best known to him/herself.

Most Van Halen fans scoff at any singer other than David Lee Roth (DLR). Indeed, the DLR era was the high water mark for the band. However, don't dismiss how well Eddie Van Halen, Alex Van Halen, and Michael Anthony performed while Sammy Hagar was the lead singer. A good friend and hardcore VH fan likened it to a sports team losing its star player, but the rest of the team upped their game to compensate. The net result was 4 really well balanced musicians.

This particular CD is one of the few commercial recordings of a live performance by VH in any era. The sound quality is superb. It is a great selection of songs, especially a few lesser known "Van Hagar" ones. Sammy does an admirable job of singing a few DLR era VH songs as well.

You won't be disappointed with this CD. And it may introduce you to a great era of VH for which you might not know all that well.

I only discovered Amy MacDonald a couple of months ago, but since then I have been listening to a lot of her music and I believe that this CD lives up to its "Best Of" listing. All her best songs are included. Highlights for me are "This Is the Life," "Slow It Down," "Mr. Rock and Roll," "Poison Prince," and "Pride." Long-time fans may have other songs that they would like to have seen included, but for me the selection is almost perfect. I think I would have preferred the studio version of "Let's Start a Band," but that is a minor quibble.

This CD does what many "Best of" collections do: it includes a couple of new songs. Normally I hate it when that is done, because I feel that the record company is pawning off on fans a couple of songs that they would like to see become hits. Sometimes the songs belong, frequently they don't. But in this case I have no complaints. The new songs belong here. "Woman of the World" is, at least in my opinion, one of the best songs that Amy has ever written.

So, if you're new to Amy MacDonald, this CD will serve as a perfect introduction to one of the best contemporary songwriters. And if you're a long-time fan, this is a chance to get her best songs on a single CD. A win for any fan of Amy's music.

This is an excellent collection from a musical standpoint, and clearly someone took the time to gather many photographs, album covers and 45 single covers. The interpretive essay is top notch. But this could have been so much more from a musicological standpoint. The recording dates and studios should have been listed. The first names of each composed could have been listed (even as an abbreviation) to permit further research. Perhaps most importantly, the musicians on each session should have been listed, if only to confirm that many of the tracks included key Wrecking Crew musicians (Hal Blaine and Joe Osborne come to mind, based upon what I am hearing). Perhaps most listeners are not interested, but I believe that Ms. Gentry's body of work is significant enough to deserve this level of documentation and care.

Comparing the sound for the albums, "Ode to Billie Joe" and "Touch Em with Love," between TGFCC and the "two-fers" from Raven-Australia, the sound is slightly improved in some respects, but a step back in others. Detail is a bit more but this sometimes is offset by a bit more edgy distortion. It also seems that additional reverb was added and perhaps a very slight bit of EQ (which can bring out the existing reverb), but it may be an artifact of using different masters. Which also brings me to another point: were the true master tapes for the original LPs used in the production of these CDs, or were safety copies used (or some other source(s)). This is important given the recent revelations of the fire at the backlot of Universal which destroyed masters, as well as original sessions tapes.

These points should not deter anyone from purchasing this box set, as this set will likely be all that will ever be released.

The sound quality is top-notch, as are the performances. Nez is in fine form here; it's mind blowing to realize he was still recovering from heart surgery during this tour!

If you're a fan of Nesmith, especially the First National Band material, you will love the performances here. So good. If you want a souvenir of one of the First National Band Redux concerts, though, you may be disappointed. Except for the story of his early days of performing at the Troubadour, all of the stories and between-song banter are cut. I was hoping to hear the story of when Mike met a couple who told him that "Joanne" was their first dance song at their wedding reception, or the famous Jif story about Red Rhodes. I'm guessing that 7a was looking to keep this recording to a length that would not necessitate a second disc.

Do you want to lower your blood pressure? I often do and this deeply relaxing CD of classic lullabies will help you daydream or stop thinking so much about stressful situations. This is perfect for listening while quietly reading.

Because this was recorded in a recital hall, it feels like you are listening to this live. On AKG headphones this is blissful. By choosing this CD you will learn more about composers from Ireland, Russia, Germany, France, Poland and America.

You will most likely instantly recognize some of these lullabies, like Frederic Chopin's Nocturne in D-flat major. But perhaps the most recognized lullaby is Johannes Brahms' cradle song which mothers everywhere know.

This CD can be used as a jumping off point to discover composers who contributed to the music of the nocturne genre.

The calming romantic violin playing of David Hays melds well with Peter Collin's precise, piano playing on a Steinway with an open heart. Together they work musical magic on the listener. If you love violin and piano you will enjoy this CD even more.

I would not say that this music was created to fall asleep to as there are still plenty of energetic moments like Szymanowski's Notturno. But this may be best for escaping the world's problems for a little over an hour. Everyone needs a break from worry, stress and anxiety which is in no short supply momentarily. This CD will make you feel you have all the patience in the world and can handle the next challenge life sends your way.

So listen to this beautiful album and enter the worlds of daydreams, visions and night dreams.

~The Rebecca Review

You have to appreciate older music to enjoy these discs, and realize that the recording equipment used in Bessie's day was primitive, to say the least. The original masters were poorly produced, to the point that her voice was misrepresented as either higher or deeper than in actuality.

There is a competing set of discs by Columbia that copies straight from these masters, meaning the audio quality is simply atrocious. The Columbia tracks are noisy and warbling. They packaging looks nice, and they feature pretty booklets.

The From recordings are remastered, with nearly all the artifacts removed and Bessie's pitch corrected. There is something of a hiss, but then there is only so much to be done when working from such humble beginnings. The Frog recordings are vastly superior to the Columbia. Bessie's other Frog discs can be purchased for reasonable prices directly from Frog Records, avoiding the price gouging so common on Amazon these days.

The Byrds were very daring when they entered this realm of the music world, a very bold step for the 60's. Rock radio wouldn't play it because it was too country, and country radio wouldn't play it because it wasn't "polished" enough. Still yet, it's an album that made it's mark in history.

I love this album and every listen only gets better. They really did push the envelope for a 60's rock band to go country. I for one understand the movement. I loved rock as a kid, but as I grew older the more appreciation and love I garnered for country music. Folk and country blend quite well, and the Byrds nailed it with this album. Very well executed.

Gram Parsons coming aboard really was a treat for both Gram and the Byrds. Together they made history by making an album that echoes through the years with heavy influence.

This album was magic, if you can stand back and appreciate it for what it is, you'll find just how great it really is. It changed rock and country music forever. I highly recommend this landmark of an album to every Byrd fan, and country fans alike.

Aside from having a band name that is either a groaner or the greatest band name ever, what can be said of Chicano Batman and Freedom Is Free? The group has a sound and aesthetic that manages a difficult trick, reaching back to the 1970s and the soul/R&B sounds of the era, without sounding like mere homage, and combining that with Latin sounds in ways that make the result feel familiar without having a single, obvious reference point. When listening to any group that so clearly reaches for an era, one often looks for a band as a reference point, or an artist, and 1970s R&B has so many. The production on Freedom Is Free, the instrumental work, all make clear the band’s fondness for the era. Yet this is not Stax, not Motown, not Muscle Shoals, nor any other clearly, specifically identifiable moment, and the movement back and forth between English and Spanish, while probably done in the era by someone, is not a thing that is a common reference point for those who think in terms of Stax, Motown, Muscle Shoals, and so forth. The vocal delivery becomes a point of departure, more psychedelic than R&B, indicating some of the alchemy behind the band’s concept. Does that work? Yes. This is all of a kind, if not by past construction, then in potential spirit, and that potential spirit is what the band summons. Call it psychedelic Latin R&B, which sounds like a genre that should have existed, and perhaps has in some quarters, and certainly does now. If nothing else, that means Chicano Batman has a thing, and once you hear it, you know the band. They are identifiable, not through virtuosity, visionary composition, nor those sparks that often mark such a band, but by bringing into existence something that one may have thought to have heard, but can’t quite place. Until now. Freedom Is Free has that feel. The feel of familiarity, like it’s an album sitting in a vinyl collection from the 1970s, as a somewhat forward-thinking oddity that came about when Shuggie Otis, Carlos Santana and let’s say the Swampers got together for a weird session. It almost sounds like a thing that happened, but it didn’t. If it did, it might have sounded like Freedom Is Free, and one can hear threads of Shuggie’s experimentalism from his post-blues period anyway, mixed with the Latin influence of maybe even Los Lobos’s experimental Kiko period. After all, once Shuggie moved away from the blues, he de-emphasized guitar anyway. And Kiko? Come on. Classic. However we think about it, it just feels right, like a project that you must have heard, over and over again. You didn’t, and you haven’t, but it has that feel.

Funny how music can work that way. Well done, but we can expect nothing less of the greatest detective from the border region.

text.5278: For some reason there is a portion of staunchly loved music from my (early/mid-seventies college days at LSU coming back home to roost in my mind recently. Specifically, the first four Feat albums, and certain of Ry Cooder’s early records. There is an unmistakable kinship between Ry (whom some reviewers here may recall played slide guitar on Feat’s first album due to a hand injury Lowell had experienced at the time) and Lowell George himself, who on these early records seems a Ry Cooder guitar/Captain Beefheart vocal hybrid. Of the Feat albums, Sailin Shoes especially is the one that separates itself. IMHP, Feat never again achieved the uninterrupted studio brilliance exhibited from start to finish on this particular recording. To the ears of the uninitiated, the record can seem deceptively sloppy and unrehearsed, but in reality is anything but, and therein lies it's brilliance. I’ve played in a band long enough now to realize just how tight the playing on this record truly is, and this is something that does not come without much rehearsal. The telepathic interplay between Estrada on bass and Hayward on drums is almost unprecedented in rock music, and when you listen to a song like ‘Apolitical Blues’ for instance, there is a wonderful spontaneity to Lowell’s vocal performance here. He suddenly converts his voice from Howlin’ Wolf mode, jumping to falsetto to sing the words ‘John Wayne’, and then immediately drops back down to Howlin' Wolf mode for ‘I just don’t wanna take no calls, NO CALLS'. Not an easy, nor studied vocal mannerism. As well, the linguistic gymnastics Lowell exhibits on Teenage Nervous Breakdown could tongue-tie the most astute jazz scat vocalist. Whew! The two Ry Cooder records of particular interest are Paradise and Lunch; and Chicken Skin Music. Roots music of the highest order! Too many great guitar licks to mention. Yet, he simplifies the language enough to make it somehow seem achievable. Man, I am digging these old records and listening to them with new ears. They have all endured the test of time.

First off you have to know I have been a die-hard Carpenters fan since the Close To You album was released in 1970 (I was 11 at the time). I grew up listening to them. I know most of their songs virtually note by note. I have every nuance of Karen's vocal intonations in my brain. The music was, and continues to be, sublime. Karen had the voice of an angel, while Richard was truly a creative genius. Any "faults" in the original recordings are PART of those recordings, and apart from simple remastering, any touch-ups are really unnecessary in my opinion. If ONE NOTE is changed from the originals, I believe I will often immediately detect it. THAT is how ingrained this music is in my head.
Now, the thing you have to understand about Richard Carpenter is that, in addition to being a musical genius, he is also an obsessive-compulsive when it comes to his and Karen's music. He has been tweaking, remastering, re-arranging, re-orchestrating and re-recording the Carpenters oeuvre since the songs were originally released. He will continue to do so as long as there is a breath left in him. He can't help himself. It's just who he is. It doesn't mean the world NEEDS it, it's just what he is compelled to do. One can only imagine what he might have done had Karen lived and he had put more of his energies into NEW music, instead of constantly trying to improve upon perfection.
This all being said, this album is a huge miss for the die-hard Carpenters fan. So many wrong choices. So many mis-inserted notes. It's hard to know how to even cover it all. I'll just choose the one that was probably the biggest cause to wince on my part....the insertion of the trumpet in the epic musical outro of Goodbye To Love...….it's just.....words fail me: it's really THAT bad. If you are a huge fan, I defy you to listen and NOT be horrified. All in all, he has taken the Carpenters sound into a whole other level of "elevator" music. (An area they were unfortunately starting to slip into with the later albums.) It's not terrible music, mind you, it's just all SO unnecessary! If you are not terribly familiar with the Carpenters sound, I suppose you will find this all pleasant enough. But for us life-long devotees, you are warned to stay away. I am so unnerved by it all that I don't even plan on keeping it in my collection of Carpenters CD's. I plan on donating it to the local library.

I feel that Coraline was Henry Sellick's brilliant response to the cringe factory that is Tim Burton's fanbase and legacy. I'll go into it, but basically (TL;DR) by going with Bruno Coulais as a composer, and using a score of french children singing gibberish (instead of the washed-up singer of Oingo Boingo) Henry Sellick confidently proves he can organize a better team, direct a better film, and treat Burton's fans to a far better experience than Burton ever has, or will in the director's seat. This score alone makes it apparent that Coraline is a film which easily out-Burtons any Tim Burton film.

"BuT whAt abOut TIm BurtOn's ThE NiGhtmAre BefOre ChristmAs? DidN't yOu likE It??"

Tim Burton's The Nightmare Before Christmas was directed by Henry Sellick.
Burton did little more than draw the characters up in his journal between napping at his desk and pulling his own teeth out with plyers while he was SUPPOSED to be helping Disney with The Fox and the Hound movie. (If you are wondering how Disney stole Nightmare from Touchstone, that's how.)

Henry Sellick, with The Nightmare Before Christmas, gave us something fantastic and special which enriched our collective childhoodnd in the '90s.

And how did we thank him?

By worshipping and deifying the first impish poorly groomed faux-introvert who was willing to take all the credit for it.

Since then, Burton has tried time and time again to insist to all of us that he actually is the dark, broody little artist you all hoped he'd be. The man is a charlatan at worst, and a fool at best, succeeding only once in his directing career with Corpse Bride (which is admittedly a masterpiece).

So Burton Finally makes his Corpse Bride, and his fans finally get what they paid for. A dark, romantic, heavily stylized piece of real art with victorian-influenced musical numbers! Now at this point we were feeling all content and sure that old Timmy-boy was indeed the broody little artist we pegged him for, and waited eagerly to see if he'd continue to impress us...which he would not.

And how does Sellick respond?
By making an intensely more intricate and interactive stop-motion set, by inventing intensely more likeable and relatable characters (an area where the book Coraline fell short), by conceiving a chillingly immersive universe for the events of the book to unfold in, and most importantly of all, putting Bruno Coulais on the payroll.

Sellick knew that, despite all of this, none of us would be jumping off of the Tim Burton Express (TM,CC,SMFH) any time soon for some Bloke named Henry Sellick whom we hadn't ever seen on the Disney channel or MTV even ONCE.
Sellick Knew you wouldn't give him a chance, which is why the Trailer sold it to you as being "From the director of Tim Burton's The Nightmare Before Christmas"

Henry Sellick is too good for us, and we don't deserve or appreciate him.

Everything since out of Burton has been contrived trash which seems geared only to keep the breathing-impaired and sweatstained returning to Hot Topic perpetually for yet another black totebag filled to the brim with cheaply made make-up and graphic tees.

If you think I am being overly critical or unfair, please listen to the Coraline film score. When you are through with it put on any one of Danny Elfman's OOM-PAH, OOM-PAH filmscores from any of Tim Burton's Hacky Films.
The latter will sound childish and condescending, I promise.

Henry Sellick & Bruno Coulais -
5 Stars, 10/10
'I bet I could Improve it, too! And that's exactly what I'll do! EUREKA!'

Tim Burton & the singer of Oingo Boingo -
3 stars. 6.5/10 (excluding Nightmare)
'Eez nice, but not so much amazing.'

P.s. also There May or May Not Be Giants...and who doesn't like those fellas?

JOURNEY-GREATEST HITS: From their jazz-prog beginnings featuring two ex-SANTANA members, guitarist NEAL SCHON and singer/keyboardist GREGG ROLLIE, on through their arena rock hey day helmed by high pitched belter STEVE PERRY, JOURNEY has remained inexplicably popular. A long string of slickly crafted singles, notably WHEEL IN THE SKY, ANY WAY YOU WANT IT and DON'T STOP BELIEVIN' are trotted out for GREATEST HITS. Although they could pump out a bloozey thumper like LOVIN', TOUCHIN', SQUEEZIN' or the harder edged SEPERATE WAYS, this quintet has always been defined by their true meal ticket, namely arena rock power ballads (LIGHTS, OPEN ARMS, FAITHFULLY). GH racks up sixteen radio ready biggies, a crash course in JOURNEY's highly commercial, multi-layered pop bombast.

RATING: FOUR HIGH NOTES

I'm passionate about piano concerti but Beethoven only wrote 5 of them; so the Choral Fantasy, with its extensive piano writing melded with orchestra and chorus, appeals especially to me. (OK, some count the transcribed Violin Concerto as a sixth.) I will defer to other reviewers as to the liturgical pieces (I liked them but won't claim much insight about them), but the Choral Fantasy is a winner. The energy, passion, and drama that Bernstein brought to his conducting (at least during that phase of his career) sweeps me along, and Serkin plays to match.

I suppose I could praise Sony's remastering "qui tollis peccate Columbia" but it doesn't entirely take away the sins of Columbia's subpar sound (which was truly a travesty, given how much better sound certain rivals of theirs were achieving). Still, Sony improves the recording to a level more than acceptable to me, if not to the audiophile. It's well worth enduring the cloying packaging bowing and scraping before His Royal Tackiness, to get the best sound in these great performances. If you ignore that deference to Carolus Non Magnus, even the CD booklet is pretty good.

Another run to remaster the first four albums. This time they come in a little box with digipacks for each separate album. Cherry Red did the last issues in nice plastic double CDs with great packaging, and here they go for a bit of a different look.

The sound seems to be better and less messed with than the last releases. Full dynamic range not much noise reduction that I can hear. I think there seems to be a better sense of clarity in the audio. That being said if you are not paying attention their last remasters were probably not too bad just a bit different.

These seem about as faithful as you will find out there. With the original masters of these albums unknown as to their use in remasterings, I am totally happy with this package. I have Zeit in just about every incarnation it has been mastered in including the double CD from the 80s. I would say this is about as good as you can hope it to sound. text.5503:
Distant Shores (1966) is the fifth studio album by the British Invasion duo, Chad & Jeremy. It was the immediate precursor to their psychedelic records.

Fun Fact! The album includes the first recording of Paul Simon's Homeward Bound, predating even Simon & Garfunkel's version!

Fun Fact! The title track was composed by their young bassist, James William Guercio, who went on to score up a long list of musical credits, most notably with Chicago.

With this album, Chad & Jeremy were finally able to craft their recordings and work with a producer with whom they enjoyed a strong rapport, Larry Marks. The result is splendid! Rich orchestrations, a dash of raga, and a harpsichord augment their gentle folk-rock, a folk-rock style that owed as much to The Brothers Four as to The Byrds and The Beatles–and always allowed room for a Broadway ballad and a bit of Brit wit. With this blend, they were able to appeal to young moderns and the occasional parent as well as the teenybopper brigade.

If Of Cabbages and Kings is Chad & Jeremy's Sgt Pepper, Distant Shores is their Rubber Soul.

Another distinguished archival job by Sundazed–complete with a heaping helping of rarities, bringing the original 11 tracks to a rather astounding 24! Bravo and cheerio!
text.5504:
This review is for "Super Black Market Clash" from THE ONLY BAND THAT MATTERS!

"Black Market Clash" was orginally released as a 10" vinyl EP in 1980. "Super Black Market Clash" is amalgamation of that EP plus the RARE 1979 U.K. EP "The Cost of Living" & B-side singles from the first 2 Clash LPs & reggae DUB versions of singles from "Sandinista!" & B-side singles from "Combat Rock."

What's MISSING from "Super BMC" is the single "Armagideon Time" from the original BMC EP. My FAVORITE Clash song of ALL TIME! So disappointing. The reggae dub version "Justice Tonight/Kick It Over" of that song from the BMC EP is included, which was originally released in 1979 as the B-side for the 12" single of "London Calling." Confused yet?

The other GLARING OMISSION from the original BMC EP is "Bank Robber." The reggae dub version is included. But, it's still puzzling. Why exclude the singles of these 2 songs but include the dub versions? CD time contraints. This should have been expanded into a 2 CD collection!

Also MISSING is "Capital Radio One" from the original BMC EP.

What's GREAT about this collection is the addition of the B-side singles from the first 2 albums, B-side dub versions & "Groovy Times," "Gates Of The West" & "Capital Radio Two" (extended version of "Capital Radio One") from "The Cost Of Living" EP. All CLASSIC Clash tracks! It also includes "Radio Clash" the B-side single from "This Is Radio Clash" which was HUGE in the clubs & on alternative rock stations back in the day. I owned the original 12" vinyl single with multiple dance remixes. (Needle drop over & over on that single back in the day. "Rewind Selector!") If they had expanded this collection onto 2 discs, the original PLUS the remixes could have been included too! With 2 discs they could have added songs that were excluded from the U.S. version of The Clash's first album. Missed opportunity!

As it stands, even with the omissions, this is still A MUST OWN addition to any CLASH fan's collection. And it still deserves 5 Stars!

(Now I have to buy "The Clash Hits Back" just get to "Armagideon Time" & "Bank Robber" & "This Is Radio Clash" on CD because MP3s are evil. Oh well. It's only filthy lucre.)
