text.5599:
Without going all would be Record Critic full of fancy verbiage but short on facts, allow me to introduce you to one of the greatest records in History.

Forget the relentless and lazy conversations about hairstyles that inevitably provide the bulk of "Reviews" for this band. 99.9% of which is recycled nonsense that isn't even remotely accurate and certainly not pertinent. This was a band of real, talented musicians with an incredible knack for fearless innovation and an uncanny ability to produce a gorgeous and unique sound that was far greater than the sum of it's parts. Not the first to blend cutting edge guitar tones and synths by any stretch, but the first to do it in such a lushly organic marriage between them. Despite the endless references to Sci-Fi themes and Space Aliens that mostly were exhausted by the time this record was made, this band had great depth. Mike Score was just as comfortable and just as effective writing gut wrenching, thought provoking or even hauntingly beautiful lyrics as he was with songs about flying saucers and Skynet (see "Man Made" from the previous album) fully two years before The Terminator made us fear the future.

Paul Reynolds is arguably the most criminally overlooked guitarist of the decade. His sound and style inspired many future legends in their own right, and his influence is still heard regularly to this day. He wasn't flashy or needlessly over indulgent. He played for the song... always, and with the perfect touch.

Frank Maudsley crafted some insidiously infectious and remarkable bass lines during his tenure as Seagull. Much like guitarist Paul, he knew when less was more, and how to play for the song. He was tireless in his pursuit of growth as a musician, and his ascension to being among the very best of the era was wondering to witness with each new release showing off his latest jump in ability... which was already mighty from the very beginning. "What am I Supposed to do?" came out of nowhere and slapped Seagulls fans upside the head with it's powerful and urgent funk assault. It's a clinic on how to steal the show without stepping on the song.

Ali Score was yet again a master of understatement and restraint as a drummer. Solid as a rock, powerful, always tasteful. Adept at blending the tried and true acoustic drums of standard Rock with the electronic drums sweeping the scene at the time, but again with subtlety and restraint that is still refreshing nearly four decades on. He was also comfortable and capable when called upon to occasionally let a drum machine do the heavy lifting while providing color and more tasteful fills.

Yes, this band was legit. This record stands out as the most "electronic", but is by no means to be confused as "Synthpop". Such a lazy descriptor never suited this band. Thanks to the success of the previous record, a bigger budget, newer and more capable toys, and the great fortune of being able to record with the legendary Mr. Conny Plank in his studio full of magic and history... this record takes full advantage of their incredibly good fortune indeed. Sonically breathtaking with it's groundbreaking flood of new and interesting sounds yet still very familiar, "Listen" requires you do just that. Listen.

From the stark first drum hit of opening track "Wishing", this record establishes itself with authority. The song then builds into a warm and beautiful adventure layered with lush synths and guitars that seamlessly interplay throughout while a deceptively steady rhythm section anchors it perfectly. The absolutely gorgeous and haunting EBow guitar outro is about as great as it gets in popular music. Magical.

"Nightmares" then changes the mood dramatically as perhaps the greatest anti-song ever. What is an anti-song? THIS is. All structure and pretense are tossed out in favor of a ghostly melody made not from typical chords or notes, but instead built with multiple layers of harmonics soaked in Chorus, delay and vibrato effects on both guitars AND bass. The minimalist drum beat just enough to propel the whole thing forward. A song that shouldn't work, but does... and does it ever! Mike Score's storytelling is the perfect companion to this atmospheric phenomenon. The 12" Extended Version included later on this release is even better, mainly for the inclusion of a longer center break with yet another Paul Reynolds EBow masterpiece.

"Tranfer Affection" wears it's heart on it's sleeve. Borrowing a bit of the melodic approach from "Nightmares", it builds from a soft, almost anemic TR-606 drumtatix drum machine intro into an evolving cascade of emotions. Both subtle and bold without too much of either.

"What am I Supposed to do?" as mentioned comes out swinging with Frank's slap bass extravaganza before unapologetically taking a hard turn towards disco. Clever layers of synths abound, and even Paul Reynolds got in on the act with his Roland Guitar Synthesizer. This song is as addictive as any drug but with no bad side effects. Pure listening joy.

"The Fall" is a dark, brooding journey into oblivion with a sparse arrangement fueled by a masterful bassline, heavily effected yet minimal drums, soft and sublime keys, and a non-stop EBow guitar line that drips with emotion throughout. Possibly the greatest "EBow song" ever recorded. Brilliant.

"Electrics" are everywhere! So too is this song. It bounces along with fiercely upbeat energy and more licks than it takes to get to the center of a Tootsie Pop. Positive proof this band could throw heavyweight punches with very best.

"The Traveler" is a two guitar balancing act performed deftly by Mike Score and Paul Reynolds. A driven rocker with a great blend of classic rock sensibilities and modern rock flavor. Do not skip it, it's a gem.

"2:30" is 59 seconds of prep time for the avalanche about to bowl you over... the border.

"Over the Border" might be their best work. Period. One could make such a case easily enough. It's an intelligent yet remarkably eager rocker that tells a powerful story while the instrumentation paints meticulously beautiful backdrops that are ushered forward with a fierce bass hook and a 1-2 combo punch of live and programmed drums. Portamento sweeps sore into the stratosphere before diving under the ice only to rise again. Syncopated arpeggios signal each new chapter in this epic adventure.

"(It's not me) Talking" re-recorded for their sophomore album and brilliantly so. This already great tune is given it's proper wings to fly higher than ever. From the almost scary sounding yet brief intro to the chaotic clanging metal outro and every where in between, this is quintessential Seagulls on their absolute A-Game. Raucous, urgent, unflinching.

"Quicksand" may as well be just that, because once you hear it, it will never let you go. Not only does this song rock harder than any head banger ever dared, but it's a sonic sledgehammer hammer that proves beyond any doubt that the way guitars were going to sound forever thereafter was how Paul Reynolds wanted them to sound. I defy any 80s "Metal" lover to listen to this song and not fall in love. However, this song isn't metal. It's much smarter, much darker, and infinitely more interesting than that.

"Rosenmontag" and "The Last Flight of Yuri Gagarin" are again familiar for those who bought this album on cassette way back when. Both instrumentals are less full band compositions and more Mike Score experimental pieces that really make full use of the technology available. The presence of Conny Plank is obvious throughout both songs as are the prohibitively expensive toys that the likes of Depeche Mode and others were yet to get their hands on. Both very forward looking in their construction and sound, they are testaments to Mike's innovation and imagination. Not everyone's cup of tea, but fantastic experiences for fans to get lost in.

This is a must have CD for all New Wavers and Flock faithful alike. "Listen" never got a proper CD release in America and the Beehive UK release from the 90s may as well be an actual unicorn. If you don't already own one, you never will. Both the remastering and track listing are far superior to the 2004 Superfecta CD release which is also quite rare itself. The packaging and inner sleeve content is also significantly better. Well worth the cost at three times the price.

Don't wait. Get yours now.

text.5662:
chief among the things i'll never understand is why comedy gets so much less respect than drama. insiders are always telling us how much more difficult comedy is. established comedy players always prove up to the "challenge" of a dramatic role, but it's anything but such a guarantee the other way around. consider Leslie Neilsen, who was pushing 60 when Airplane! catapulted him from one of those vaguely-familiar-face dramatic actors to full-fledged household-name comedy superstar. whereas when Jerry Lewis plays a dramatic part on Law & Order, it came and went with little more than shrug. it was like a commercial airplane pilot riding a bicycle, or a renown neurosurgeon giving a tetanus shot.
the difference: drama is a process, whereas comedy is a gift. in other words, drama can be taught, can be given to you, whereas comedy, well, you pretty much either got it or you ain't, period!
it applies to musicians as well, nowhere more exemplified than in Ray Stevens. despite his stature as a musical humorist on par with "Weird Al" Yankovic or Tom Lehrer, he's often wasted his gifts on less exceptional "strait" fair, and actually netted himself some misplaced acclaim for, most obviously, that sappy "We Are The World" of the '70s, "Everything Is Beautiful."
which is where this cd comes in. this long-overdue compilation is for the discerning listener who relishes the inspired lunacy of "Gitarzan,""Ahab The Arab," and "The Streak"...but can live without the mushy "Misty," for instance, or the sanctimonious "Turn Your Radio On,"
(for one thing, the three essentials are all Stevens originals, whereas the other two are covers.)
but alas, there was a slight lapse in judgement. they didn't dare overlook the three aforementioned essentials, that would be tantamount to omitting, say, "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "We Will Rock You" from Queen's greatest hits. for the most part, though, it focuses on a couple years in the mid-90s. there are certainly gems therein of social commentary ("Tabloid News," "Teenage Mutant Kung Fu Chickens") as well as nitpicky minutiae ("The Motel Song," "Where Do My Socks Go?"). but consider, that's a pretty narrow sliver of a career spanning at least six decades.
so on the whole it's a fun compilation, but we need a Volume 2, a "20 More Comedy Hits" to accommodate, for instance, "Along Came Jones," "Can He Love You Have As Much As I?," and "The Ballad Of The Blue Cyclone."
so just who do i speak to about getting that ball rolling?

My love affair with Chaka began in 1975. Don't get me wrong. I am a 66 year old black man who has been hopelessly in love with the same man for 35 years and counting. I was a student at the University of Tennessee in the fall of 1975. Rufus performed at the student union. A young lady I was dating at the time & I got sro spaces in front of 2 massive speakers. I probably have permanent hearing loss from that show. I knew I was witnessing the birth of a supernova one Chaka Khan.
The 70's had my favorite cousin & I attending 2 Chaka Khan concerts in my hometown of Louisville Kentucky. This cousin passed away a couple of years ago and I dearly miss her. I had really built up this new talent to my cousin. Unfortunately, this was the time when Chaka was dealing with her demons. She frequently pushed the microphone out to the audience for them to sing. After 2 trys, I thought I was done with her.
But she managed to redeem herself to me. With a string of megahits, I, once again, became a megafan. She can do it all. In the mood to dance, put on Chaka. In the mood for romance, put on Chaka. She is your one stop shop for incredible music. The essential is a great Chaka collection. Long live the Queen!

I just discovered and finished listening to what has to be one of the greatest musical tributes and innovations I have ever heard. And I do not say that flippantly or without knowledge of the subject of which I speak- at risk of sounding patronizing or arrogant, I studied music performance and composition at some of the finest music schools in the world (including The Juilliard School).

And I am quite serious when I say: this album is one of the most clever and well-done musical undertakings I have ever listened to. The use of the original tunes as the "structure" for the holiday songs is brilliant- because while it's obvious this is what is being done, it's done in a way that seamlessly blends the sound and harmonic basis of the foundations with the harmonic progressions and lyrics of the carols and Christmas favorites.

That's all to say: neither song (the Beatles classics and the holiday tunes) are subverted in a way that feels like a betrayal or perversion of its original self. Instead, on every track, the two are melded flawlessly- giving the listener the impression of it truly being what The Beatles themselves might have done if asked to record a "traditional" holiday album.

Bravo to EVERYONE involved in this artistic undertaking. While I am a diehard Beatles fan (and a growing fan of the Fab Four), I can say, objectively, without bias, and with the knowledge to make such a proclamation, that I am absolutely thrilled by this album and look forward to it being a regular part of our yearly winter celebrations.

Cheers, lads. Thank you- and happy holidays!

text.5837:
Bluegrass comes in many varieties. Some is startlingly virtuosic. Some is just plain, comfort music. Yonder, despite its participants, falls into the latter category. It is worth revisiting once in a while, and any time one does, it will provide comfort. It is strange, but that’s what it is.

Jerry Douglas is, without a doubt, the most accomplished dobro player in the history of the instrument. Even Jimi Hendrix is an insufficient comparison, given the development of the field. Perhaps Art Tatum is the only real comparison for Jerry Douglas and the shadow he casts over his instrument. And Peter Rowan? His voice is not that of a classically trained, or jazz trained virtuoso, but it has a kind of unique and otherworldly beauty that simply cannot be appreciated except on its own terms. If there is a living exemplar of the high, lonesome sound, it is Rowan. So put them together, and in a genre known for showboating, they’ll showboat, right? Wrong. They do the opposite. They lounge back, and play to the sweet spot of back porch country, with just the right amount of virtuosity to remind you of who they are, but never enough to overwhelm the purpose, which is nothing more and nothing less than to put a simple smile on the face of those who appreciate the broad category of stuff called “folk” music.

That means one can come to Yonder with the wrong mindset and miss the point. Look for Flux’s best dobro runs, and be both misled and disappointed by one’s own expectations. Look for Rowan to let the pipes show, and the same holds. This is back porch music, played as if at a house concert, if one just happened to be so fortunate as to live in a neighborhood with great virtuosos, but when they just felt like playin’ some tunes rather than impressing anyone.

In that, it feels as though Jerry and Peter made this album for themselves. It feels intimate, and enjoyable for that very reason. Will it stand as the greatest bluegrass album ever made? No, but it doesn’t need to. It is unassailably good, as long as one understands its purpose.

text.5861:
More than a decade removed from the genre they helped to proliferate, Murder By Death has managed to make a career out of their one-time novel approach of channeling indie-folk through an American(a)-gothic lens. The band’s latest album (and 8th overall) The Other Shore finds singer/songwriter Adam Turla and Co. offering a slightly different take on their trademark sound.

Opening with an ode to wanderlust, “Alas” is essentially everything you’ve come to expect from Murder By Death in a five-minute package. With thundering drums, a sublime cello-solo, and Turla’s ever-reliable rasp, the band is clearly in fine form right from the start. Meanwhile, the upbeat two-step “Chasing Ghosts” and the tom-driven “True Dark” provide the album with a riveting opening salvo.

From there, The Other Shore settles into somewhat familiar territory, with Turla guiding his cohorts through mid-tempo romps (“Stone”, “Space”, “Bloom”), and tender balladeering (“Travelin’ Far”, “Only Time”) all the while exploring the plight of two lost souls in a not-so-distant dystopian future. It’s heavy-handed stuff for sure, but hardly the first time Turla has tackled a longwinded, densely layered narrative.

The saving grace here is that unlike many of their previous releases, the eleven songs that comprise The Other Shore work just fine when removed from the context of the larger story. Diehard fans that choose to dig deeper will certainly be rewarded, but passive listeners will immediately find enjoyment with the record’s accessibility. The melodic juggernaut “I Have Arrived” might be the best Grateful Dead song that band never wrote, while the string-driven “New Old City” is one of the most satisfyingly sparse arrangements in the Murder By Death repertoire.

While the band has always excelled at finding a way to balance the bevy of folk instruments they employ with their traditional ‘guitar, bass & drums’ setup, The Other Shore also benefits from one of the best production-jobs in their catalog. Sarah Balliet’s cello cuts through like a hot knife through butter, no longer battling with the band’s rhythm section (drummer Dagan Thogerson, bassist Tyler Morse) in the way she did on previous releases. And for his part, Tulla’s voice soars above the rewardingly dense, but never cluttered mix.

While the record is sure to elicit differing opinions from the masses (fans may loathe the ‘departure’ while there is little here that will bend the ear of an already-decided critic), for their part, the band sounds like they are having a blast (and maybe that’s all that really matters?). Both decidedly dynamic and meticulously concise, with The Other Shore, Murder By Death has finally managed to unravel the secret of ‘less is more’.

Roger Waters’ dystopian lyrics loosely based on George Orwell's book “Animal Farm”, describing the various social classes through three animals: Predatory dogs, Despotic pigs who hire the dogs to maintain their control, and the sheep who mindlessly follow the pigs rule.

There are only 5 tracks on the album but the main three songs total almost 40 minutes with Dogs coming in just over 17 minutes.

This is definitely required for all Pink Floyd fans.
text.6052: 1976 was a very good year for rock music. Not quite the heyday of the early part of the decade but even with the onset of disco and punk influences there were some great classic rock albums released that year that still hold up well today. Agents of Fortune by the Blue Oyster Cult is a great example of a rock album that is known primarily for the single Don't Fear the Reaper but wont make to most lists of greatest albums of 1976. This is a shame as it really has ten very good and sometimes great (add E.T.I. and Morning Final) songs that often sound like they are all from different bands altogether. BOC has the unique distinction of having each band member serve as a lead vocals on at least one track. Add to this the song writing credits are different for each song and you're gonna get variety. Some people might call it lack of continuity but it makes for an interesting set of songs. Don't Fear for example doesn't even sound much like any of the other tracks but as a whole the album stands up well and cements BOC as one of the 70's very good rock bands that remain largely underappreciated outside of those who know this album to be a rock classic.

text.6094:
Next to The Beatles, The Hollies are probably my favorite British group to come out of the '60s. They were among the Beatles' strongest competitors, even far outliving that indescribably popular and successful (in the U.K. and the U.S.) but relatively short-lived band, although they didn't get to be anywhere near as big as the Fab Four, at least not where the Star-Spangled Banner flies. While the group did have several U.S. hits, their success here was sadly small compared to their U.K. success.
Like most of the truly decent Hollies collections that have been put out (that I know of, anyway), this CD is an import release; it comes from the U.K., and I think most of the other import ones do as well.
This compilation was first released in the U.K. in July '78, and this CD reissue came out, I believe, a decade later to the month (if not the day). Over 40 years after its original release (and over 30 years after this reissue was released), this is STILL a great collection in my opinion. I'd say it's one of the best single-CD Hollies comps that I know of (not to mention one of the best single-vinyl ones). It contains 20 tracks, all in stereo, and plays for a full hour.
Of course, since this was (and is) a U.K. compilation, its aim is (at least I presume) to collect the U.K. hits, although most of their U.S. hits also appear here, as some of these songs were hits in both places. In fact, one of the tracks here, "Long Cool Woman In A Black Dress," was a much bigger hit in the U.S. than in the U.K.! (It reached #32 over there but made it all the way to #2 here!) One of the other tracks, "He Ain't Heavy, He's My Brother," was released as a single twice in the U.K. (once in '69 and again almost 20 years later); it hit high there each time, reaching #3 the first time but going #1 the second time (which was, I think, after this CD came out), becoming the Hollies' second and (as far as I know) last chart-topper there! (The first one was "I'm Alive," which landed at that spot in '65.) They didn't score any #1s in the U.S. as far as I know.
It's interesting to note that the recording here of "Yes I Will" is an earlier, longer take than the hit (in the U.K.)version; it was first released, by mistake, on the Hollies Greatest compilation (in the U.K.) in '68. (There was a skimpier, like-titled U.S. comp in '80.) This song was also recorded, in a more "sentimental"-sounding fashion, by The Monkees (under the title "I'll Be True To You") with a vocal by, of course, Monkees heartthrob Davy Jones.
The U.K. and U.S. Top 40s that don't appear here in any form include "Just Like Me" (the first Hollies single), "Searchin'," "King Midas In Reverse" (the oddest exclusion, in my opinion), "If I Needed Someone" (their rather bland version of the Beatles song), "Hey Willy," "The Day That Curly Billy Shot Down Crazy Sam McGee," and "The Baby" (not to mention the "Holliedaze" medley) among the U.K. ones, with "Pay You Back With Interest," "Long Dark Road," and "Stop In The Name Of Love" being the U.S. ones. Not all Hollies tracks that were singles in one place were singles in the other, although there weren't many tracks that appeared on singles in the U.S. but not in the U.K.
This is, I think, a VERY fine collection (even if it does use the wrong recording of one song!); however, while it's longer and more comprehensive than most of the domestic Hollies comps than I know of, it isn't as much so as the '93 U.K. comp The Air That I Breathe, which I would say is the best of the best of the single-CD Hollies collections I've seen (or heard), making this one a close runner-up. Air That I Breathe includes all of the songs that appear here (with the "correct" version of "Yes I Will") as well as most of the other U.K. hits I mentioned, along with a "new" (at the time) recording, "The Woman I Love." ("Stay" is in mono on it, though; the rest are in stereo, with "Look Through Any Window" in a different and, I think, better mix.) But if you want a single-CD comp that isn't too short but isn't as long as that one, this one is a great one to get, in my opinion. If you're the audiophile type, the sound on this CD and on that other one might not work for you. But if your ears aren't hard to please, I think you'd enjoy either one.
It's a shame that there have been so few really good domestic Hollies collections on CD or even vinyl (at least that I know of); reissues of the group's albums (the U.K. versions or even the U.S. ones) also seem to be almost non-existent here in the good old U.S. of A. The group really deserves to be treated much better here than they have been! If they had hit as BIG and HARD here as the Beatles did, you can bet they wouldn't be so criminally neglected!

Viewed with hindsight's benefit, "Jazz: Red Hot and Cool" is an important transitional album in the Brubeck Quartet's astonishingly prolific output, recorded in 1955 at New York's Basin Street nightclub. Although the band—Brubeck at the piano, Paul Desmond on alto sax, bassist Bob Bates, and Joe Dodge on drums—had refined their quartet's sound over five years, this, if memory serves me, was the first of Brubeck's albums for Columbia, his mainstay label throughout the '60s.

This is a rock-solid album of mostly jazz standards, done with Brubeck Quartet's special touch. The originals, composed by Brubeck, are "Closing Time Blues" and "The Duke," first recorded here, in a briefer, more easygoing version than that which would become canonical. The Quartet is tight as drum, so to speak, with each performer given a chance to shine. In "Sometimes I'm Happy" Bates goes to town with a terrific solo, showing his chops when not keeping the group right on the beat. Desmond had not yet perfected—or, at least demonstrated—his patented, "dry martini" sound: here his marvelously inventive solos are almost buttery, though not oleaginous. Depending on the improvisation, Brubeck swerves from a Count Basie minimalism to some delightful creative quotations of Bach's "Eine Kleine Nachtmusik" and Pachebel's Canon in a superb track, "Fare Thee Well, Annabelle." The set is kicked off with an up-tempo, Gerwishneque jazz waltz of Rodgers and Hart's "Lover."

Although Brubeck displays on this album his signature, unexpected chord progressions and occasional, nearly 12-tone noodling on the keys, "Jazz: Red Hot and Cool" is not the breakout, multiple time-signature masterpiece of "Take Five" of four years later, which scared Columbia Records to death until they couldn't press albums fast enough to keep up with popular demand. "Red Hot" may also be a trifle misleading. This is firmly West Coast jazz, cucumber cool. But—this band knows how to swing.

"I hated the studio and loved live performances," Brubeck said (in the liner notes). "Even with the horrible pianos you find on the road, something else just takes over [before a live audience] and you play the piano the way [the music] demands." He and his band rose to the occasion on this album. While not the first Brubeck record you may wish to start with, "Jazz: Red Hot and Cool" is brimming with expert musicianship and joy. It's an album that belongs in every jazz lover's Brubeck collection, perhaps in every jazz lover's collection, period.

Eddie Cochran and Carl Perkins were George Harrison's guitar idols. Eddie was finishing a tour of England when he was killed in an auto accident. Gene Vincent was crippled. George made sure he saw them live on this tour.

Cochran was a triple threat. He played guitar. He sang. He wrote his own music. Just before his death, he was scheduled to go into the studio with a new wunderkid guitar prodigy, Glen Campbell. Eddie was to produce this fleet-fingered, country boy's album.

Today, Eddie Cochran is best known for his teen lament, 'Summertime Blues'. That song deserves to live for all eternity, but he was much more than just that one number. George Harrison's audition piece to join John Lennon's Quarrymen was a note perfect rendition of 'Twenty-flight Rock'. Paul McCartney set-up this introduction and prepped Lennon concerning little Georgie's prodigious guitar talent.

This collection of Eddie's Best may be debatable, but the only true Best of...would also be a complete gathering of all his work. As far as early rockers go, Cochran was not just influential, he was/is The Gold Standard.

text.6138: This recording of Meistersinger has been a matter of derision and complaint almost since it first appeared (domestically) on an RCA version.  However, I was in Germany (had been there a month) on the day Kennedy was Assassinated (the 22nd).  It was nighttime in a very cold, wet, and dank Germany.  German televisions "spoke" but the screen was black.  The next day black streamers flew with German flags which were flying all over the city I was in.  The streets were empty and the town I was in appeared like a ghost town.  Kennedy's death was as big a blow to the Germans as it was to my family back home.  So it was in this atmosphere (unfortunately) that the Munich National Theater reopened after its destruction in WWII the very next evening.  The observance of the combined events...from other reviewers here...was very much in character with the "spirit" of the day.  Later, I was in Germany again on my honeymoon in 1968 and on our trip we saw Lohengrin at Bayreuth.  We had arrived early and wandered around the normally sleepy little medieval town.  We happened into a record shop where we bought some vinyl souvenirs of our visit.  This album was featured because Meistersinger had been premiered in Munich almost exactly 100 years to the day (plus 3 weeks) before that date.  So we bought the complete linen Meistersinger album (the Eurodisc version).  Others have noted that there is a true sense of "theater" and "live performance" in this rendering.  On modern stereo equipment (better than 1968) it sounds quite splendid.  Keilberth was certainly an estimable Wagnerian but I suppose I bought it as much for Jess Thomas as anything.  Later my wife and I saw Thomas as the two Siegfrieds in San Francisco.  But when I lived in Germany ('63-66) his picture (usually as Lohengrin) was in every record shop.  He was VERY popular in Germany during those years.  His biography was written in German (which I have) and he was a very interesting person.  Heldentenors of his quality have been very rare ever since he retired.  Back then they (the media) complained that he wasn't Melchior, but with the virtual demise of this class of dramatic tenor Jess is certainly missed.

text.6171: My old Supreme CDs were in bad condition so I decided to replace them with this collection, which has all the biggies along with a few head-scratchers. Disc One includes 2 of their best pre-major-success tracks, of which "When the Lovelight Starts Shining Through His Eyes" is the clear winner. This track sometimes gets included in the list of the group's pre "Where Did Our Love Go" chart failures, but I believe it was the pivotal track that announced, with great musical zeal, the girls' imminent breakthrough..  The musicians involved seem to have had a blast delivering this Motown classic. "Run, Run, Run" always seemed to me like Motown's attempt to harken to the Phil Spector sound of its seemingly template track "Da Doo  Ron Ron".  Disc One also includes both "There's No Stopping Us Now" ( a rather routine album filler track) and the not quite strong "Standing at the Crossroads of Love", which has the slow cha cha feel of a record like "You Beat Me to the Punch". Side Two delights with the group's later hits but also includes the not particularly appealing (to me) track "The Sha La Bandit" and a rather dispensable re-make of The OJays'  "Love Train".  Motown did a lot of such re-makes. Personally I  don't come to a Motown album in order to hear a group with killer songwriters like HDH do re-makes of already well exposed songs like "A Lover's Concerto" or "Aquarius" etc. but it was part of the business plan apparently.  What's amazing is how fantastic most of the familiar hits still sound. So I recommend this CD happily; it's a winner. This is no ordinary pop music collection, it is the stuff of legend. You can't go wrong with this one.

Scale The Summit is an interesting group, with at least potentially some broad appeal. To be honest, I’m here for Yvette Young. The guitarist from Covet, with some solo work, makes an appearance on the first track with her very distinctive style, and without that, I probably would not have listened. Scale The Summit is operating within a very difficult niche. They are playing a kind of progressive instrumental metal that, when done well, can appeal to those of us who do not normally listen to metal. Bands like Animals As Leaders and Polyphia manage the trick. They do so with wildly creative compositions, combined with technical mastery that is peerless. One can listen to these bands with the mindset of listening to classical music— not “neoclassical,” but classical music— and appreciate it from the perspective of composition. Math rock, where Young normally makes her mark, has a similar appeal. All of this is important because these groups and artists do not draw very heavily on that critical source of rock— the blues. Scale The Summit plays a style of music that is similarly removed from the blues. The extent to which they succeed, then, is connected to the extent to which their compositions require close attention. The players, after all, are technical masters. Yet there are many technical masters. What separates Abasi/Reyes/Garstka, or Henson et al. from the progressive metal pack of the day is the complexity of their compositions in addition to their technical mastery. Young maintains enough of a groove, through math rock, that there’s still something else there beyond her guitar calisthenics, but it’s all a complicated thing.

Coming to the album at hand, with a lot of guest artists, including Young, Angel Vivaldi, and some others. Nobody is simply playing scales. Let that be clear. There are fascinating ideas here. If there is a complaint to be made, though, one should note that this is very “clean.” Clean, written with quotation marks. The album is recorded to a high degree of precision, and while one may put the music into an analysis program, who really cares? Has it been snapped to a grid? Beat doctored? If so, so what? If not, then they practice enough to try to replicate that level of precision. Is that a good thing? A bad thing? A matter of taste? Perhaps there is something to be said for the human element of imprecision, and perhaps there is something to be said for approaching perfect mastery. Either way, the sound is very clean, and approaching mechanical.

The extent to which that detracts from anything is the extent to which the compositions call for such precision, and whether they are sufficiently complex, drawing on classical theory in such a way that they benefit. Scale The Summit plays with remarkable precision. They are clean. Young, in contrast, alters her tempo intentionally, because that is something that one does in math rock, thinking through the structure of the time of the composition. Different approaches. That contrast made In A World Of Fear an interesting listen, for one brought here by Yvette Young.

Again, the genre can be played with precision. Consider Animals As Leaders. Consider Polyphia. The question is, what substitutes for “the human element” of imprecision? This is a strange question to ask of a genre that has demanded more and more precision over time, yet the fastest sweep picking merely fast picking. Every genre has technicians.

Where does the album stand? It is good. It is interesting. There is something here. For someone coming here for Yvette Young, though, with more of a jazz or math rock perspective, the precision has the following effect. Nothing puts the listener off balance.

There is structure, movement, composition, and all that good stuff. Technical mastery. Yet nothing to keep the listener surprised.

To be sure, that’s asking a lot. And this is a very good album, well played (or rather, well beyond “well played”). Surprising, though? Not as such, and part of that is how clean everything is. Is that good? Bad? Taste, really.

If you want well-played progressive metal, though, this is that. With some very good guests.

GARBAGE! That's why you'll see the sales rankings of this and the above-mentioned acts at about 15,000th or 50,000th, whatever. Because most people today DO NOT KNOW OR APPRECIATE REAL MUSIC. All they care about is shattering windows of the car next to theirs at an intersection with their stupid subwoofer blasting out their rap spewage. This album is absolutely astounding! EVERY SONG is a winner, and I don't throw out that phrase too often. It's like Slash's latest studio effort, Living The Dream...sounds like a greatest hits album, but it's all new material...amazing! This review is for "Days Of Future Passed [2 CD/1 DVD Audio][50th Anniversary Deluxe Set".

Whether you are a passing fan or a die-hard fan, "The Days Of Future Passed" was one of the best experiments in music that was ever tried. The good news is, it passed the test. This Moody Blues classic started a trend that has spread to so many bands and music artists worldwide.

This album was a unique blend of big orchestral, a little classical, and a lot of the Moody Blues style of rock and folk music. I tried to pick a favorite from the album, but I couldn't. They are all equally my favorites. Of course "Nights In White Satin" has always had a special place in my heart.

There are 3 discs in this collection.

DISC 1. The first is an Audio CD that contains the original 1967 mix remastered in stereo. The main 7 songs of the album sound great. There are 2 bonus tracks also in perfect stereo sound. Then there are 7 more bonus tracks taken from live performances on the BBC. These BBC tracks are only in mono, recorded back before anyone had stereo TV.

DISC 2 is also an Audio CD carrying the same original 7 songs from the album. The difference is, these tracks are from a slightly newer 1972 re-mix. The quality is as good as the original CD mix, but if you are a real fan and very familiar with the original mix, you might be able to notice a few subtle changes in what sounds comes from which speaker, or what is new and what is missing. But you won't be disappointed. This CD also carries 4 alternate mixes that were never released before. And there are 6 more bonus tracks that are the A & B sides of original 45 RPM record releases. These 6 titles are all Mono Single Masters.

Now for the bread and butter of the collection. Disc 3 is a DVD that will play on any DVD Video and BluRay players. This disc will NOT play on any CD player. Treat it as any other DVD.

All 7 titles of the Days Of Future Passed are included. The beauty is that they are special mixes of DTS true 5.1 discrete channels. There is also the original 1967 remastered stereo mix. Both versions are full 96KHz/24bit mixes and they are uncompressed. Little to no video on a DVD leaves a lot of room for uncompressed mixes of 5.1 audio. 96KHz and 24Bit plus no compression provides us with close enough to studio perfection audio that we all can appreciate.

I am in total awe of the sound that I hear. There is very noticeable separation of all 5 discrete channels, and the subwoofer is very alive and clean. Form the first title "The Day Begins", it instantly gets your attention as it opens with an eye opening big bright crystal clean orchestra that surrounds you. If you close your eyes, you can point at specific instruments in several directions. All the way through my favorite, "Nights In White Satin - The Night". NIWS starts quietly on just the front channels, almost as mono. Then the full orchestral strings comes in and surrounds you bright and clean. All 7 titles will give you the same effect. The closing music that ends the album is breathtaking. The gong at the very end is by it self on the left rear channel as it fades out. It almost makes you want to turn around to look at it. I had to listen to the full album 2 more times and I still wanted more.

I have the Days Of Future Passed" as a live concert on BluRay. But not even the BluRay DTS Master Audio 5.1 track sound as good as this DVD version. That amazed me. Get this 3 disc version. If you have the surround equipment and love this album, buy this 3 disc set and enjoy. It will show you what your surround system can do. It will put you in the middle of the music.

text.6224: The 2016 album, Guidance, stays within the comfort zone of Chicago-based Russian Circles, who take their name from a hockey drill rather than the country.  The band has meticulously honed a Venn diagram overlap between post rock, math rock, and progressive metal in something vaguely like post-metal, but with a distinctive sound that does not quite match any other group within that subgenre, save perhaps Pelican.  Some of their albums veer toward post-rock, and some toward metal, with their most successful works finding effective ways to blend their influences in coherent ways.  Guidance is an effective blend, with the following distinguishing factor.  While one can hear each element that makes up the group’s constructive process, the most important aspect here is their use of dynamic range in order to build.  Dynamic range is nothing new to any of these genres, but what makes the dynamism of Guidance particularly interesting is how the group uses changes in volume, tempo and mood to shift from one side of their influence to another.  Shifting from an even-keeled post-rock sound as they build to something bigger, and louder, and more metallic not just in volume, but in construction is something that demonstrates a creative process going beyond merely cranking it up to 11.  That process shows how the group combines their influences coherently.  Even Pelican doesn’t quite do it like this, staying more within a sound on each piece.  Russian Circles, though, finds a way to combine those subtle time, volume, and tone changes within a composition to take the listener on a journey, musically, across subgenres as well as within the composition.  It is a fascinating trick that few in post-rock manage, fewer still in any style related to metal, and it demonstrates the value of both leaving out the vocals, and playing with the kind of restraint that Russian Circles does.  This is not the kind of music that immediately invites dropped jaws in response to technicality, nor a response to headbang, mosh, or whatever.  Rather, this is the subtle museum piece from which one first walks by, but then returns, and cannot help but continue to analyze and admire for its subtle beauty.  Sometimes, that’s more rewarding.

A Tercentenary Concert on 17 October in the Sheldonian Theatre brought the musical culture at court to life in memorable renderings of works by J.S. Bach, J.J. Quantz, F. Benda, C.P.E. Bach and Frederick himself. The London Handel Players are currently the foremost ensemble performing the music from Frederick’s on period instruments. Their inspiring concert marked the musical highlight of the international tercentenary year.
Frederick established a rich musical culture at his court in Berlin and Potsdam. After ascending the throne in 1740, he immediately set in motion lavish plans for an opera house, attracting some of the finest singers of his day. At his beloved Sanssouci palace in Potsdam, inaugurated in 1747, he surrounded himself with an impressive entourage of outstanding musicians. These included various members of the Graun and Benda families, accompanist Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach, and the renowned flautist Johann Joachim Quantz. Flute lessons, which had previously taken place clandestinely, now became part of the daily schedule together with concerts at which Frederick reportedly played several sonatas and concertos every evening.

This 1982 album is the last of 3 that were recorded at Compass Point Studios on the sultry islands of the Bahamas. I noticed certain elements - reggae touches, bongos and other percussion, and lyrics - that give some tracks an "island" feel. But just like on the album that preceded this one ("Nightclubbing"), genres used on this recording are blended to form tracks that defy easy labeling. Every track is upbeat to some extent, as far as tempo goes, but the tone of some of them is serious. All have strong bass lines, some are funky, and some have a hard rock beat. Grace's sung vocal in "The Apple Stretching" is smooth and easy, but then the same song has spoken sections that get pretty rowdy. "Cry Now, Laugh Later" makes me think of Macy Gray, due to the bluesy arrangement and the party atmosphere. "Inspiration" is decorated with shimmering, celestial electronica. "Unlimited Capacity For Love" has busy electronica chattering away in the background, but later there are some beautiful, melodic synth lines.

The album's title is "Living My Life", and that life seems to be in New York City. The boyfriend of the singer, "My Jamaican Guy", takes her out: "Take my life for a drive/Never need to change his tools/Him drive like a stubborn mule/Dat way him now go plop plop." "The Apple Stretching" describes New York waking up in the morning: "The sun comes swaggering across the harbour/And kisses the lady waiting in the narrows/And she already plenty shaky stands there/Blushing, clutching the torch of liberty." The story gets a lot more specific and a lot more lively after that, including a dump truck accident, a bag lady, a Jesus freak and a cop who fires his gun and yells, "Freeze!". In "Everybody Hold Still", the protagonist is mugged: "I know I shouldn't have left the apartment/I know I should've stayed in watching TV...Everybody hold still/Nobody gets hurt/Please don't take all of my money mister." And as the title implies, "Cry Now, Laugh Later" touches on more troubles: "I don't know why I'm laughing/Immigration breathing down my neck/Ain't got no money for a pay off/Stay in jail until they send me back." Grace wrote or co-wrote every song except "The Apple Stretching", and the songs paint a colorful picture of the life of this alien in the Big Apple, enhanced by creative arrangements and Grace's overarching persona.

rock & roll's most tragically unsung hero, the one-hit wonder who most deserved more, is of course Warren "Werewolves Of London" Zevon. it's harder to cite a first runner-up, but i'd say Norman "Spirit In The Sky" Greenbaum was certainly in the running.
he was famously inspired to write a hymn of some sort by a television performance of Porter Waggoner (probably best remembered now as Dolly Parton's mentor/hero). it's even often hinted as a sign of a puckish sense of humor, a singer with so obviously Jewish a surname singing how "i've got a friend in Jesus." and there is indeed a certain whimsy to much of Greenbaum's work. he's no "Weird Al" Yankovic or Tom Lehrer by any stretch, but he does live up to the court-jester approach of, say, Joe Walsh.
Greenbaum is now famously ambivalent about the song, because however much revenue it might generate him, it can still easily pigeonhole him as something he's not. ("it made and destroyed me in one stroke.") one of the more kick-ass rock grooves of it's time, it's even hinted that the "fuzz" guitar was invented specifically for the recording session. also, it's come to represent a brief movement called "Jesus rock." not to be confused with the more sanctimonious "Christian rock" of recent decades, Jesus rock was actually a sincere effort to make room for Our Savior on the pop charts without reducing the music to a sermon. (it's other poster-child is "My Sweet Lord" by George Harrison.) but to Greenbaum, it was a mood of the moment rather than a dogma.
(i could also recommend a song called "Jesus" from the first Queen album. hey, if Greenbaum the Jew can serenade our Redeemer, why not Mercury the Zoroastrian?)
which brings us to the inevitable disclaimer. both musically and thematically, "Spirit In The Sky" is the anomaly here. his more typical music style is easiest to describe as jug-band a' la The Lovin' Spoonful, with just a pinch of R&B for texture.
(to give you some idea, he'd played in a novelty act called Dr. West's Medicine Show & Junk Band, of "The Eggplant That Ate Chicago" fame.)
that sense of whimsy, for instance. "Tars Of India," apparently a brand of cigar or something, is his contribution to the how-to class of song, a' la "So You Want To Be A Rock & Roll Star" by The Byrds or "Rock & Roll Band" by Boston. it promises, with tongue firmly in cheek, that said cheroots are all it takes to make" what's in you come out."
"Good-Lookin' Woman" is the tale of a less-than-stud assuring a goddess he has the "money to keep you around." he then approaches from the other end of the spectrum to advertise his "School For Sweet Talk."
he can be sincerely romantic as well. "Alice Bodine" is a wistful ode to a childhood flame, while "Marcy" takes the "She Loves You" route. "("Marcy knows you love her.") then, "Save Me For A Rainy Day" makes for as plaintive a folk reflection as anything Peter Paul & Mary had to offer.
interestingly, he seems to of shared Al Yankovic's conviction that food is inherently funny, as in his ode to "Chocolate Milk" and his tale of a farmer's enthusiasm for his new "Milk Cow." "Canned Ham," from what i hear the closest thing Greenbaum had to a second hit (charting somewhere around 60), is a desperate plea for his "baby" to act on a promise of old to purchase said ham for him. (again, the punchline refers to his Jewish heritage.)
i'm not sure if Greenbaum had it in him to be a legend. (he's always quite firmly stated he never regretted his lateral shift into goat farming at the end of the decade.) but he definitely could've gone a bit farther, had Fate been kinder. every song herein is somehow interesting and/or contagious. the likes of "Junior Cadillac," "Jubilee," "Marcy," and "Skyline" had similar single potential to be tapped, even if no one ever bothered to do so.
the man's music certainly has spirit.
in the sky and otherwise.

text.6648: Haunting, explosive, hard-hitting, charming and uplifting, this debut from the Los Angeles-infected quartet is a modern masterpiece of alt-rock perfection with cinematic strokes. Year of the Rabbit is a new band conjured up by guitarist/composer/vocalist Ken Andrews, who also happens to be an avant-garde producer/recordist/mixer, having injected his eccentric ear-tweaking talents to albums by the likes of Blinker the Star, Pete Yorn and Jimmy Eat World. Andrews (the "alternative Phil Spector”) was also the brainchild behind the much heralded group Failure, who arguably are the genesis of the chromatic processed guitar sound (currently perpetuated by former member Troy Van Leeuwen who took it to A Perfect Circle and Queens of the Stone Age), and whom also earned accolades world-wide and gained great support by the likes of other left-field dark rockers such as Tool. For his new band (also featuring members formerly of Shiner, National Skyline and Cupcakes), Andrews and company further explore the depths of otherworldly guitar sounds, and assemble them into a giant wall of chromatic sound. The somewhat androgynous, exotic and universal radio-friendly songs within the self-produced album are held together by luminescent psychedelic pop hooks, strange yet friendly grooves and titanium drumming that creates wild and wonderful collisions and blends of machinated textures and arrangements though still staying richly organic. It is rare for a band to come up with a solid first appearance that is not spotty, but somehow YOTR have achieved it by judiciously mixing art and commerce and have come up with an instant classic that is akin to the timeless feel of the Cars' debut (somewhat of an influence here, and certainly inspired by the haunting aura and concepts of early Gary Numan records) or even Nirvana's major label debut. There is not an ounce of trying too hard or a pretentiousness syndrome within at all; everything (even with the mandatory slow songs) flows beautifully to the point where the CD player might very well execute the repeat function by itself. It’s that good. Astronomy alt rock at its finest. (Elektra records)

text.6762: First, you have to "hear" what's going on. Paul Weston and his wife, Jo Stafford, were always invited to Hollywood parties; but then, they were always pressured, he to play piano, she to sing, and it ticked them off. So, they created this album (vinyl) to take with them to parties. Now Jo Stafford was one of the best singers ever, and had perfect pitch. But in here, Weston deliberately hits the cracks between keys, and she goes alternately flat and sharp, sometimes in the same phrase. One tune is aimed at Doris Day's hit. My brother in law (a professional musician with his own group playing in Vegas) bought this when I was in high school, and we would laugh until we hurt. This is so much fun...but be ready.

text.6765: I've had this disc sitting in my collection ever since it was originally released in 1998, and I can remember pretty much every music magazine you can name, live or dead, every website proclaiming this as one of the best albums of the decade, revolutionary, etc., just about all of the superlatives in the dictionary.  So, finally, it rose to the top of the giant pile of "to listen to," and "to read" and "to watch."  For the most part, it lives up to the hype.  Compared to where punk rock was in the '90s and early '00s, the reviews are correct - this absolutely pushed things farther than anyone else was willing to go at the time.  The innovative use of samples and loops, well it reminds this old guy of Wire, Mission of Burma, and I think I even hear a little bit of Television.  This was, and this is not a pejorative, "art punk" - I mean this as a compliment.  The record _sounds_ great.  The one thing that holds it back, and yes I know it's still a punk album, are the vocals.  I don't just mean the screaming, which is about 75%, but even the spoken word and sung parts - it's just  - it's the weak spot, trust me.  Dynamics means a lot more than just "quiet part" and REALLY LOUD part, and screaming, I think even back then, doesn't give a band as much mileage as they probably thought it would.  On the whole though, very glad I listened to it finally, I think it mostly (but not quite) lives up to all the praise heaped on it for all these years.

text.6770:
I recently saw a program on PBS touting the brilliance of this Kinks album, and so I bought a used CD to see if it was really that good...

It's pretty BAD, and pretty derivative of the Beatles' "Sgt Pepper." (It came out the year after.) Ray Davies tries desperately to capture childhood memories (a la "Penny Lane" or "Lucy in the Sky"), but instead of being evocative, he knocks us over the head----for example, in "Do You Remember Walter?" he tells us that his former childhood friend is probably fat now. Oh. OK. "Picture Book" is similarly smug and emotionally inept.

There are echoes of "Penny Lane," "Strawberry Fields," "Lucy," "Mr. Kite," etc., all over the place. Davies tries McCartney's straightforward music-hall memories, and he tries Lennon's psychedelia-tinged memories, and he even goes Dylan at one point ("Last of the Steam-Powered Trains"). But it's all sloppy, inept copy-cat attempts at relevance.

I'm mad at PBS, and anyone else, for recommending this.

I bought a copy of this CD at the Al Dimeola concert I attended 2/6 in Fort Lauderdale, and listened to it twice before actually reading the liner notes today. I think this is ADi's most ambitious, personal, and accomplished effort yet. It draws from a wide range of influences — flamenco, Middle Eastern, classical, world, etc. — all fusion-blended in a heady mix that evokes a more diverse emotional palette. Rapidly changing sequences demand attentive listening. What struck me as odd was some of the drumming. It sounded really pedestrian in contrast to the technical mastery exhibited by the other musicians throughout, and in was mixed too loud in my opinion. That was disappointing and a distraction, the only blemish, really, in an otherwise outstanding effort.

DiMeola is currently touring with an acoustic trio, accompanied by a Cuban piano player and an Italian accordion player. Their technical mastery of the material and rapid fire seamless interplay was in full force throughout the two sets. If you get a chance to see them, jump on it.

One of the first attractive features of the cd is the audio quality. Just listen to RC’s rich overtones throughout all the tracks.
The entire cd, including the alternate takes, provides real enjoyment. The sound of PD’s alto is breathtakingly beautiful. CB’s playing on open trumpet is exquisite. JH’s performance throughout is one of restraint.
I have heard many superb renditions of Concierto de Aranjuez, and this one can be placed in the category of Masterpiece. I recommend any music lover to listen to a copy.

WARNING: DVD is in PAL (won't play on most US DVD players)

This is from a reunion concert in Nottingham in 1990. It is the original quartet with occasional fifth member, Jimmy Hastings (same group as on the first three albums). It is just under 60 minutes and the sound quality is very good to excellent.

The DVD is in the European format, PAL instead of the US NTSC, so it won't play on most US DVD or Blu-Ray players. You might be able to play it on your computer. I do have a universal DVD player, so I can watch it. The format is 4:3 (not widescreen). The video quality is OK (better than a VHS tape). The filming and editing are good for the most part....not a lot of zooming and pan and scan like most videos today. There are few times when the video is concentrating on the wrong person. Much of the filming was done by two guys with hand held cameras that get right up next to the musicians. At times it is a little creepy and I don't see how they can play with a camera sticking right in their face.

It is nice that this is a reunion concert of the original group, but I still think it would have been better if Geoff Richardson had been there. This is a very good performance and when this was first released in 1993 it was one of the best live Caravan albums available on CD. But, there are a few weak songs on it, featuring Richard Sinclair, like Videos of Hollywood. Now there are many wonderful Caravan live albums out on CD, like Live at Fairfield Hall (previously hard to find LP, Greatest Hits Live).

This concert was originally released as Caravan Live on CD in 1993 (unless there is an earlier version or maybe a VHS tape that I don't know about). At least I am 95% it is the same. This older CD has slightly better sound quality and some of the cheering was edited out. But, comments between songs are exactly the same, although come of the comments have been edited out of this newer release.

Access All Areas is a series of CD/DVDs (all in PAL) but out by Edsel and distributed by Demon Records. They find old taped concerts and release them.

I hesitated to buy the original Rhino Handmade edition of this release, as it was very pricey and what I heard of the material didn't impress me. But I grabbed this up during the Covid-19 lockdown, and I have to say, I'm very impressed.

For a band that was just past its first album and not even with its second under its belt, Iron Butterfly show themselves to be a virtuoso, charismatic quartet, capable of holding a stage and a listener for an hour at a time -- between Doug Ingle's organ arabesques and Erik Brann's Hendrix-influenced lead guitar, there's plenty of bluesy psychedelic flexing going on, all of it backed by Lee Dorman's imposing bass and Ron Bushy's relentless percussion fills. The balances aren't always 100% ideal, but hey, this is a pair of live shows from 1968. I'm just glad the tapes survived, and disc two, containing the second show from April 27, 1968, offers some extraordinary playing and probably the best rendition of the yet-to-be-released "In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida" ever heard .

The producers of the CD have also taken a portion of a page out of the Woodstock album, in leaving a pair of very compelling stage announcements intact at the opening of two of the sets presented here.

text.7003:
Growing up in the Mid-South, I've been faintly aware of the Louisiana Hayride all my life as the Grand Ol Opry's kissing cousin, and also the country radio show that welcomed Elvis Presley with open arms after his being denied from coming back to the Grand Ol Opry. I also knew that a lot of my favorite artists like George Jones, Hank Williams, Johnny Cash, and Johnny Horton most all carried on between the Opry and the Hayride in order to make their songs known and heard to a wider audience with live performances. As far as knowing about the radio station itself, though, I had no clear idea of the Hayride or what it was about. Buying this huge, monolithic box set has finally given me some insight on just what this radio program coming out of Shreveport was. At twenty CDs and over 24 hours of music, artist banter, and radio advertisements, this sprawling set that includes a large, beautifully illustrated book feels like an informative, self-paced museum tour. In fact, you might say I paid for a ticket back in time to hear these wonderful radio broadcasts. I will comment on the sound of some of these recordings and say that a few (most notably some Elvis tracks) sound like they were recorded through a pile of mud from my grandfathers pasture, but that is to be expected especially considering that some of these tapes were probably stored in un-air conditioned environments in Louisiana (humidity, anyone?) and that they survived at all is a miracle. Not that this affects all the tracks, in fact I'd say a high percent of them are rendered and remastered very clearly for this collection, and they retain a certain nostalgia as you really feel like your listening to an old broadcast and not a compressed CD. As for audience noise, the only time this really inferred with the listening experience was on a few Elvis tracks (surprise, surprise) and when Hank Williams performed Jambalaya on the Bayou, which on that song in particular the audience is only really overzealous on the instrumental breaks. All that being said about the sound quality and audience noise, you must keep in mind that these are taped broadcasts from the late 40's to 60's, way before the introduction of the better and more crisp concert recording technology that would come in later years. That these CDs sound as good as they do is a testament to the Bear Family and their will to present the best sound quality and product possible.

One last note is the price, which can be a bit of a turn off considering not everyone wants to spend over $200 dollars for a massive CD box set, especially when digital music is really much the "preferred" medium. However, if you are reading this review and have looked at this product then you are obviously interested in owning this time capsule of history, and like me probably don't mind parting with that amount of money every now and again to buy a set this large. I was skeptical of buying this at first, but after owning it for a few weeks I'm glad to have this in my collection and don't regret shelling out the dough for it.

text.7029: I, too, was introduced to the music of this maverick composer in music school at my 20th century lit. class.  I wanted to find a recording that was more sonically up-to-date than the original "Music of Harry Partch" on Columbia.  I listened to many of the more recent recordings, however, I kept finding CDs that had too many Western instruments like sax and trumpet, or solo voice.  What I really wanted was a heavy dose of Partch's instruments in a truly resonant environment.  So I was very surprised to find that this live recording from 1969 was the most illuminating sonic environment for his instruments along with some chamber choral singing (which compliments the instruments perfectly).  At first I balked at the hefty price tag of this CD, but it's clearly worth it !

“Level Headed,” released by the English glam rock band Sweet in January 1978, sees the band move in several musical directions and delving into both California-inspired easy rock (as heard in “California Nights”) as well as art rock. For the latter, Sweet uses baroque-based instrumentation on the track “Fountain” sung by guitarist Andy Scott, who also wrote the lyrics. The one lone US/UK Top Ten hit “Love Is Like Oxygen,” co-written by Scott, is featured in both the original 6:53 version and the 3:43 single version. This was, sadly, to be lead vocalist Brian Connolly’s swan song with the band as various health and personal troubles took their toll on the beleaguered singer. This left Scott and bassist Steve Priest to handle the brunt of the vocals.

“Dream On” (not related to the Aerosmith song) is a tender love song written and sung by Scott, followed by the aforementioned LILO. Steve Priest does an admirable job on “California Nights,” which reflected his desire to live in the USA permanently. The song “Strong Love” is a blatant attempt to capitalize on the exploding disco scene that dominated the remainder of the 1970s. Starting with “Fountain” and continuing onward, Sweet delves into areas of art rock and slight elements of mysticism as heard on the track “Anthem No. 1 (The Lady of the Lake).” Two more “typical” Sweet songs, “Silverbird” and “Lettres D’Amour” highlight the last glory of Brian Connolly (aided by female vocalist Stevie Lange).

After a stringed instrumental titled “Anthem No. II,” we arrive at the most unusual Sweet track ever. It’s a futuristic, science fiction track called “Air on ‘A’ Tape Loop” which may give off a strong Pink Floyd/Alan Parsons vibe. In fact, the space rock track would have fit perfectly for the popular science fiction television series Doctor Who. (Why the BBC didn’t notice the power of the Sweet track is anyone’s guess.)

Anyone who listens to only “Ballroom Blitz” and think they know everything about Sweet, truly ought to listen to Level Headed. The transfer is good for my ears, and the raw power is immeasurable.

Have loved this album since high school. I read all the negative reviews before buying and decided the low price made it worth trying, even if the pressing turned out to be crap, mostly because all the videos/pictures with negative reviews showed the record being playing on suitcase players. Sure enough, the record plays beautifully on my Audio Technica LP60, which is considered a starter turntable BUT it's still infinitely better than a suitcase player and has served me well with no issues.
No cracks, no pops, no skips. The music has that delicious "warm" sound you'd want from a record like this and it delivers. I absolutely recommend buying and I'm very happy with it.
If you have the appropriate equipment you're probably fine buying this (although that's not a guarantee--sometimes Amazon just isn't reliable when it comes to vinyl) and it's pretty cheap for a record. The problem is people playing records on crap turntables and being surprised when a lot of records sound horrible on them. Sometimes you land a genuinely bad pressing or it comes damaged, but most of the time, it's your suitcase player.

text.7281: In 1977, The Brothers Johnson had a big hit called "Strawberry Letter 23". Recently I looked to see who wrote it, and I was amazed to find that it was Shuggie Otis, an artist unknown to me. I felt compelled to delve into the work of this person who wrote that very mind-bending song, so here I am. In my research, and on this collection, I found a very talented singer, guitarist and songwriter. He wrote or co-wrote all but 2 of these 18 songs.These recordings, which I would sum up as blues and funk laced with 60's pop-rock, were made in the period 1969-1974, which means that Shuggie Otis made them from age 16 to 21. Not too shabby, I say. I am impressed by the range of styles in the performance and the composition of these songs. His singing voice is not the most polished or accomplished in the world, but what he lacks in finesse he makes up for in mood and style. Examples: He projects innocence and wonder ("Strawberry Letter 23"), traditional male blues ("Me And My  Woman") and playful James Brown funk ("Hurricane"). He certainly doesn't lack finesse on the guitar. On most of the tracks he burns it with traditional hot bluesy licks, but he can be mellow ("Island Letter") or cross over to blues/rock of a more psychedelic nature, as on "One Room Country Shack", which calls to mind the guitar sounds of Cream. You can also hear 60's sounds in "Aht Oh Mi Hed" and "Ice Cold Daydream". Some of the songs have hallucinatory lyrics, like these from "Strawberry Letter 23": "In the garden, I see/West purple shower bells and tea/Orange birds and river cousins/Dressed in green." He goes from a somber love ballad like "Jennie Lee" to a hit-the-road blues number with the improbable title of "I Can Stand To See You Die". The instrumental track "Oxford Gray" is very unusual - bluesy to an extent, dramatic, with an orchestra, sounding like a film score in places. A tremendous debut EP from Sudan Archives. It kicks off with “Paid,” which features rather conventional instrumentation and lyrics. Having been lulled into relaxation by the conventional, we are then gobsmacked by the remainder of the EP, none of which sounds like anything I have heard before. “Come Meh Way,” with its monster violin riff, might be the career-crowning achievement for another artist; for Sudan Archives, it’s just the second song on her first EP.
The remainder of the EP is drawn from the same vein as “Come Meh Way.” We hear another monster, but yet plaintive, violin riff on “Oatmeal.” Some ocean ambience. Electronic and acoustic percussion. Strumming and plucking on the violin. Sounds from all over the globe- West Africa, Northeast Africa, Japan, Ireland, Cincinnati, LA. This EP by this American artist is the some of the most mature, truly “world” music I have heard.
Sudan Archives is one of the most significant artists active now. Right now, while we are all alive to hear and see her. Don’t miss the chance to experience a future legend now.

text.7368:
This is a reissue / remaster of the 17th album by iconic American guitarist / composer / bandleader / visionary Frank Zappa, originally released in 1973. The sessions that produced this album also produced the 1974 album “Apostrophe (`)”, which was Zappa’s next album. The album presents seven original songs, all by Zappa.

Zappa assembled an absolutely brilliant lineup of musicians to record the album, which included French violinist Jean-Luc Ponty, keyboardist George Duke, trombonist Bruce Fowler, trumpeter Sal Marquez, multi-instrumentalist Ian Underwood, percussionist Ruth Underwood, bassist Tom Fowler and drummer Ralph Humphrey. The vocals were performed mostly by Zappa with a little help from several singers, including the uncredited appearance by Tina Turner and the Ikettes. The unique and exemplary guitar parts are of course his.

This album marks a new approach in Zappa’s convoluted musical path and marks his passionate affair with Jazz-Rock Fusion, which has its sources some years earlier in "The Hot Rats Sessions", but came into full bloom starting with album and dominated his 1970s output. He managed to combine a very complex music, both harmonically and rhythmically, with a seemingly Rock or even Pop glam, to expand his audiences, without losing an iota of his musical integrity.

In retrospect the music on this album sounds a bit pale in comparison to the numerous live recordings of the same material, which was often expanded into lengthy improvisations and offered an explosion of energy and spontaneity. Nevertheless, these are the original versions of that gorgeous material, and have not only a nostalgic tinge, but are true Classics in every respect.

Overall, although almost fifty years passed since this music was recorded, this album remains an absolute Classic in every respect, which stands proudly as an icon of superb music, which still shines brighter than almost anything else recorded since. Zappa’s genius, not only as a musician, but also as a visionary and a brilliant observer of the human condition and American folly and deceit, remain completely relevant and are even more actual today than ever.

text.7385: I recently reviewed the very famous and highly reviewed version of La Boheme with Pavarotti and Freni.  I called it "La Boheme Lite".  The reason is that it is inferior in every way to this recording, except for the sound.  The sound of this 1959 Decca stereo recording is good, but since it was recorded in 1959, it is not great.  Nevertheless, this is the recording that really turned me into an opera lover.  For one thing, Renata Tebaldi is at her most inspired, sometimes bordering on genius, and she has THREE arias, making this very much a soprano's opera.  In the aria "Mi chiamano Mimi", Tebaldi builds, layer upon layer, a mountain of sound with that huge voice of hers ending in a tremendous, thrilling climax.  Carlo Bergonzi is in excellent voice with beautiful, loud, and clear high notes.  His sobbing at the end of the opera is heart wrenching.  Gianna D'Angelo is a very young, fresh-voiced and kittenish Musetta.  Ettore Bastianini is peerless as Marcello.  In the second act, after Musetta says that it is her foot that hurts, Bastianini's singing could be compared to a lion's roar.  When Cesare Siepi sings his aria saying farewell to his old coat with his rich bass voice, it is enough to make you weep.  I gave away "La Boheme Lite" to a friend.  It just couldn't hold a candle to this recording.

text.7401: The Beatles split pretty acrimoniously in 1970 as everyone knows and ‘Let It Be’ was their apparent swan song. By anyone else’s standards, a very good if not great record but not as good as their best. Some might rate it as high as maybe ‘Abbey Road’ or the ‘White Album’ but I don’t agree with that. That the LP has several classic songs is without question as the title track, “Across the Universe” and “Get Back” all appear here. However they are not the same versions as the celebrated single releases, not that that’s a bad thing. Other standouts include the two George Harrison songs, one of which, “I Me Mine” seems to be a dig at either Lennon or McCartney; not sure if that’s true or not but would it surprise you? They were pretty intolerant of each other by the end. Not much more I can add here though “I’ve Got a Feeling” deserves special mention as it proved even in the nadir of their working relationship, John and Paul could still work together and create a standout song. ‘Let It Be’ has been overpraised by many, as has the post breakup careers of the Fab Four (I’m sorry but could there be a more overrated canon of work by four individual artists ever?) but it does please quite often - so like Georgie Wood says, dig it, dig it, dig it...

text.7585:
Many of us who listen to radio back in the 70's also remember the TV show "Soul Train" with Don Cornelius as the host. To see Rufus for the first time with their beautiful lead singer Chaka Khan on Soul Train was a real treat. There was nothing like this group before. Their songs were energized, electric and full deep heart felt emotion. "Rags to Rufus" hit the record shelves in 1974 and had their greatest hit, "Tell Me Something Good" which was written by Stevie Wonder. The lusty, sexy song captivated its audiences all over the radio airwaves with its hooks and funky guitar and keyboard work. The best song on the album is their follow up single, "You Got the Love", which starts off the album. The song starts off with this loop track with the guitar and plays tricks with your mind when all the instruments come in on the off beat and alternate whith the shuffle beat and the kick drum.
Every song on this albums is great, from the instrumental title track to the heart felt, "Look Through My Eyes" and "In Love We Grow". There is even a classic spiritual, "Swing Down Chariot" which adds another dimension to the album.
Buy this album it is iconic Funk and Soul. You will end up playing it to death. Remember to crank up the bass. The CD version seemed to be a bit shy on the bass. The vinyl on the ABC label seems to sound the best.

Back when I was a teenager, I fell in love with Natalie Merchant's voice. Leader of 10,000 Maniacs, Natalie's genre of music was mostly alternative and abstract, yet she still had the most accessible lyrics that any fan could enjoy. With her pop sheen sensibilities like "Trouble Me" or "Like The Weather", it was no "wonder" (no pun intended) that she gained such a serious, loyal fan base.

However, Natalie felt constricted after just a decade and permanently left the band, all to branch out on her own. And it certainly paid off. 1995's "Tigerlily" and 1998's "Ophelia" went on to sell millions of copies. And with her voice becoming even BETTER in the 2010's, she continues to release Grammy-winning award compositions. This particular box set is a real treat for hardcore Natalie fans, including 2 additional never-before-heard CD's. Truly WORTH the $50 that I spent!! :)

just hearing this for the first time, and i'm blown away that this isn't more well-known. Excellent tunes and fantastic playing throughout, including Jose Neto on guitar, Mark Egan on bass (with his Jaco-like tones), Kei Akagi on piano, and of course Joe Farrell, who plays both flute and sax on what is, sadly, his last recording before his death. As expected, Airto and others bring a dynamic percussive blend. "Treme Terra" kicks off with an off-kilter rhythm and melody and beautiful Flora-Airto vocal combo. "Misturada" is equally off-kilter and super funky. "The Return" begins with Flora's other-worldly voice, cutting to a slower, somber bass groove leading into a sweet flowing tune. "Three Way Mirror" is a gentle swingin' tune, funky enough to get you moving. "Sao Francisco River" is just lovely, with lilting guitar strum from Jose Neto, lively bass, and exquisite vocals by Flora.
"Lilia" starts sparsely and flows into a fantastic jazz groove with everyone firing hot on piano, bass, flute and Airto on vocals, and some fantastic percussive moments.
"Plane to the Trane" brings it home with a rhythmic swell and some seering/searching solos worthy of Trane.
