text.8187:
Stanley Jordan is a difficult guitarist for me to wrap my brain around. Mind-bogglingly gifted at a technical level, he just doesn't always do it for me. Here's the thing. The one-man-band thing, if done wrong, can sound gimmicky, and there are times when Jordan sounds gimmicky. This one is Jordan sounding right.

When you can play two entirely separate lines on guitar, sometimes on two different guitars, through tapping (which is a big thing again thanks to math rock), what do you do? There is an intrinsic tradeoff with tapping as a technique. It opens up melodic lines that you couldn't play if you weren't tapping, and obviously, if you are Stanley Jordan, you can accompany yourself, but it is a tonally limited approach. When you consider the importance of tone for musicians like Bill Frisell, whether or not that's worth the tradeoff depends on what you do when you open up those melodic possibilities. The risk is that if you don't do enough, it's just the one-man-band gimmick.

A few years down the road, Charlie Hunter would come along with his 8-string guitar/bass hybrids, and play guitar and bass parts simultaneously. He would avoid the gimmicky one-man-band thing by just playing totally in-the-pocket jazz-funk, and being funkier than everyone else such that the one-man-band thing doesn't even matter, just as it didn't really matter with Roland Kirk.

Stanley Jordan burst onto the scene doing covers of pop tunes and not always opening up the melodic possibilities to the degree that he could. That way lies gimmickry, to my ear. And with the tonal limitations of tapping, he hasn't always done it for me.

Live In New York, though, started to show a different Stanley Jordan. You've got a couple of Coltrane tunes here, starting out with the first track. Impressions. You have some old jazz standards. I don't really need another jazz cover of Over The Rainbow at this point, but whatever. Really, it's just the smooth jazz cover at the end that I find off-putting. Then, the accompanying band. They free Jordan up to really cut loose melodically and show the possibilities of tapping so that he isn't just doing it for the sake of doing it. Hey, look what I can do, right? No. Not here. And with bass deity Charnett Moffett leading the backing band, at least to my ear, Jordan has the kind of setup a musician can only dream of.

This is what tapping can do in jazz. Stripped of anything like gimmickry, this is Jordan just playing, and showing what kinds of melodic lines open up. And, with the band, I don't feel like anything is missing because of the tonal limitations of tapping. That's sort of the irony here. Tapping allows Jordan to accompany himself, but because of the tonal limitations of the technique, I don't feel like he should. With a band including Charnett Moffett, I couldn't really ask for more. That low end is really taken care of with Moffett.

So, while I don't always dig Jordan, this one works.

I am substantially re-writing this review after a lot of careful listening to this recording. My initial impression isn't changed, however, I think Buniatishvilli is a wonderful pianist but not yet a substantial artist.

I wrote that she is gorgeous and to ignore this would be disingenuous.

I listened repeatedly to this recording and compared it to Horowitz's recording of the Rach 3rd, Wild's fabulous live recording, Bolet's live performance in Indiana, the composer's recording of the 2nd, Moiseiwitsch's of the 2nd and Valentina Lisitsa's recordings of both 2 and 3. I mention the last because she is a sort of rival to Buniatishvilli in terms of repertory and recordings, she is also an attractive female and relatively young.

Buniatishvilli always takes the fastest possible tempo it seems and this proves to be (perhaps) her undoing. Fast passages lose clarity, she doesn't always seem in sync with the orchestra, and lyrical passages lose their dramatic power. She is much quicker, for example, than Horowitz under Ormandy. She seems to ignore or at least not emphasize what Schonberg called "inner voices". Finally she lacks a dramatic tone, which further works against her. i would raise the same criticism with Lisitsa btw, lest anyone think I am partisan, except Lisitsa's tone is better and her orchestra, The London Symphony, is incomparable.

At this point I am fascinated by Buniatishvilli's voluptuous beauty and her pianistic skill, I would love to see her perform, and I will eagerly anticipate further recordings. But I do not expect the great artistry or beautiful sounds I get from my favorite recordings of old.

I am reading a fine biography, "Rolling Stones": 50" I will review shortly. As is usual when I read music biographies, I get very interested in the music, where some people are into the gossipy, debauched and crazy behavior angle. However, with the Stones, the two are inseparable, and the fact they created a stunning volume of albums starting with "Beggars Banquet", "Let It Bleed", "Get Yer Ya-Ya's Out", "Sticky Fingers", "Exile On Main Street" and wrapping it up with "Goat's Head Soup" show that their talent and vision couldn't be derailed even in the most toxic situations, usually around Keith Richards, who famously was in the throes of a prolonged heroin addiction, not to mention any other recreational substance that was within reach, but still managed to stay alive and write some great music.
Where "Exile On Main Street" was a very gruff affair, and full of bluesy power, "Goat's Head Soup" carried the same intensity but introduced some funky keyboards courtesy of Billy Preston, and rocks as hard as anything the band ever did. "Dancin' With Mr. D." starts off with a blues lurch, and the real rocking gets going with "Heartbreaker" and a funked up horn section that propels the tune into the stratosphere.
One ballad, the hit "Angie", written by Keith Richards, was discouraged by their label at first as a single, but the band insisted, and the song today is one of their most beautiful tracks, not exactly what you'd expect from Keith especially at the time. "Silver Train" keeps the rock and roll humming, and after a few slower tunes, the album closes with the infamous "Star Star", and the salacious chorus I won't repeat here. But aside from the swipe at the jet set society from Jagger, which is a bit disingenuous considering he was a major league rock and roll playboy as much as Richards was a strung out junkie, the song is one of their most lively and furious rockers.
The Stones would falter a bit after this, but regroup for the excellent "Some Girls" after a couple questionable albums, "Black and Blue" still one of the most debated as an overlooked classic or a real low point for them. But "Goat's Head Soup", while not usually hyped very much, is a superb album, and is truly among their greatest albums. Why punkers would shortly start criticizing the Stones as old "farts", it is really quite hypocritical for those bands to do so, when one considers that while the Beatles, Beach Boys and The Dave Clark Five had the pop scene pretty well nailed down, The Stones represented the raunchy side of the street - the hard blues, country hard livin' on several tunes that nobody in Nashville today could begin to touch, and real garage band mentality, with their very rough and tough edge. Punk simply was not possible with the garage bands they did acknowledge, but for all who love that edgy side of rock and roll, denying The Rolling Stones is like insisting the earth is still flat.

text.8435:
For those wanting to listen to the original cues composed by Pete Rugolo for the classic ABC series, "The Fugitive" (1963-67), this is the real deal. I have deducted one star for the reason given by another reviewer. Mr. Wrong is right: missing is one of the series' most tender cues, for strings and harp. Not only is it intrinsically lovely; its inclusion would have given this album some needed variety. In musical terms we have here a master class in orchestration: how many different ways could Rugolo, Stan Kenton's chief arranger, play the same sixteen bars of music, an A theme ("Th' . . . FU-gi-TIIIIIVE!") and its B bridge (a wistful tune: "He runs—if he's caught, he's dead—ahead of Gerard, to find Fred!"*)? It's a tribute to Mr. Rugolo's talent that he could create so many variations on such brief motifs—brassy, sweet, melancholic, jazzy, romantic, mysterious—to accompany the series' visuals. The result is invevitably repetitive yet listenable on its own terms (and, for Boomers, a musical wayback machine to the original series). As Jon Burlingame, premiere film soundtrack musicologist, explains in this album's liner notes, executive producer Quinn Martin commissioned Rugolo to execute what was then, and remains, an unusual assignment: instead of tracking multiple episodes with different music each season, the composer created about 50 minutes of cues that could be repeatedly "needle-dropped" into episodes throughout the series' four-year run. Rugolo scored them, then supervised Harry Rabinowitz to conduct their performance by The London Studio Symphony Orchestra. Most of the rest of the music was borrowed from the CBS library, with compositions by Jerry Goldsmith and Bernard Herrmann. (Those cues are not available here, though the tracks are obtainable in compilations for "The Twilight Zone." The cue Mr. Wrong and I miss may have been drawn from that library; if so, this album's producers should not be faulted.) The music is of uneven quality: themes for Lt. Gerard (Kimble's nemesis) and Fred Johnson (the one-armed man) are loud but dull, while departures from the series' theme, such as "Youthful Innocence" and "A New Love," are melodic and well arranged. The album's longest track (5:11), for the final episode's confrontation between Kimble and Johnson, begins sadly, then cuts loose with full orchestral dynamism. To sum up: These are Rugolo's original cues as originally recorded, capturing many moods of the woebegone Richard Kimble and complementing the deep empathy that series star David Janssen brought to his signature role.

* These are my crummy lyrics. Can I now become a member of ASCAP?

Back when cds came out there weren’t a lot of choices. I ended up buying the Cleveland/Dohnanyi (or however you spell it), Brahms First, and the Vienna/Bernstein Brahms Second, Third and Fourth. I always liked the Dohnanyi, but have been lukewarm about the Bernstein, and found myself usually listening to something else on Spotify.
I decided to look for a good integral set and after extensive internet research, ended up with this Philharmonia/Klemperer set for under $20 which also includes the Requiem, Alto Rhapsody, Haydn Variations, Tragic Overture and Academic Festival Overture.
The performances are uniformly outstanding, and the Requiem is considered by some to hold benchmark status.
My desire for a satisfying set of Brahms symphonies is now fulfilled, and I don’t think I will be looking into other Brahms symphony performances for a long time.
Hard to get more for $20, and the sound is clean, too.

text.8526: I was initially looking at one of the more expensive compilations that had some of the newer Rick Rubin produced songs, but the price made me consider this album instead.  This is a great selection of Cash's work up to about the 1980's.  I am 60, and much of this is music that my Dad liked, and which I would never have listened to when it came out.  Yes, its not complete.  It does not have every single good song he performed.  But, you cannot get all the best songs on 2 Vinyl discs, so I think the selection here is great compromise.  I like the duets with June Carter Cash, and Bob Dylan, and there are some great standards like Folsom Prison Blues.  As I listen to the tracks over and over, I may decide to buy a few more of his records, but for now, this quenches my musical thirst for The Man in Black.  The recording quality is very good, but not spectacular.  Some of these songs were recorded in studio with a single mic, or maybe only a few mics.  Often they were mixed intended for mono playback, and then re-mixed for stereo, but the sound is very good for the age of the recordings.  It varies from song to song as I imagine the master tapes varied in quality.  As some reviewers here noted, the quality control of the vinyl could use improvement.  I returned the first set because they had warps and off-center holes which make the disc spin in a way that the cartridge moves left and right because of the disc, and not because of the grooves.  Amazon is great, replaced it in 2 days, and the new one was much better, but also as noted, the holes were not drilled/punched properly.  This is not the only new vinyl I have gotten with this problem, so I keep a drill bit handy that I use by hand to clean out the center hole.  Once that was done, the new discs played well.  Very happy with this purchase

I hardly even noticed when it went missing during one of my many apartment moves.  A bit further on up the road, however, and after getting into his The Smoker You Drink LP, I went out and repurchased Barnstorm and began to really appreciate its highpoints, of which there are many.  It just may be Joe Walsh's quietest work, but in many ways, it may also be one of his deepest.  Glad to finally have it on CD and back in my collection.

text.8583: La quinta sinfonía de Bruckner siempre ha sido una de esas composiciones que para mi concepto destacan la genialidad del austriaco en cuanto al contrapunto. Además, es una de esas piezas sinfónicas que, bajo la batuta de un director detallista logra momentos de gran belleza; principalmente, por su sonoridad algo oscura y su impresionismo en algunos pasajes, que recuerdan a la música de camara... en el caso de esta grabación, el maestro Sinopoli no solo lo ha logrado, sino que además, nos presenta una propuesta conceptual, en dónde la atmosferica musical adquiere tonalidades misteriosas y enigmáticas, dentro de la densa tesitura sinfónica. Creo que todos los movimientos se ejecutan a buen tempo, aunque reconozco que Sinopoli, al querer destacar cada timbre o solo instrumental, estos tempos tienden a ser algo más lentos y reflexivos... en fin, es una estupenda interpretación. Muy recomendable.

text.8673: I am a huge fan of this band, and I will say off the bat that this is not my favorite album of theirs, it's their debut album and the band had yet to come upon the signature "Jethro Tull sound". Not only does it include the entire first album (both a remixed version plus the original mix), it's also got all of the non-album singles and b-sides, plus a few outtakes, alternate versions, and previously unreleased recordings. It's also got a 96-page booklet detailing the early incarnations of the band, details on the recording of the album, interviews, lyrics, etc. So it's an extremely comprehensive set detailing the band's earliest years. text.8681: Heifetz is supposedly one of the greatest violin virtuosos of the twentieth century. It's a reputation that is mostly deserved. But these performances are a huge disappointment. The greatest piece on the recording is Mozart's sublime K. 364 Sinfonia Concertante. Heifetz rushes through it. There is no majesty, nothing touching or moving. The sound engineering is very poor. Also to be avoided in the K. 364 is the painfully slow and mannered performance of Vengerov/Power under Vengerov's direction; and the period-influenced rendering of Carmignola/Waskiewicz under Abaddo, which is a cursory run-though with no vibrato. Alternative suggestions for the K. 364: Oistrakh/Oistrakh (their 1972 version with the Berlin Phil.); Lin/Laredo; Fischer/Nikolic. Except for the rather underwhelming accompaniment of the Israel Phil., the '80s recording of Perlman/Zuckerman is also very fine.

Note: The playing gets = 4 Stars. The recording quality = 3 Stars

Admittedly, I jump into classical reviews only when I’m torn and confused about what I’m hearing (see my review of Scriabin’s complete piano works by Maria Lettberg for similar concerns). I picked up this box set because there are surprisingly not many complete renditions Brahms’s piano works (most pianists record opp. 116-119 and the occasional op. 76), as compared to, perhaps, Beethoven’s sonatas or Chopin’s sum total. I’d been listening to Katchen’s for ten years and all the opp. 116-119 that have come out in the 21st century. That satisfied me, but the Katchen sounds older and older every year next to the great advances in recording quality beginning in the mid 2000s. With modern recordings of the total Brahms, you can choose the Chandos champ, Barry Douglas or this lively outlier, La Dolce Volta’s Couteau. Douglas’s recordings are the complete opposite of Couteau’s—large and booming (as are all Chandos piano recordings, including the most introspective Debussy tapped out by Bavouzet). Douglas is solid while not distorting a unique sensitivity, at least not usually. If Douglas sounds bigger than life (and personifies this on his album covers), he’s only partially responsible—as noted, the recording sound is Olympian without respite.

Couteau comes from a very different place. His label La Dolce Volta is coming into its own in France and only French magazines have touched this album. Not that all reviews matter, but his reviews on the company webpage (all in French—sorry), are quite vague (including the one on this Amazon page). They are full of metaphors, like Couteau is the captain of our ship, taking us (the passengers) through the life of Brahms. They all praise the act of making this album. Out of the dozen reviews (again, only existing in France), however, there is almost no word on the quality of the playing and certainly none on the sound. The closest is a review saying they listened to the discs straight through and then put them on again— sanguine, to be sure.

To my ears? The playing seems entirely sensitive to this music. It seems so natural, even right at disc one with the andante of the second sonata. It’s a softer touch, again, somewhat the opposite of Barry—but Brahms can succeed soft or loud. The composer’s output seems to celebrate full-chested behaviors as well as quiet moments within one’s own skull.

My concern is absolutely the recording quality, which is why I think reviewers are struggling to nod at this one. It’s like a tragic botch. At the end of the day, the recording is extremely “tight,”— no air between the sound and microphone whatsoever. The result is extremely mechanical, as if you’ve programmed a Yamaha synthesizer to play Brahms very well, and plugged the output cord directly into the recording device. Indeed, it almost sounds recorded in mono, again on an electronic keyboard. This really saddened me, and left me confused. This box should be momentous and a celebration of lesser known Brahms finally being recorded for the “now”—and Couteau is the pianist to do this. But the soul of these works was removed in the studio, so all of Couteau’s hard work is being played down a well, and we’ll never know what it was supposed actually be like.

You can hear a bit of what it could be like, as Couteau is making recordings of Brahms’s chamber pieces as we speak (first 2 discs already avail). But, even then the first disc of chamber works has a recording from this piano box set on it, and you can compare right there---the pleasant air of the chamber works and the glove box sound of the solo piano piece. I’m going to continue listening to Couteau. He knows his Brahms. It’s just uncomfortable at times to know that this could have been among the greatest sets in a long while.

Fabulous 80s album with just a bit of cheese. Rio is a standard bearer for the pop synth decade, and it still holds up quite well, way better than most of Duran Duran. You have a lot of hits, you've got sophisticated melody and choruses to die for, and you have a finally decent mastering with good EQ.

That in itself might be the push to get the more expensive version, but it also comes in a nice digipack foldout with book and great extras. The auxiliary features include US Remixes, demos, alternate versions, and plenty of good material to sift through. It's the perfect way for the album to be capsuled for future audio enthusiasts. Dynamic range is good, and the overall EQ is quite a bit better than the older release. Highly recommended.

There is NO percussion, piano, guitar or early sampling instrumentation to date the music!
Just one man a few keyboards in what I imagine was some sort of lucid connection to the cosmos improvising a beautitude of deep contemplative music that really hold no specific nation, culture or religion at the focal point of its origins.
This is quiet instrumental music at a penultimate level, not really wallpaper but not too distracting either. Iasos layers his tonal alchemy intelligently and his elixir of compositions will leave you refreshed, reflective and your ears and mind properly nourished!

I've been a huge fan of The Ocean for about 6 years. Easily on my top 3 favorite bands of all time (right next to Between the Buried and Me and Eluveitie). Based on those bands, you can see I really like melodic style metal, combining clean and harsh vocals, melodic and heavy music, and lots of good atmospheric sound intertwined with aggressive metal. Anthropocentric has been my favorite album of The Ocean since I discovered them. Pelagial gave that album a run for it's money, but although an outstanding effort, it was just not quite the perfection that Anthropocentric was. Then along comes this album and although I can't name it my outright favorite, it's a contact back and forth between the two. This album is an absolute masterpiece and easily takes album of the year for 2018. It's dark, moody, aggressive, powerful...everything these guys are able to deliver. Loïc Rossetti's vocals are some of the best in metal and he really knows how to pour his passion into every word. The production of guitars and drums are perfect on this album. Notes are clear, drums pack a huge punch without being jumbled together.
If you are a fan, I guarantee you'll love this album, if you've never hear of The Ocean I can't recommend this album enough, you won't regret checking them out!

This was quite a revelation to me. First of all, I never knew that Meat Loaf didn't actually write the songs on this amazing album. They were, in fact, written by his very talented musical partner. For decades, I had always assumed that Meat Loaf had done most (or all!) of the writing.
For some reason, I had also always assumed that Meat Loaf had a string of successful albums; this was NOT the case. "Bat Out Of Hell" was indeed a smash success. But there was a kind of void after that. In fact, his next album, in 1981, did very poorly. This led to Meat Loaf filing for bankruptcy, which I also didn't know! In fact, he was somewhat in financial limbo until the release of "Bat Out Of Hell 2", several decades later.
He is most definitely a fascinating guy, and clearly very talented. His on-stage performances are simply spectacular. He obviously put his heart and soul into every song, and every musical gesture. It must have been stunning to see him perform live, at his highest peak, in the late 1970s. That would have been mind blowing.
All in all, if you don't already know a lot about Meat Loaf's life, aspirations, artistic expressions, career, and personal highs and lows, this is a must-see video. You will also learn a good deal of vital information about his talented partner(s), and about producer Todd Rundgren, who is a brilliant talent on his own. This was all quite an eye-opener for me. This is definitely recommended viewing.

text.9153:
Rock critic and author of the "Rock and Roll Book of Lists" and the "Part 2" edition Dave Marsh, in the first volume of a really great pair of books, listed the greatest and worst live albums in his opinion, and I have always remembered how he described "Get Yer Ya-Ya's Out". I'll try to do the quote accurately but just in case I miss a word or two, we can call this paraphrasing when he listed the album very high on the best live list and described it as "being recorded on a night when The Rolling Stones may very well have been the greatest rock and roll band in the world".
He was right. Actually the album is over a two night triumphant gig at Madison Square Garden in November of 1969, and what a fantastic album!
Fans of the Stones often cite the years with lead guitarist Mick Taylor as their best, the exciting and extremely bluesy and talented Taylor lifting the band to heights of power they would probably never equal, although they certainly have turned out plenty of fine music after Taylor left. There can be no doubt they were never any tougher, tighter and powerful, especially on this superb set.
"Jumping Jack Flash", one of my favorite Stones tunes, is a great opening track, and as "Carol" takes off, they remind us while doing a fine cover of the Chuck Berry classic that they were steeped deeply in blues every bit as much as the Yardbirds or Eric Clapton and also remind us that the beat and propulsive energy is as integral to the feel of the best blues if not more so than virtuoso soloing run amuck.
To that end, Taylor is the epitome of playing the right notes exactly at the right time, allowing some room to strut his stuff but never getting carried away and always knowing critically when it's time to get back to the groove. "Love In Vain" is the slow blues number from Robert Johnson and features Taylor at his best, and possibly the most soulful British blues player of the whole late '60's rock scene. Not until Robin Trower (yes, Robin Trower) emerged a few years later would the emotional impact of the soloing match that of Taylor's, Hendrix', and Jeff Beck.
"Midnight Rambler" is a delight and a showcase for rock and roll's tightest rhythm section in Bill Wyman and Charlie Watts. Wyman was the quiet one of the band, but he let his bass tone and incredibly reliable steady grooves do the talking. And the sound - very deep, very robust, is a bass tone I personally slobber over. Add Watts, as close as a human can get to perfect timekeeping, and the Rolling Stones had a foundation that could withstand any earthquake.
Side Two continues the great show, finally culminating with "Street Fighting Man", and leaving the audience screaming for more rock and roll, as the Stones probably delivered live at that time probably better than anybody.

text.9285: Danny Kaye was one of kind, and this collection does offer a good cross section of career.  But, as another reviewer noted, the sound quality is inconsistent and at times flat out bad.  At least one track ("No Two People") was mastered from an electronically rechanneled stereo release, which plops Mr. Kaye smack in the middle of an exaggerated echo chamber, and a few other tracks appear to suffer from excessive noise reduction EQ.  A competing compilation by Jasmine was similarly mastered from CDs and vinyl, but the sound quality is more consistent.  Unfortunately, it's likely that the original masters for ALL of Kaye's recordings for Decca were lost In the 2008 fire at Universal, your best bet is to seek out pre-2009 releases from MCA/Universal, mint condition vinyl or the Jasmine collection.  In the meantime, this one will make do...if you're desperate.

text.9357: It is a tragedy the world will not get to hear and see JTE sing anymore. To me no other artist in my lifetime(almost 50 now) can bring honest vulnerability with such painful heart on the sleeve words and sincerity. Every word he sings takes you into a real story about someone feeling such real emotions In such a troubled confusing unkind world. You almost feel as if you are there going through what each of these characters are. Sometimes we can easily relate with what these characters are going through because we too have gone through it. Others times we are made to feel compassion with every listen. To me Midnight at the Movies was JTE’s ultimate masterpiece start to finish. “Mama’s Eyes” is the best song he’s ever written that discusses his complicated family dynamic and his own guilty conscience about his part in it. “Someday I’ll Be Forgiven For This” he also deals with this guilty conscience by rationalizing that both people in the situation will inevitably do the same thing to each other when they step out of their relationship. It is a very self reflecting song about how and why relationships end and the feeling involved and how they transpire from one person to the other and they end up being the same. Hard to find blame with both are the same in the end. “Can’t Hardly Wait” is an amazing cover and feels like JTE wrote it himself. He gives the original replacements great justice. There are so many old time music sounds throughout this album that really showcase just how much of a genius and historian of traditional music JTE was. I love all of his albums and listen to them weekly. I was lucky enough to meet him a month before the pandemic hit at a show. I will cherish that always. These songs and these words are second to none. Truly one of the greatest ever who will forever be missed

Recently I've gotten into vinyl in a big way. The Stones are one of the all-time great bands in that 70% of their albums are hits and even the fillers are listenable/good.

Normally, I am not a huge fan of Best Of albums because as a vinyl enthusiast, I thi k respect of the original listeming experience is part of the retro charm of listening to vinyl. I've come to enjoy Doors songs I've never enjoyed before because when you spin a record, you have no choice but to get through the hits and the fillers together.

The Stones are such a prodigious band with so many hits that sometimes you just want to hear the best of hits and it would take hours of listening to go through that many albums. There are three bands whom I have a best of album ... The Stones, Motorhead and Nirvana. This doesnt count live albums like Doors Live at the Hollywood Bowl, White Stripes Live or Nirvana Unplugged which are great albums to own live. You may be able to make the case for a Hendrix or Janis Joplin compliation as well.

I was a bit bummed that this was issued on clear vinyl as black vinyl is reportedly the most sturdy and will hold up best. But, sometimes The Stones sound great with clicks and pops so I'll go with it.

The mix is good here ... the bass will be a bit lacking but in the 60s and 70s most were listening to vinyl on small portible record players as the high fi experience didnt occur until the mid to late 70s, so this treble happy music is how most heard the stones on vinyl. The bass was pumped up in live shows and in hifi systems. Most music today is remastered to thump a lot more as that is just expected from post-rap era of the 80s, 90s and 00's where people wanted to feel the music through primal bass beat.

You cant argue with the selections here which contain the best of The Stones' early hits. A lot of songs like Ruby Tuesday and the like have been lost on newer Stones fans. Brian Johnson's influence can be fely on this album. The only inclusion I miss is 'She's a Rainbow' which is one of the most underrated of The Stones' early hits ... a song that will stick in your head for days.

This is a nicely produced album which any vinyl collection will benefit from. There may be better Stones complilations on CD but for vinyl ... this one works great. Happy to have it in my collection.

text.9541: Nice 3 disc offering. Highly recommended and well worth the purchase price. Being familiar only with TM's later work I was floored after hearing disc 1 (Taj Mahal) and 2 (Natch'l Blues). They are the natural progression of the 50's and early 60's blues of Muddy, Wolf, Sonny Boy II and the like. They are not Blues Rock albums. Though they contain a slight rock sensibility, the traditional blues sound of the afore mentioned performers remains well intact. His vocals fit the music perfectly and the songs feel loose and roll right along providing a great listen. Bonus points given because the personnel include guitar guru Ry Cooder and studio legend Jesse Ed Davis. Interesting fact- per Gregg Allman, while his brother Duane was convalescing due to having a broken arm and severe cold Gregg had left a gift of the Taj Mahal album and a bottle of cold medicine Coricidin at his door and left. Six weeks later the cast was off Duane's arm, and he was playing Jesse Ed Davis's slide guitar parts with the album playing. He used the Coricidin bottle as his slide. If it was good enough to motivate Duane to pick up slide guitar (and later establish himself as the first Bonafide slide guitar giant in classic rock), then it's good enough to be in any collection. IMO disc 3 Mo' Roots misses the mark. It is more of a world music, easy listening album. That is not the complaint, I listen to all types of music. Though the sound production and musicianship are good, the songs are missing something and fall flat. But don't let that stop you, music is subjective so listen for yourself and make up your own mind. Besides, the other 2 albums are stellar essential blues. Buy it.

text.9562: Steelheart was a mid 80's to early 90's Power/Hair rock band. Their strengths were a lead singer that could knock out their lyrics and a drummer that provided the pulse or back-beat of their music. While the lead guitar produced the higher guitar riffs the rhythm guitar gave us a rhythmic pulse that backed up the drummer. From what I remember, the goal of these types of bands was to be load in music, loud in voice, and provide the music that made you want to get up and air-guitar and air-drum. Some of their songs are in the form of a rock ballad that may have been soft in story but hard in music and back-beat. I don't remember any of the songs on this album being on the Rock or Top-40s charts but they were not one hit wonders with the quality and variety of their music. During the mid 80's into the early 90's there were many good hard rock bands, hair bands, and power-rock bands to choose from so their music may have been over looked by the music world.

Prospective buyers of 'Turas 1980' would be interested to know that the release of this album is endorsed by the band members. It's an official release. According to the liner notes, Moya's husband, Tim Jarvis, co-ordinated the album and her daughter, Aisling, edited the original recording. Each surviving band member has written a short response to the album in the booklet.

This concert was recorded at Bremen University, Germany, by Radio Bremen in January, 1980, not too long before the band broke world-wide.

The sound quality is very good. You can tell it's been recorded professionally. The sound is probably as good as on any other mobile recording from that period. It is also at least as good as the sound on Clannad's earlier albums on the Gael-Linn and Tara labels.

If you look over the track listing, you would notice that the concert is fully comprised of the amazingly atmospheric and awe-inspiring traditional songs for which Clannad is well known, some sung in Irish Gaelic and some in English, and others, a mix of both languages. A main feature of these songs is the power of story-telling. You become fully absorbed in the tales being told through the lyrics, if you aren't already hypnotised by the vocals or the instruments. Personally, as well as being fascinated by the stories sung in English, I love the sound and rhythm of the Irish Gaelic words, although I don't understand them. Making the experience even more fascinating are the spoken introductions for most of the songs, explaining the content, especially before the Gaelic songs. These are probably mainly spoken by Ciaran or Pol, maybe sometimes spoken by one of the twins, and the guys' wonderful dry humour is most entertaining.

People who know a little of the history of Clannad would know that they travelled Ireland in their early days, collecting traditional songs from the elderly people of the day, before the old people and the songs died out. Therefore, we get a real variety of songs here - some jaunty and uplifting, hinting at mischief and love of life, some sombre and melancholy. I have all the Clannad and Moya Brennan albums, from 1973's 'Clannad' and 1974's 'Clannad 2' up to the most recent, and I can confirm that there are some songs on this concert recording that don't appear on any of those LPs.

The final things to comment on are the main features of the recordings. The instrumentation is great. The family plays all their respective instruments with vigour and character. The group is is also in fine voice.

Most importantly, the crown of any Clannad recording, the beautiful voice of Moya Brennan, shines and captivates. Moya sounds as magnificent as always. Obviously, the sound is just a bit thinner, because the studio enhancements of the later famous studio albums haven't been employed here. However, her voice is as pure and musical as ever it was. She doesn't miss a note. That heavenly, light vibrato is in full flutter and she sounds just fantastic.

I would fully recommend this album to anyone who is enamoured with Clannad's traditional Irish music, with traditional Irish music in general or with the Irish Gaelic language.

By the way, I gather that 'Turas' means to tour or go on an expedition or odyssey - hinting at the odyssey of Clannad - from their beginnings to the far reaches of their career and full circle back to their beginnings, here on this recording - although I hope there's much more to come.

text.9705:
With so many recordings available of Carl Orff’s cheeky Carmina Burana, how do you choose? For me I prefer 1. A strong, symphonic-sized chorus that throw themselves willingly at the music and aren’t too flung back in the sound, 2. Either vocally beautiful soloists that can handle Orff’s extreme ranges with ease or soloists that are characterful, despite the ranges, 3. A closely captured orchestra that affords inner detail and doesn’t skimp on a forward percussion section, and 4. A leader that strongly characterizes Orff’s earthy music rather than luxuriates or smooths the edges.

Eugen Jochum’s famed 1968 stereo recording, here on its latest DG Originals release, previously found [[ASIN:B00000E414 on DG Galleria]], is the grandaddy of Carmina Burana performances, despite many recordings existing before this one, including a 50’s mono already set down by Jochum, also [[ASIN:B002K4WQWE on DG]]. Some of the hoopla is Orff’s personal rubber stamp on this particular recording, making it a prime choice, although Orff approved other recordings as well, such as the mono Sawallisch [[ASIN:B000002S39 on EMI]].

The positives of these performances far outweigh my nitpicks: the chorus is full-bodied with only occasionally wobbly singing from the sopranos, but giving an all-in performance. The famous O Fortuna is effectively sung, particularly the whispered quiet section that is still full-bodied, and the ‘puellula’ male semi-chorus, which often sinks recordings, is strongly sung. The German opera chorus tends to staccato their accents, but a small nitpick against characterful singing.

The soloists are also excellent: Fischer-Dieskau is beautifully lyrical here, mixing his high range effectively for some suave singing with no hint of his notorious bark; Gundula Janowitz soprano is also gorgeous, well-controlled vocally with only the top note of Dulcissime not working, and Gerhard Stolze, a tenor whose sound I have never relished, liberally pours on quirky character in his one solo. Excellent all around, and the studio location gives effective use of their qualities.

Eugen Jochum leads this music efficiently; he rarely dwells, but instead pushes ahead rather consistently. Jochum might miss some moments of repose, but the Berlin German Opera Orchestra sounds great, and all of the percussive effect are clear to the fore. DG’s sound is excellent across the board with a strong bass line, the chorus are perfectly understandable, the soloists are in front of the orchestra, and the instrumental voices speak pretty clearly with no fear of mushy, hissy, or boxy sound.

I think this recording is an easy first choice among a host of other fine performances. Personally, I also like Leonard Slatkin [[ASIN:B000003FH3 on RCA]] for his fine soloists, Michael Tilson-Thomas [[ASIN:B07ZQGYMZL on Dutton]] or [[ASIN:B00000253D on Sony]] for his sharp-edged modern outlook, Riccardo Muti [[ASIN:B00001ZSXC on EMI]] for his joyous surface excitement, yet there are so many others with varying qualities.

This recording, though, is an excellent introduction to Carmina Burana that can trace its source directly to Carl Orff, but it is also an excellent performance on its own. It doesn’t hurt that it still comes in great sound some 50 years later. Highly Recommended!

One of the things that's really admirable about Leopold Stokowski is the way he championed the cause of "new music" as a conductor. He was the conductor who gave the American premiere of Mahler's Eighth Symphony ("The Symphony of a Thousand"), as well as the premieres of music by several other 20th Century composers -- music which was new and unfamiliar to American audiences.
In this CD, he tackles music which, although familiar to him at this point, was still unfamiliar to American audiences at the time, including Respighi's "Pines of Rome" and Shostakovich's First Symphony, which the composer wrote at the age of 19. "Pines of Rome," as played here, is so good you almost don't want to listen to the rest of the CD. The Symphony of the Air is, essentially, the NBC Symphony Orchestra after Toscanini retired -- an orchestra noted for its precision and clarity -- and Stokowski eschews his usual romantic approach to bring out that orchestra's strengths. The mutual respect between conductor and orchestra is one of the great joys of listening to this CD.

text.9875: I purchased this recording for two reasons:  Ildebrando D'Arcangelo and Elina Garanca.  Not familiar with the opera, but knowing, and liking these two singers' voices, and the fact that Vivaldi is usually good music,  I thought there would be enough to surmount my dislike for the counter tenor voice, which unfortunately occupies the vast majority of the opera.  There was NOT!  Not to say that either was not in their usual great voice, there just was not enough of them in the score.  There is something about the counter tenor voice which for me is unnerving.  Trouser roles by mezzos are much easier to handle.  While I have seen David Daniels live in Los Angeles, I cannot honestly find fault in his vocal talent.  I guess, as in mezzo trouser roles, if you are going to sound, dress, and sing a male role perhaps countertenors should dress like women since they sound like them?  Might be easier to deal with.

text.9905: When I was in my teens, I attended a series of opera movies, one a week over the course of a summer. Prior to that, I was only familiar with the big three middle Verdi operas and Aida. Seeing.....and hearing those movies was a revelation. One of them was an old (even at that time) black and white performance of La Forza Del Destino. I haven't a clue whose voices I heard in that movie. No matter! It was love at first sight...and hearing, and it has remained one of my favorite Verdi operas...no small feat considering that Verdi is my operatic God of my idolatry. Some years after that movie, this recording was issued...on LP of course. By then, Leontyne Price had become on of my favorite sopranos, along with Sutherland and Moffo. I quickly bought a copy, and it took pride of place in my collection. I repurchased it a couple of years ago, now on CD. Price was in her absolute prime, and this was one of her signature roles. For me, she is (or was) Leonora. As for the others, Tucker had a beautiful voice, but did have his mannerisms as others have noted. His voice sometimes had a metallic edge as well, hence my slight caveat. I always loved Merrill. Others find him uninvolved in this recording. I don't. And Shirley Verrett is wonderful. Again, others have quibbles about Schippers. I certainly prefer him to Muti, whose opera recordings I avoid. As for the recorded sound, I find it holds up reasonably well for its age. Perhaps not perfect, but far more than adequate. In any event, having the young Leontyne is a PRICE beyond pearls! (Sorry 'bout that!) I have three recordings of Forza...and this is by far my favorite, slight flaws and all, so pay the PRICE and she will repay you in kind.

text.9966:
Being born in the "wrong" generation does have its upside(s), not the least of which is the ability to objectively react to the music for MUSIC's sake; I wasn't with Lep from the very beginning (on account of not existing), I wasn't with them in their more "metal-ish" High N Dry days (barely born), I wasn't into them during the Pyromania era (still barely born), and I was tragically too young to enjoy Hysteria in all its real-time glory. Nor did I confuse musical value with imagery (mostly due to being a straight male...). Sadly hailing from the "grunge" generation, I was only getting serious about music once it had already become the painful ordeal to publicly admit one's self a Def Leppard fan in the 90's. But for getting serious about music, I do have Def Leppard - and more specifically, this album, to thank. People writing them off for aspects such as at-times trite lyricisms aren't truly listening.

Some of the first songs for which I ever hunted down piano sheet music were "Let's Get Rocked" (permanently in love with all those sixteenth "Bach Tchaikovsky Violins!!" triplets & the dizzying heights all the key changes take the song to in the end), "Stand Up Kick Love Into Motion" (in my opinion the BEST version of the E Major affair they'd tried [and admittedly succeeded with bigger hits, please kindly continue down the hall for reviews more popularity contest-influenced...] twice before with "Photograph" & "Armageddon It" and once later with the still-solid "Promises"), and my all time favorite Def Leppard ballad - the song I feel just tugs at the heartstrings more than any other - "Have You Ever Needed Someone So Bad." One of the most frustrating experiences as a teenager (and let's just say there was ample competition in that department...) was running around to all the music stores with my grandmother every week after "Tonight" was finally released as a single, NEVER finding it released for piano. I'm not kidding when I say that devastated me. So in order to learn the song, I bought the guitar tab and learned guitar too.

BUT. My supporting evidence for favorite Def Leppard album - and, more controversially to be sure, the daring word of "BEST" - resides in one 7 minute epic known as "White Lightning." This is the inner sanctum of being a Def Leppard fan for the MUSIC: Key changes abound; adventurous twists and turns; stellar soloing; all signature vocal harmonies & top-of-the-line production values in check; and dark haunting lyrics in honor of fallen comrade Steve Clark. It's all out the window, of course, if the cumulative summation of the parts doesn't yield a gut-wrenching emotional catharsis, but I didn't write all this to say it doesn't. All the elements of this masterpiece (a term I try not to abuse) contribute to one hell of a musical experience - the same way the 10 tracks of ADRENALIZE work together to create a fluid & satisfying rock album top-to-bottom.

I have respect for each and every Def Leppard album (although if brutally honest, I do struggle with "X"). I'm well aware of what "Pyromania" is, what "Hysteria" is, all the groundbreaking history those albums are so deservedly in the books for, and I understand what I do to risk putting "Adrenalize" - the "runt in the trilogy," according to Rolling Stone's David Fricke - up so high, but this album speaks to me musically more than any other, and it's something I must stand by. SOLID album with the distinction of continuing to offer something new with every listen - even almost 30 years (!) later.
